The Tickwatch E is my first foray into the world of WearOS and on the whole I've been very happy with it. I picked this up during the Prime Day special and took my first test drive with the watch at San Diego comic con. I had some initial reservations due to some of the other reviews, especially the ones noting poor battery life... my previous watch was a Fitbit blaze with a typical battery life measured in days and a lot of the reviews for this watch pointed more towards hours. Fortunately with my normal usage (media control, notifications, texting a few times a day) it seems like there is plenty of battery life at hand. That said, when you start to tax it more (things like: navigation, google fit workout mode w/heart rate, phone calls from watch,), it can start to suck down battery a lot quicker, but never enough that it hasn't gone through a whole day with battery life to spare.

Good:
- Fantastic entry level watch with great pricing.
- Battery life is good
- Extremely feature rich at this price point
- Does not have tons of pre-loaded apps I'll never use

Not so good:
- Watch band fit, but just barely (6'3" with a large frame)
- WearOS can be a bit quirky... I really don't need single gesture watch face switching
- Incoming calls don't always buzz the watch before the call has been missed (this might be a phone issue)
- Dismissing notifications by swiping to the side can be more miss than hit, it often thinks I'm pulling up or down slightly rather than straight across.
- Not waterproof, holds up fine to splashes though.

Other thoughts:
- Even if the band fits you just fine, you may want to spend a couple extra dollars to get a new one. I didn't find the included one to be terribly comfortable. (shop for 20mm bands)
- It's not the most stylish design and it's plastic... you wont want to pair this with a suit, but for a function forward casual every day watch, it's perfect.

Review:
First off, yes it has 4GB storage but 60% of that is taken up with the pre-installed apps, many of which cannot be uninstalled! Just wanted to make that clear off the bat since all the reviews trump the 4GB storage and make no mention that in reality, you’re left with much less free space than that!
Despite this, my impressions of the Gear Sport after 5 days are extremely positive. I should say that this is my first smartwatch / fitness tracker but I did my research, compared with it’s main competitors and knew what I wanted. I chose this over the Fitbit Ionic and the Garmin Vivosport as I am always impressed by Samsung products and it was closest to ticking all my boxes. It’s not perfect but overall it’s everything I could’ve wanted. In short, it’s comfortable and has hit a sweet spot in terms of size. I personally find it a very attractive design that should appeal to both sexes. I am very impressed with the battery life, smartwatch functions and most importantly, the accuracy of it’s fitness and sleep tracking (having prepared myself for it not being very accurate). More details below.

OS:
So it uses Tizen OS and I have to say it is very fluid and responsive and very user friendly. Yes there are options galore and menus within menus but once you know you’re way around and set up your favourite widgets etc.. it’s a zip to use. And the rotating bezel works brilliantly in this regard. Well done Samsung for making it a very pleasant user experience! The apps ecosystem is not that great unfortunately and I guess that’s because Tizen isn’t currently as popular as Android or IOS. However, I anticipate this will improve but for now I couldn’t really find anything very useful apart from maybe a calculator and stopwatch. The good news is that the Gear Sport already comes pre-installed with all the most useful immediate apps.

Battery:
In short excellent. I can easily get 3.5 - 4 days usage out of a full charge which is more than the stated 2-3 days in the online reviews. Now I should say that by default I have Bluetooth and wi-fi turned off; heart monitor off; light sensor (for automatic dimming) off, wake up gestures off and screen timeout set to 15 seconds. I only use GPS, during workouts which obviously also kicks in the heart rate sensor, and I only use Bluetooth when I need to pair with my smartphone. In one 36 hour period, with the above settings but having it track my sleep, 30 lengths swimming, 2 lots of 45 minute walking workouts with GPS, and a 45 minutes gym session with treadmill and rowing machine tracking, the battery went from 100% to 68%. I think that is excellent.

Sleep tracking:
Very pleasantly surprised with the accuracy here. I nearly went with the Fitbit Ionic as I wanted good tracking here and read they were the leaders in this regard but the Gear Sport impresses me with it’s results. It doesn’t let you know what sleep stage (e.g. REM) you were in at what time which is a shame, rather it breaks your sleep into three different stages which it terms restless, light and motionless. It has accurately recorded jaunts to the bathroom in the early hours of the morning and nights when I know for a fact that my sleep has been quite restless, it’s shown this in the graph the following day. It also appears to accurately record my falling asleep and waking up times. So altogether impressed though I hope more research goes into this area and they can soon record your actual sleep stages like the Fitbits can apparently do.

Fitness tracking:
Again, very impressed with the accuracy though there are some anomalies. I compared the heart rate monitor with the treadmill at the gym, which has the metal handles, which tend to be more accurate than wrist based trackers. Each time I compared the two, the Gear Sport was only 1 or 2 bpm out, usually behind. Impressive! However there was quite a discrepancy between the machine and the Gear Sport when it came to calories burned (both had accurate weight inputted). When the treadmill said I had burned off 60 calories, the Gear Sport only read 43 calories and the Gear Sport was consistently behind in this regard over the course of the session. The treadmill was on a 15% incline so I don’t know whether the Gear Sport was able to discern this? I am unsure which tracker gives off the correct reading…
Walking workouts recorded GPS accurately and provides a useful map of your route and range of useful data such as heart beat, average speed, calories burned etc.. It would automatically detect pauses and resuming such as when stopping at lights.
Swimming tracking works well, you input the length of the pool beforehand and then go. I did sometimes seem to be a length behind but then it would recalculate on the next length and fix itself! Anyhow, it records lengths accurately and again provides useful data at the end of the session such as calories burned, a breakdown for each length and even recognises what stroke you did!

Screen:
I am slightly disappointed with the screen to be honest. Yes it is OLED, vibrant, responsive, bright and blacks are inky black but at around ~310 ppi, the resolution is not nearly as high as the latest smartphones and so when up close you will definitely see pixels. And this means that many of the more complex watch faces available are not as clear as they could be, lines and small rounded text can be difficult to discern. I believe that this is something all current smart watches suffer from, I have read this is one of the better screens so I guess we will have to wait for the next generation watches before we get a significant bump in resolution.

So to wrap up, I think overall this is an excellent fitness tracker smart watch for the casual user. I am impressed with the accuracy of it’s sleep and fitness tracking, the usability of the OS and the look and comfort of the watch. It’s chock full of latest tech although it lacks in some key areas such as LTE and doesn’t have a speaker so you can’t have phone conversations with it, though you can of course send SMS messages once paired to a phone. The improvements Samsung need to make for the next iteration would be far more storage (really 4GB these days is measly), a higher resolution screen, more in depth sleep tracking information and a better app market.

Review:
I've been regularly using the watch for 2.5 months and generally I'm very happy with it. I had previously used the widely-panned Garmin 410 and I can very strongly say this watch is a tremendous improvement (the "touch" feature of the 410 was completely frustrating). Nice solid mechanical buttons are the way to go. I use the watch with a Garmin footpod to capture my running cadence, the bike sensor, and of course the HR monitor. All paired easily and work just great. Switching sports is very easy and the time-to-GPS lock is quite rapid. I enjoy uploading my data to the Garmin website to look over what I've done and compare performance over time. The upload process is very easy to do.

The only aspect of the watch that holds me back from the fifth star is swimming. In a pool it simply doesn't accurately record my laps. This complaint has been documented frequently online and Garmin's apparent response is that people should learn to swim better. No matter what I seem to do, it nearly doubles my swim distance. This of course renders all the data captured completely useless. I am admittedly a poor swimmer, but I would have hoped for more from a $400, top of the line watch.

UPDATE: After 7 more months of use - and a lot more swim training - I believe the 910XT has earned a 5th star. I'm a passable swimmer now and the watch virtually never misses a lap. There's the occasional lap added, but that's usually a tip-off that my form is slipping and I'm getting tired. If you're a half-decent swimmer (something I'm still striving for) you won't have a problem with the swim aspect of this watch. It continues to perform extremely well for running & on the bike. I continue to love the watch - my electronic training partner.

Review:
Looking for Christmas gift for my wife, I ended up researching smart watches and trying to figure out what could be the best bang for the buck.
I first found out about the brand through a YouTube tech reviewer and liked what they had to say about this particular product. Some more reading, and the fact that Mobvoi was running a special finally led me to take the plunge and get the Tickwatch E for her.

The Tickwatch E Shadow is a very nice device. The black shell is not polished, it has a soft and slight textured look and feel to it and she loves the fact that you can change the wrist bands to make it look a bit more upscale than just a sports looking watch. Unlike other devices I looked at while doing research, this watch is an Android Wear device which means full integration with our Android ecosystem. The device has one physical button on the left which is used to power on the watch, return to home/watch face screen, access the system menu and activate Google assistant.

The overall experience my wife has had with this watch has been fantastic, she loves the responsiveness of the watch which translates to her being able to respond to notifications with ease, the chat apps we use work as they should, the fitness tracking is excellent overall although the heart rate monitor is a bit slow sometimes and the IP67 rating gives her peace of mind that she can work out in almost any condition without worrying about getting the device messed up. Battery life is also excellent, she turned off the gestures so that the watch doesn’t activate by accident and has managed to get a consistent 1.5 days of use out of a full charge.

Not all has been sparkles and happiness though. As with any new product and a small company that releases said product, there are bound to be issues from time to time. As it was in our case.

Our original device did run into a problem when charging one night, the watch rebooted a couple of times and turned off. The following morning the watch was a tad warm which was odd since it’s normally cold after it’s done charging, and when trying to power it on the display colors were off and there was a graphical artifact in the middle of the screen. I did some searching online and found another user that had the same issue, but the forum post at that time had no answers or directions on how to proceed. After attempting to troubleshoot the device and factory resetting it a few times with no avail I promptly started an RMA process with Mobvoi to get the watch replaced, this is where the sparkles dimmed and the happiness turned into some confusion.

This is the part where I think Mobvoi needs to mature a bit more, though they did a great job in returning emails and finally getting the watch replaced, the actual RMA process through their site is very problematic and not very intuitive. I actually ended up emailing support first prior to submitting my case through the site because their site was not working with all the browsers I had tried (Chrome, FF, Edge, IE, Opera), it was malforming the page to the point where I could not continue to submit the problem. After finally guessing and submitting the form most of the communication ended up via email anyway because their ticket status page never updated again. This turned what should have been a quick RMA process into waiting almost an entire month for a replacement watch.

Again, many thanks to their support team for taking care of our issue.

For anyone looking for a smartwatch packed with features, great battery life, a good price and backed by a great customer service department, the Ticwatch E will not disappoint.

I have a Ticwatch Pro that I purchased in 2020 that I have loved because of the dual screen feature. I still use it today even though I have newer Garmin and Samsung watches. This Ticwatch doesn't have the dual screen feature or any outstanding smart watch feature, but is a solid watch that is responsive, good-looking and very light and comfortable to wear.

I've been using this watch for about 5 weeks now and it's been a great experience. This watch uses the Wear OS platform and works well with it. It also works with the Mobvoi app to provide additional versatility with the health and fitness features of the watch. It has a 1.3" bright LCD, sharp resolution and glass screen. The watch body is polycarbonate and comes with a silicone strap. It worked fine during my daily wear in a mostly indoor construction management environment. It's IP68 certified and I used it several times in my hot tub or in the shower without a hitch. The watch lasted me 2 full days wearing it continuously even during sleep and with normal use. An extra day would have been appreciated, but that's about the norm, even though my Garmin Venu watch lasts me 5 days+ with normal use.

Review:
I had a love hate relationship with this fitness tracker smartwatch. I loved that this unit tracked your steps and gave you notifications once you've reached your goal. It integrated great with the S health app that comes on the Galaxy S4 and above phones. You could also download the Gear Fit manager and install third party apps to help give the gear fit more functionality. For instance I found an app that would allow you to dial your contacts from the gear fit and then all you would have to do is pick up your phone. Another thing I liked was the sleep tracker. If you wore the watch to bed it would track your movement at night and give you a percentage of how much you were motionless through the night. I found if I was around 92% or above I got a pretty good nights sleep. Below 92% I could tell the next day! Finally this watch was the best alarm clock I've ever had! If you set an alarm on your phone and changed it to vibrate only, the alarm would vibrate on the watch! This was amazing because I could set the alarm and it would only wake up me and not my wife when it went off. I could dismiss the alarm or snooze it right from the watch. By far my most favorite feature!

There were several things that I did not love about the Gear Fit. For one, notifications were awkward to read. While you could change the orientation to be vertical or horizontal it seemed strange either way you looked at it. In vertical mode the big words would be hyphenated over several rows which made it even harder to read at times. The heart rate monitor wasn't very accurate at all. If I did three readings in a row the results would be random from 60-90 BPM on average. The Gear fit is a little bulky when it comes to thickness or height but the thing I hated the most and what ultimately made me decide to send it back was the watch band itself. The clasp just snaps into a hole on the band I kept finding that sometimes the band would get caught on something and come right off! It was enough to make me worry about losing it. I looked for alternative bands that would lock on but there were none to be found. Aside from that, wearing this band caused my skin to breakout and itch. I don't know if it was from moisture and rubbing or if it was from the plastic/rubber compound itself. I could wear the Gear Fit for a couple of days but had to take it off for at least a day to give my skin a rest.

I really wanted this watch to work especially since I got it at a great price on sale. I don't think I would have ever paid full price for it because for a few dollars more you could have gotten a full size Android Wear or Galaxy Gear watch with more features! Speaking of which I replaced the Gear Fit with the Asus Zenwatch which I am totally happy with!

If you're considering this watch I would really do as much research as possible. It may be a good fit for you but again if you pay full price for it there are much better options for a few more dollars. If you want a great tracker that has some integration with your smartphone and if you can find it on a good sale this might be a worthwhile buy.

Review:
This smartwatch is a big improvement over the previous umidigi smartwatch. The touchscreen is much easier to navigate and the app for this smartwatch is also much better. The app has less personalized customization than an app for a fitbit but is very close. You can change the face of the smartwatch by tapping and holding down on touchscreen. The clock hands move exactly like a real quart sport watch.

The sensor on this smartwatch is not accurate but is very close. When moving, the steps is almost accurate but when exercising such as lifting weight, the step measurement is wrong. I was staying in place but it clock at 150+ step. The heartbeat seems accurate when measuring it alone but seems wrong when exercising. It takes like 5-10 seconds for the sensor to pick up the actual heartbeat. I compared my heartbeat by measuring it by hand for one minutes and it comes pretty close to the measurement on the watch which is 3-5 heartbeats higher. There are several common exercising options in the watch for choosing when exercising which has a few extra measurement. I do not do some of those exercise so I do not know if it's accurate or not.

Your biometric data when exercising cannot be view unless you pair it with the app. The graphs on the app is very useful for knowing whether you reached those crucial benchmark (ie anaerobic exercise) for burning calories. You can also monitor your sleep pattern but you must enable it on the watch by swiping up and click on the moon icon. The sleep monitoring is not accurate. The light sleep detection is wrong. I was awake in bed but it display as light sleeping. I think the error is around +/- 30 minutes.

Your notifications does pushed to the watch but only from a few selected apps. Not all of the notification from the phone is pushed to the watch which is the downside of it. What I do not like about the app for this watch is it always runs in the background. You cannot stop the app. This will have an affect on the phone battery life.

Time and weather will not update unless you pair it with the app. You cannot manually set the time. You can set an alarm in the app but the watch vibration is very low that if you are deep asleep, it will not wake you. Vibration is barely noticable.

I have used the watch for 4 days. The battery went from 96 to 69 percent. The screen will turn on when I made a heavy movement with my arm. If it turn on less often, it would last a little bit longer but not much.

I like the watch. It has a high quality build. It is a little bulky which most people will not like. It's perfect for
someone with a larger build like an athlete.

There's a few cons but I cant fault it because most of the high end smartwatch has pretty much the same cons. This watch works almost as good as a high end watch for fitness purposes. There are quite a few functions that I wish it have but as smartwatch gets better, I could see them being implemented.

Review:
Two weeks into my using the Forerunner 35 and I'm happy, especially after using the Garmin Vivosmart HR+, which had a number of design flaws and eventually, either a mechanical or software failure that resulted in its return to Garmin after 8 months.

The Forerunner 35's large, flat screen has much better readability than the Vivosmart. It is sleeker and doesn't get caught in sleeves and pockets like the Vivosmart did, offering more ergonomic sensibility.

Forerunner 35 has a battery level indicator on the main screen--no need to sort through a couple of menus to find out how much power you have left on this rechargeable device. The Forerunner 35's battery life is much better, too, I just ran it two weeks on one charge, while the Vivosmart HR+ barely made it six days before hitting the charger. Forerunner 35's normal watch-button controls are easy to use and much more reliable at navigating menus than the touchscreen that the Vivosmart HR+ had. The touchscreen is unfortunately subject to anything conductive brushing across it, even shower water...not a huge problem, but you have to navigate back to the homescreen. Not an issue with the Forerunner 35's button navigation...just like a digital watch should have.

The GPS connects quickly and accurately. The heart monitor is good and I haven't had any troubles with how it records activities like sleep...all good, there, too. I'm a runner, so the device has come in handy for training. It works well with Garmin Mobile Connect on my iPhone, keeping track of data.

I have to give a shout-out to Garmin's US-based support crew for helping me with the issues I had with Vivosmart HR+, even when they weren't able to find a quick fix for the watch, they remained in contact and were helpful and courteous. I decided to give Garmin devices another chance (buying the Forerunner 35) because their support team was nice...stuff like that is important to me.

I would recommend the Garmin Forerunner 35 comfortably with four stars. I'll update with any further observations or critiques.

I've had this watch now for about 4 months. It has become such a big part of my daily routine that I feel naked without it!

Background: I use this watch daily to track my steps. I also work in a busy healthcare setting where I'm a bit paranoid about touching my phone (and dragging all those nasty things I touch across my face), and we are also not allowed to check our phones on the floor. So having both a functional watch and notification filter helps me prioritize when it might be necessary to take a quick break to answer an important call.

Functionality: I was one of the original backers of the OG Pebble on Kickstarter, and loved the idea. The watch has come a long way--the color screen, the sturdier build, and sleeker designs are all great improvements in my book. The userbase has exponentially increased too, so there are a lot more watchfaces and apps coming out on the Pebble Store. My top 3 used apps: Timer (perfect for a quick snooze), Pandora (lets me change volumes and like/dislike), and Health (built-in Pebble app that tracks steps and gives you a breakdown). It's simple and does what I need it to do without all the expensive fluff. I'm lookin' at you, Apple.

Durability: I attached a military-grade NATO strap to my Pebble, and have taken this thing EVERYWHERE. It stands up to constant alcohol-disinfecting (wiping, not dunking in the stuff), hand-washing every 15 minutes, and on my hikes and trips to the beach. It's not an invincible watch--if you get sand in it or swim in salt water I don't know how well it'll survive. Use common sense and be gentle with it when you can, and it'll go miles.

+ Well-priced compared to the competitors. I got it for $160 during a sale.
+ Simple yet elegant. I don't need bloat or expensive add-ons.
+ Sturdy steel frame with steel buttons
+ Glass is very durable--there have been many times where I thought I had scratched it
+ Plays well with Android OR iPhone
+ Has a microphone when you're too lazy to type out a message. Voice recognition isn't perfect but good enough for quick messages.

Cons:
+ Bluetooth needs to be on all the time to talk to your phone, and the app needs to be on in the background. Keep a spare charger handy if you're using it a lot
+ I'm honestly trying to find something here. Can't think of anything.

Review:
I've been using this for about a month now, and really, REALLY like it. If I had one complaint, it's that the bluetooth radio in this watch doesn't seem to have quite the range of my Pebble Time Round, so disconnections happen more often. That said, bluetooth runs on similar wavelengths to cordless phones and microwaves, so various devices interfere. If I'm in the kitchen and the microwave is turned on, it's not uncommon to lose the connection. Nature of the beast with bluetooth.

Still, the screen is MUCH brighter than on the Round, so I'm happy with the trade-off. Don't know if the color on the round adds a layer, but that would explain it. Contrast is much better. Add to that the battery life (I hit 60% after FOUR DAYS, but I also probably get fewer notifications than most people), and I'm sold. The heart rate sensor is what it is -- optical heart rate measurement at the wrist is inherently unreliable at this point in the technology's development. That said, I find it tracks fairly accurately, though especially in sweaty, jiggly moments (exercise), the numbers can fluctuate. It's not a chest strap, and it's pretty unreasonable to expect similar results in my opinion. Voice reply to text messages (I'm on android, if that matters), was a surprising home run. Hint -- if you say "Question mark", etc, it adds the appropriate punctuation.

Software could use tweaks and development, but since Pebble went under, don't plan on that ever happening. Fitbit is currently committing to keeping the services running through thet end of 2017, or at least that's how their press release reads to me, and the Peppble developers hired by Fitbit claims they are trying to make the watch less reliant on cloud services (UPDATE: This has been done, though certain cloud services may still go away at some point), and the developer community may also work on these things, but right now I'd assume that if you buy this, plan on some functions not working after 2017. Which is sad -- I love these watches. Still, if you can find one used or on sale at a serious discount (like I did), it might be worth it to you. Also, there is a third party Android app that purports to run most of the watch's functions without the Pebble app or cloud servers (Can't remember the name, and I haven't used it so can't say how it works) that some like. At any rate, it seems some of the fuctionality of the watch that is not cloud-based will contionue to work well beyond 2017, but things like weather updates and voice-to-text services? To be safe, I wouldn't plan on it.

If the company was still up and healthy, I'd recomend this watch to most people in a heartbeat. If you're looking for a watch that does notifications with tremendous battery life and is always-on, it seems that these functions will continue to work. But it's still a gamble -- there is NO guaranteed support continuing into the future from either Fitbit or Pebble -- and that includes warranty support!

Oh -- and get a screen protector. Yes, it's gorilla glass, but that stuff isn't indestructible. Scratched the hell out of my Pebble Time Round absentmindedly brushing it against a stone wall as I walked. All it takes is a single moment of distraction to thunk your wrist against something, and your watch screen is now scratched.

Review:
So, I will preface this with the fact that this is my first smartwatch, and first real experience with Wear OS from Android. I got this as my job has me texting with other coworkers a fair amount, and I wanted a way to check my notifications and respond without always pulling out my phone.

Set up: Ok, so this should have been a LOT easier to be honest. I had to do this twice (got a new phone about a week after I got the watch) and it took a long time each time for the phone to see the watch to complete setup (yes, Bluetooth was on and discoverable on both). I had to do a hard reset of the watch to get it to pair with my new phone. Once the Wear OS app could see the watch setup was easy and worked well.

Use: The watch will work just like any other Wear OS watch from Android. It did update to a newer version of the OS shortly after initial setup which made swiping from each direction have a new function. The responsiveness to taps is good, and I see little lag. The apps do take a bit of time to load up, and the screen often times out before it is fully loaded (I wish the screen timeout interval was adjustable). Otherwise it works well. I get quick notifications of texts and emails coming in, which is what I really need the watch for. I have found that the Google Assistant functions are really helpful, and voice recognition excellent. Responding to a text while I walk down the hall and talk to my watch (despite sounding dorky) is very helpful for me and efficient. The voice recognition is certainly faster than trying to tap out a response slowly on the tiny on screen keyboard. My favorite moment so far was while mowing my lawn, I was using my phone to stream music from Google Play Music to my bluetooth headphones, and then being able to change the volume or track from my watch.

Specifics to the TicWatch Pro:
- The dual layer screen is the reason I got this watch and it works as advertised. I use the LCD screen most of the time to see the current time. My main complaint is the LCD screen does need a fairly good source of ambient light to read clearly, but the time area is quite large and easily read.
- Size: I was concerned at first that the watch would be too large on my narrower to average sized wrist. After wearing the TicWatch for the last 3 weeks or so, I don't notice an issue with it. The watch is a bit thicker than I was expecting, though I don't really notice this much (though it does get stuck on the cuffs of my dress shirts). The overall size does have a nice solid feel to it that I really like.
- Straps: Nothing fancy. A leather-like outer with a rubbery inner lining. I hope it holds up ok. It does have the quick release function, if you want to change out straps.

- Durability: so far, so good. I like the fact that the bezel is raised slightly over the screen and should help protect it from scratches.

I chose to turn off the "Tilt-to-wake" gesture (which keeps the screen off more of the time), and do not have the screen set to always on either. Value: I got this TicWatch Pro as a gift to myself after seeing a *great* price on it on Thanksgiving. At the price I got it for, it is a fantastic deal. At full retail, its an OK price point, but it remains much more affordable than an Apple product or other Wear OS competitors.

Final thoughts: Great device so far. I think the hardware is solid and I have really enjoyed the ability to leave my phone in my pocket or on my desk, but remain able to check notifications. Hopefully it holds up for a long time to come.

Being as it has all the hardware a health tracker needs(unless you're hardcore cardio and want third party stuff like chest HR sensors which the watch doesn't support) and right now the only thing limiting it is software, it can only improve with time.
Functionality:

downsides are the notification management needs improvement and responding can be a pain because of poor voice recognition, which should be the bread and butter of a smart watch and done with ease.

If you're looking for a great price for a practical smartwatch with a long battery life, this is the one. The battery life definitely lives up to the 7 day expectancy. The watch works great as a notification center and remote for your phone. I use mine with an iPhone 5s. The only limitation is that you can't reply to text messages from the watch with iOS phones unless you have AT&T, Verizon, or T-Mobile. Android phones get this function for all carriers though. However you can still send SMS and the built in microphone works well for this function. The watch is water resistant and is fairly sturdy. I've bumped it a few times and haven't noticed any scratches yet but if you're wearing it actively they have protective skins you can buy. I purchased the watch strictly for the notification function so I don't have to take my phone out of my pocket to see who's calling, what a text says, what event is coming up or currently happening, or what email just showed up. Since all push notification go to the watch, I even get my auto updates from the Google App and IFTTT which is great. The silent alarm function is great for not waking my wife up in the morning when I get up for work. I love being able to control (skip, pause, play, go back) my phone music from my wrist when I'm driving so that I can keep my eyes on the road or when I'm doing yard work. The health tracking is not the reason I bought the watch but it's an added bonus. I enjoy seeing the steps and HR numbers and the sleep tracking. All seem fairly accurate for a wrist device. I'm enjoying playing around with different watch faces to always have a quick glance of weather, steps, time, date, location, battery life, and bluetooth connection. Just having the screen always on and a long lasting battery life for close to $100 is awesome. I would not own a smart watch if it wasn't for pebble. This is the right price and functionality to motivate me into the smart watch market.

Update: A little over 1 year after purchasing this watch. I've used it every day since I bought it and I still really like it. It's a shame the company is no longer around. Here's a few updates after year of use. One of my favorite aspects that I didn't mention in the original review is the buttons. The four buttons with customizable shortcuts are a fantastic piece to the watch. I much prefer this over any kind of touch screen function. I can do a number of things without ever looking at my watch. I know the shortcut sequence and can do things like change songs, send canned texts, or snooze an alarm without ever looking. I also switched to a pixel phone 3 months ago and I can say that the android experience with the watch is much more enjoyable than the iPhone. With the iPhone you have to keep the Pebble App open all the time to keep getting notifications. This is not the case for android phones. I never bought a screen protector for the watch and I am starting to see a few minor scratches but nothing that is very obvious. I've bumped the screen quite a lot so the lack of major scratches and scuffs is a good sign for the screen durability.

After using the phone for over a year, I still recommend it and I still think it was more than worth the $100 I spent. I've attached a look at the watch after a year if you're curious.

I have owned this watch since September 2021 and it has been nothing but trouble. I got it because I do a lot of hiking in Alaska and was impressed with the reviews about its GPS function.

Lately, the trouble has been that I can't trust the battery level indicator. Four times it has said battery level in the mid-range, I go for a 3 to 5 mile hike and it freezes before even a mile in and I find out later that the battery quit.

It often randomly pauses or goes to another menu option - for a while I thought that I was accidentally pushing a button when I flexed my wrist, but this has happened with controls on the side of the watch opposite my hand, so it seems like it just decides a button needs to be activated every so often.

The elevation gain is highly inaccurate at times - see attached photo. Apparently I was hiking Denali here in Alaska that day (sarcasm) - the real elevation gain on that hike was about 1000 feet.

The heart rate monitor is always 10 to 20 beats per minute low. Last week my heart was pounding and it said I was at 69 bpm. When I counted, it was over 130.

I tried using it when I lifted weights and that was really inaccurate as well and not in an intuitive way - for example, push ups would be fairly accurate (I don't fuss unless it's more than + or - 2 off), but one leg dips would be WAY off. No arm movement at all with push ups, but up and down with dips - so why more accurate with push ups? I was spending as much or more time editing the reps as I was working out, so I quit using it for that.

Also, the controls are not intuitive and if you push the wrong one, there is no way to back out of it or reset without shutting it down. If you push, say a navigation or waypoint button accidentally, you have to go through with it and even then it won't take you back to where you want to be. There are many hikes I just gave up recording because that happened.

Before the Instinct, I used a Vivoactive 3 and it was even worse. I don't have a basis for comparison because I have only ever owned anything but Garmin watches, but it is time to move on to another brand.

Review:
So I got this on Amazon Prime Day, and have had it for about 3 weeks now. I'm thinking of returning it. I'll first mention the PROS of this watch, and then tell you why I'm returning it with the CONS. Here's some background on what I do and how this watch fits in with my daily life. I have a Samsung Galaxy S7. I walk my dog for about 45 minutes every morning at 2.5 miles total. Then I work from 9-4 like most other people. Get home. Relax. And then play some adult league sports around 7pm. But the place I play sports is about 45 minutes away from me, and because of traffic, I often take varying routes to get there, and listen to music along the way. I get home around 9-10 depending on the sport. And then shower and my weekday is over. On weekends, I am a sports official. I mostly intended to use this watch to assist me in my officiating with a referee app that a coworker of mine, developed but only for android. Its a great app and Ive seen him use it. Sometimes I'll only officiate 1-3 games a day. Others will be 5-6 or all day tournaments. I needed a watch that could last a full 24 day on either a weekday or weekend with all these intended uses. I like to track my fitness so all the active stuff I mentioned, I wanted heart/some gps/and needed to be connected to my phone the whole time for data transfer. I needed to be able to get AT LEAST 7-8 hours of heavy use.

Pros:
+ Look/Feel: The minimalistic all-matte black finish is right up my alley. In terms of looking neutral and not flashy enough to draw attention, but looks sophisticated and elegant enough that if people do notice, I've had people ask "Hey what watch is that?" Couple it with your favorite watch face and its a great accessory to basically any outfit. The silicone band is standard enough. Good for wearing normally or for doing sporty things like I do. They are 22mm bands I think so they can be switched out with any 3rd party bands. For the price and for someone who doesnt want something too flashy but still stylish, this gets a 5/5 from me.
+ Play Store: Because this is Android wear, you have the option of all the apps that android gives, and are not in the extremely limited range that some other watches have (cough* samsung gear)
+ Heart rate monitor
+ Magnetic charger
+ Speaker to take calls/listen to music
+ If you have a samsung phone and have the fast lightning charger (or any fast charging block I suppose), this thing will go from 15% to 100% in about 30 minutes. However, that's only if youre near an outlet.

Okay. So why do I want to return this even though I got it at a somewhat good deal? (Currently $160, bought it for 99)
Cons:
1) The damn battery life. I read at least 60-70 reviews and watched a large handful of youtube videos about this watch before buying it. The stances of people on battery life were very mixed but mostly negative. Some people said they got great battery life after they altered some settings and did a few power cycles. Some people said they couldnt get a day out of it (but had all the heavy features on like wifi, gps, always-on display, etc). Others said they disabled those heavy settings and did the power cycles and still didnt get a full day out of it. Because of all the inconclusive comments on battery life, I decided I would try it out for myself and remain optimistic that I could get decent battery life out of this thing.
- For my weekday use, starting a day at 100%, using the built in fitness app, I do a "fitness walking" workout when I go with my dog. 45 minutes later, ITS AT 77%!!!! Just doing a 45 minute workout, which basically just consists of walking around a few blocks, burns 23% of my battery. I dont have much time to charge it. So I go to work. Luckily at work, I dont have much use for it there, as I have my laptop and what not. By the end of the work day, after using it for the occasional notification and time-check, I'll have about 55%. Then I come home. Relax. And go to the adult league sports. I activate another workout to whatever sport, and by the time I get back home, I'm usually done to 15%.
- Keep in mind, I do deactivate all the "unnecessary" features when not in use. In other words, when Im not using it for fitness, gps is off, heart rate is off, always-on display is NEVER on, I have it at medium brightness, but its always connected to my phone via bluetooth. I also did 6-7 power cycles when I first got it, and updated everything to the latest software. I go from 100% to 15% from TWO workouts that barely eclipse 150 minutes total, plus a workday of notifications. I think thats horrendous.
- Not to mention that my weekend use is much worse. Now granted, this officiating app I use, does use GPS and step tracking, but it doesnt use heartrate monitoring. But it does have a timer I set for a game, and when a team scores, I input a score. If they get a yellow/red card, I input that as well. I needed this watch to be ableto last my SIX 80-minute games. Now I dont do 6 games every weekend, but I needed it to be able to last that long just in case I do. I started it off easy and used this + officiating app for TWO 80-minute games. I guess GPS isn't optimized very well because after two back to back games (started at 100% battery), I was at 30%!!!!!!!!!!!!! THREE ZERO. I know the app takes a lot, but youre telling me that after ~160 minutes, the watch needs another charge before I can do a 3rd game? Cmon man.
- Conclusion: Unfortunately, the battery life is as bad as people say, IF YOUR USE IS BEYOND THAT OF the average joe who just wants to be able to check notifications on their wrist. If thats all you want, then you may be just fine with the battery life. But if you want to use this for fitness or want to use it for a specific task that involves pairing with an app+phone and heavy use, then this is NOT the watch for you. The battery life is the #1 deal breaker for me and ultimately the reason why Im returning this.

2) No default messaging app or connection???? When I get a text to my galaxy s7, I do get the notification on my watch, and Im able to reply to it if I open it immediately out of that notification. However. If acknowledge the notification and close it, there is NO way to get back to that message and reply to it or even view it again. That doesn't seem to make any sense to me. I actually love being able to reply right on my watch and not have to walk back over to my phone, or take it out of my bag or whatever. But if Im currently occupied, cant reply at that moment, I am forced to go and get my phone after acknowledging the notification. There needs to be some kind of messaging link so that I can open up the message later. Its very annoying to read the notification, then be busy for 20 minutes, and then when youre ready to reply, you have to go and get your phone to do so. To me, this sort of defeats the purpose of a smartwatch. I want to be able to leave my phone/desk and if Im in another room, be able to stay in that room and address the message regardless. Pretty disappointed that I cant do that.

3) OLED screen burn-in. Disclaimer!!!! This did not happen to me. I dont ever have my always-on display specifically to avoid this problem. However, I have seen and heard it is extremely common in this watch. If you use a 3rd party watchface and activate always-on display, or make the mistake of NOT turning on screen-saver for the built-in faces, your watch is in danger of getting the screen burned in. I highly recommend that NO ONE turn on always-on display, even with 1st party watchfaces. I tried activating the screen-saver in the developer options and for some reason, it would always glitch and never activate. Im so scared of the burn in that I just turned off "always-on" altogether.

4) Finally, and this is just me nitpicking and being critical, lack of "defining features". One of the reasons why Im so close to getting a samsung gear watch (other than it pairing perfectly with my phone and despite the bottleneck app market), is that rotating bezzle. A bunch of other watches have that "1 feature" or "those features" that truly make the watch stand out and a joy to use. This watch is about as basic as it gets. Obviously for this price range you cant ask for too much, and I honestly dont know what feature Id want in this watch for it to bring it to the next level. (BETTER BATTERY LIFE MAYBE???). In all seriousness, the watch is extremely standard. Looks neutral like I previously stated. But the single button and touchscreen just make the most "ehhh" of smartwatches. Nothing memorable to exciting about using this.

BOTTOM LINE:
All these things being said. Depending on your use, I dont know if I could recommend this to anyone. If you just want a smartwatch to be able to see notifications (and be forced to reply immediately or else...) and dont plan on using any fitness features, then maybe this is the watch you want? Although there are seemingly better alternatives in this relative price range I believe. Idk what they are, but if you look hard enough you could find something that better fits your use. For everyone else, I'm sorry. I tried to be open-minded despite the critical reviews. But they were unfortunately right. The battery life downright sucks. And if you need to rely on this watch to last you just ONE day, let alone two, it wont happen. I would be fine with single 24 hour use. Because I could always charge it overnight. But not even a single day on a weekend when I actually use it for 5-6 hours straight? Not okay. Pretty disappointed. Because I got it for such a low comparative price, I may keep it just for weekday use. But Im definitely not gonna count on it for anything other than that.

The watch is easy to charge and has an impressive battery life. The wristband is easy to remove and reattach (or presumably swap out with compatible wristbands). The watch is low-profile and nicely fits both men and women's wrists.

I chose this watch because, unlike others, it offers O2 saturation readings, which I need everyday, along with BP and HR. I can manually perform the latter two readings, but not the first, and I was already looking for a fitness tracking watch to try out that didn't break the bank. It also boasts a better waterproof level, but please be aware that the manual stipulates it is not intended for saltwater swimming, nor water with harm chemicals; so I'm not sure if it's even safe for pool use—the Amazon page certainly leads you to believe it can be use in a chlorinated pool. I do note that on the Amazon page and the watch itself, interestingly enough, that "swimming" is not one of the 9 programmed activities of the 8 that can be visible at a time.

Unlike some other reviewers, I found setting up and pairing the watch with my iPhone 5SE quite easy. The manual provides clear instructions for Bluetooth pairing and downloading the free mobile phone app. I do wish that the manual provided more explanation around other watch features and functions, however—such as what each icon represents (and what happens when you press it) when, from the starting dial face, you swipe right left, up, and and right, and right and then down and then down—beyond just the the sport feature.

The challenges I encountered were syncing the VeryFitPro app with Apple's Health app—VeryFitPro still does not appear in Apple's Health app as a 3rd party app as VeryFitPro's instructions lay out, so I have not been able to import my watch's data into Apple Health. Next, despite following VeryFitPro's instructions, no alerts other than phone calls appear on my watch. (I have enable proper settings in the app and in the Bluetooth settings on my phone). Finally, this watch does not include a wheelchair push activity tracker. I am wheelchair-bound and had been looking for a lower-priced alternative to Apple's offerings, which I believe DO have this feature. I hope that the developer is able to add wheelchair (pushes) as one of the "sport" options to track and make this an ACCESSIBLE, INCLUSIVE app for people of ALL ABILITIES.

Review:
I personally am a big fan of the Garmin Fenix line. I started with the Fenix 2, moved on to the Fenix 3HR, then the Fenix 5X, and now the Fenix 5X Plus. Although the Fenix is a great line of watches, they are pretty costly and they're also a heavy watch. Those two factors make me wary of using them as my everyday watch, despite being very rugged.

So instead, I was looking for a "daily driver" watch that had a subset of the features of the Fenix line that I wanted to use every day. Things like, heart rate monitoring, activity tracking, on the fly workout if I didn't have my full kit (I also have a heart strap and run dynamics with my Fenix), etc.

The Garmin Instinct has all that and more! If I were to compare, it's very close to the Garmin Fenix 2 with the monochrome screen, very long battery (a feature I miss in the newer Fenix models), workout tracking, etc with the added plus of the heart rate monitoring and sleep tracking. Although the sleep tracking isn't as good as some other brands I've used, it's usable as a rough analysis. The Instinct doesn't support run dynamics like the new Fenixes do but neither did the older Fenix 2 so it's not a huge loss.

In in all, the Garmin Instinct is an all around great watch for those not looking for the Fenix price tag but want many of the Fenix features, particularly outdoor. Even though it's polymer instead of metal, it's also still a rugged watch and also lighter than the Fenix. I highly recommend this as a starter Garmin watch over the VivoActive or the ForeRunner (unless you are primarily a runner).

Review:
Up front, let me say that I bought this device because my doctor suggested I use a FitBit to track my weird heart rate. Clearly, this is not what the device is designed for and not what most people use it for. Still, I think I can help others determine whether it is the right device for themselves.

SET-UP: Pairing and set-up were fast and easy. The instructions that come with the device are clear and easy to understand.

CHARGING: I love how this device charges. One side of the wrist band comes off, then the charger can be plugged in for charging. This is so much less cumbersome than using a cord. The tracker charges fully in 1 hour.

APP: The app is self-explanatory, easy to use, and makes it easy to see your stats at a glance. It has one little defect, which I will discuss in a moment, but for most people, it probably would not make a difference. Through the app, you can take your blood pressure (which, when compared to my old school blood pressure cuff, seems surprisingly accurate), see your heart rate throughout the day, see your sleep data (including sleep duration, how many times you woke, when you fell asleep and when you woke, how long you were in deep sleep and how long you were in light sleep), and your "sport" info (which I did not use). There's also a running mode that shows you, through GPS, how many miles you've run. In addition, you can set the device to alarm (vibrate) when your heart rate goes above a beat per minute that you designate.

COMFORT: The band on this device seems sturdy and is soft enough to be comfortable. I had no trouble sleeping in it. It's a lot more comfortable than my FitBit.

CONS: The big con for me was two-fold: First, while the description on Amazon says that the device monitors your heart rate continuously, you have to tap the screen several times to "scroll" and get to the screen where your heart rate is displayed, then it takes several seconds for the heart rate to appear. In addition, the app only records and graphs your heart rate every half hour. For me, these features just wouldn't work. I needed a tracker that would quickly and easily let me see my heart rate and would graph my heart rate continuously throughout the day.

CONCLUSION: If you just want a fitness tracker and are debating between this and a FitBit, buy the ZURURU! The price may seem to be too good to be true, but honestly, I far prefer this tracker and its app to the FitBit I ended up with. IF the makers would just allow me to see my heart rate more easily, and include in the graph ALL my hearr beat data, I would still be using ZURURU .

Below is my initial review of this product. Everything in that review still applies. So, if that's the case, then why am I updating my review and changing my recommendation?
The charger.
This should be such a minor thing that doesn't even need to be mentioned. In fact, if you look at my previous review, I don't mention it because it didn't appear to be an issue. Yes, it was a little finicky but nothing unexpected from your standard magnetic charger.
Oh, I was sooooooooooooooo wrong about that.
The charger is a nightmare. It will connect right up, its magnetic connections coming together with a nice, satisfying little *click!* and a graphic on the watch that shows it's charging.
Then the nightmare begins.
The screen will, if you're lucky, stay there and your watch will charge normally. This is what happened 80% of the time for me. As time went on, however, I kept seeing the screen switch from the charge screen to the clock face. Another thing I noticed was that, when it switched to the clock face, it was NOT charging.
This started becoming an issue. The watch would switch on its own all the time for no apparent reason. Sometimes, it would just switch back and forth. It was insane.
It has now gotten to the point where it connects and displays the charge screen for a few seconds and then goes right to the clock face. Getting it to charge takes forever and there appears to be no good solution to the problem. I've cleaned the connectors on the phone & charger and it makes no difference.
I've been noticing this kind of problem a lot more recently. A desirable, high-end electronic device is brought to market and originally offered at a price point higher than much of the market could afford. Other companies see this and make high-quality, less expensive versions of the product and concentrate so much on making their device do everything and more than the originals that they forget about the basics. In this case, they shove a cheap magnetic charging setup into an otherwise very good item and it destroys the whole thing.
It doesn't matter how good it is, how deep it'll dive, or how well it controls your media if you can't charge it.

Review:
I have had my Gear Fit for just over a week now. I use it both as a smartwatch and as a fitness tracker. It does a fairly good job at both. I give it 4 stars because it's nearly perfect for what I use it for, but if you're looking for the ultimate smartwatch or the ultimate fitness tracker, you won't find that here.

First, some background: I use a wheelchair. Literal "steps" mean nothing to me. So I can't tell you if the pedometer is accurate. During the average day, the Gear Fit tells me I've done ~ 5,000 steps, if I go for a brief roll sometime during the day (in addition to my usual routine of going to work and coming home). So, that works for me as a relative measure, but if you're looking for something that will keep an accurate step-for-step count, you might be disappointed.

The Gear Fit has a heart rate monitor that distinguishes it from bands such as the Jawbone UP24. I use it mostly to tell me how hard I've been exercising (which for me consists of mostly lifting weights or rolling really fast). I've gotten pretty consistent results for that.

All of the fitness functions tie into S-Health, which is why you're going to want a Galaxy phone to pair the Fit with. (There's an open source alternative to the Gear Fit Manager so you can use it with other phones, but I can't say if that's going to give you the same experience.) Fortunately, S-Health is much improved from its earlier incarnations. Now you can track your sleep,and it pairs fairly painlessly with the Gear Fit. The one area where S-Health is lacking when compared to, say, the UP software for the Jawbone devices is, the food tracking is a bit more laborious. The S-Health software doesn't have the UP's ability to scan bar codes, so you're reduced to typing more than you'd be with another device.

The thing that really sets the Gear Fit apart form devices like the Jawbone UP devices and the FitBit is the screen. If you move from one of these bands to the Gear Fit, the first thing you'll notice is how much easier having a screen makes your life. You don't have to rely on vibration patterns or blinking lights. The information is right there on the screen to read.

The Gear Fit's screen is curved nicely, and it's easy to read indoors. Outdoors in bright sunlight, you have to crank up the brightness. (I use a 2 setting indoors, and a 4 or 5 outdoors.) But you have to stay cognizant of the conditions outside before you go out. If you have the screen set at 2 for brightness, good luck going out in bright sunlight and trying to adjust the brightness then. An ambient light sensor would really help in this regard, and I'm hoping it's added to the next version.

The Gear Fit Manager allows you to change the wallpaper, colors, and watch faces. There are a variety of watch faces to choose from, so you're almost guaranteed to find something you like. I do wish the home screen (where the clock resides) was a bit more customizable, though. In particular, you have to go to the Settings menu to see the battery level. It would be nice if you could have things like the battery level and the Bluetooth status on the home screen, so it was more accessible.

The Gear Fit Manager software allows you to send notifications from almost every app to your Gear Fit. You get a little vibration on your wrist, then you can swipe to the Notifications icon, tap on it, and see your notification. Keep in mind, though, that the more apps send notifications to your Gear Fit, the more of a hit the battery takes.

Speaking of the battery, you can probably expect 2-3 days of battery life with regular use. If there's one piece of advice I could give you, it's this: Turn the Bluetooth off when you're sleeping. That greatly improved my battery life, even when I used the watch to track my sleep.

The Gear Fit lets you view text messages and e-mails, but there's no software keyboard or voice control here, so you have to reply from your phone. In fact, most of the functions of the watch will involve your smartphone. That's not too different from most other smartwatches, but it would've been nice if Samsung had at least included a GPS so that you didn't need your phone for basic fitness activities like running and hiking.

All in all, I'm very happy with my Gear Fit. It does everything I want, and I paid a reasonable price for it.

Review:
i wanted a new watch (my old one broke) primarily to know when someone calls, texts, or emails me, and also to keep track of my walking and workouts. this watch does all that, it's waterproof (i wash it after each workout), looks elegant (looks a lot like the apple watch), and costs under $25. plus the battery lasts a very long time, which is a huge plus. you can recharge it for 10 minutes while you're in the shower every few days, and it will never run out of battery. will last even longer if you turn off heart rate monitoring. excellent bright screen, with adjustable brightness. "find phone" feature is nice too (i've already had to use it twice). for these reasons, i'm giving this watch 5 stars, though it's far from perfect.

i have two main issues with this watch, though at this price-point i wasn't going to knock down a star for these issues:
1 - heart rate sensor is ok (fairly good actually) for establishing average and resting heartrate. however, it's not at all accurate for tracking heart rate during workouts. maybe this can be fixed with future firmware updates, maybe not.
2 - the watch navigation and faces aren't customizable. the weather location isn't customizable (which is very important, given that it got the wrong location for me). i'm guessing this can be fixed easily in next app update. there is no way to delete which workout types show up on the watch, to make stopwatch more accessible (currently takes 5 actions to start stopwatch, but only 2 to do a breathing exercise. i want that reversed). and there's no way to make it so the screen stays on during my entire workout. all these customizations should be in the app, so i'm hoping the companion app will improve over time.

other things to note:
it has music controls, breathing exercise, sleep tracking, and a lot of exercise modes. i will never be using any of these features.
it has a standard quick-release watch band, so you can customize your watch band and get fancy or funky ones. i'll stick with the default watch band, but it's a nice-to-have feature.
the watchfaces you can choose from are cool, but i wish there were more.

tldr; if you need a watch to track your heart rate accurately during workouts, or to have highly customizable watchfaces, this is not the watch for you. if you want an elegant-looking smartwatch that will vibrate and display all your calls and messages, with a clean, bright display, week-long battery life, and exercise tracking, all for under $25, this watch is for you.

Review:
TL;DR: Watch is basically perfect for tracking runs and basic workouts.

Purchased this watch as an upgrade to the Withings Steel HR Sport. While that watch was serviceable, it also relied on phone-based GPS and had somewhat unreliable heart rate tracking. This meant that the data gathered during my workouts was highly variable and could only be used as a rough approximation of reality (for example, running the same 4.3-mile route daily would give me distances of anywhere from 4.2 to 4.6 miles with my speed looking like seismometer output and my heart rate measurements sporadically dropping out). I decided after a year of a semi-serious running habit (20-25 miles/week when not injured, sick or otherwise indisposed) to pick this up. In short, it was worth it.
Pros:
The GPS is on point. My 4.3 mile route is 4.3 miles every day without fault, and the map of my run is totally accurate.
Garmin connect presents a ton of useful information. Most workout programs will tell you the aerobic/anaerobic benefit of your workout, and the app tells you your training load and infers your “body battery” from activity and heart rate throughout the day. There are hydration and calorie-counting widgets if that’s your thing. The data visualizations are clear and coherent.
Having music loaded onto the highly waterproof watch removes rain as a potential excuse not to run. Spotify integration works reliably, though it isn’t nearly as easy as simply strapping your phone to you for the run.
The watch face is customizable, and there are custom widgets/workouts you can download from the Connect IQ store.
Battery life is generally pretty good. I’ve only had the watch die on me once, and that might be due to my watch face not really conveying battery info.
Cons:
None for my purposes!

Disappointments:
Google fit integration with Connect would be nice, so my phoneless runs could be added and then sent to Pokemon Go.
My preference is to listen to audiobooks while I run, and this doesn’t seem to be possible with the 245.
I’ve been dealing with achilles tendonitis most of the time I’ve had the watch so I can’t enjoy it as much as I'd like!

Review:
I should preface that I have a bias towards Garmin as this is my third tracker - I have the smart scale and a lot of friends on the app, so take that into considerations when reading my review. That being said, I did a lot of research before I landed on the Vivio with Music, especially compared to the Apple Watch 4. While the watches share a lot of the same basic features - GPS, Waterproof, Work with iPhone, on wrist heart rate monitor, etc. - for me, the Garmin was the right product.

The key takeaways that put the Garmin ahead of the Apple Watch for me were:

- Battery Life: the Garmin has consistently provided five days of charge. That’s with at least three workouts in that five days, GPS use during at least one of those workouts, and the heart rate monitor always on. The Apple Watch only claims 18 hours per charge. **If sleep tracking is a big deal for you Garmin is the only real option.**
- Notification Fatigue: I am a techie and love my features but I thought the Apple Watch was just to much Smartwatch for my wrist. The Garmins preset widgets, push notifications and Garmin Pay were the right speed for my needs. There is still quite a bit of customization, but not so much that you find yourself overwhelmed by options.
- Design: This is entirely preference based but I prefer the circular facing on the Garmin to the soft, square display of the Apple Watch.
- Ecosystem: As I is said before, I’ve bought in to the Garmin system - figuratively and literally. I have friends and family in the ecosystem and find it to be easier to navigate than Apple health (which still seems like it’s in Beta).
- GPS Accuracy: I’ve heard the Garmin GPS technology is more accurate. I have no way to prove this but given they pioneered consumer GPS products I’m going to give them the edge here.
- Spotify Integration (coming soon): I have a premium Spotify account, and have no desire to switch to Apple Music. This was a big selling point for me. Fingers crossed this support launches soon. (As of Jan 20, 2019 I am still waiting).
- Price Point: this wasn’t a huge point for me but the Garmin is $120.00 less than the standard Apple Watch 4.

All things considered, the Garmin isn’t perfect - I was disappointed with the plastic watch housing, button, and screen display. For $300.00 I would have liked more. That being said, it does keep the weight of the watch down.

If the takeaways I detailed above make sense for you, I’d recommend this GPS tracker in a heart beat, pun intended.

Review:
Alright so I came into this purchase with mild expectations and I have since been blown away. Now, I will start by saying that I was looking for a smartwatch that was gaudy or too futuristic looking so this seemed to fit my criteria nicely. This doesn't have any incredibly outstanding features like the Apple i-Watch or any of Samsung or Motorola's watches, but it does exactly what I wanted it to do. It alerts me to a number of different notifications that my phone receives such as text messages, ESPN score updates, phone calls, and yes even the occasional Tinder match. The thing that the Martian Notifier does best is hide the fact that it is a smartwatch in plain sight. The piece, I feel, is first and foremost a timekeeping mechanism, and secondly a smart watch. There is an LED notifier light that will blink on the watch if you get a notification, which you can turn off in the app or on the watch menu itself, but that's as close it comes to alerting the casual passerby or onlooker that what you have on your wrist is a smartwatch. The notification system itself is a small OLED screen at the bottom of the watch which will light up ever so slightly when you have a notification, and then proceed to scroll your message across the screen.

Now, the only reason I am deducting a point is not functionality based, but purely an aesthetics matter. The watch band is rubber and while some may like the casual aspect, I find it difficult to dress up if I need to while wearing this watch. What I would like to see in the future is a more dressy looking band that comes with the watch; I know you can buy a band and replace the stock one, but that's just another step in the buying process that I'd like to avoid. I'd also like to see them start to compete with some of the fitness trackers, as I would like to work out with this on and have it track at least my steps and distance. One more side note, as has been mentioned in other reviews this is splash proof, not completely waterproof. I will definitely follow this company closely and see where the go from here with this tech.

Review: For starters, I should say that I have previously owned a Samsung Galaxy watch and, before that, a Fitbit Blaze. My Galaxy watch broke recently, and rather than spending another several hundred dollars, I came across this smart watch for only $39 ($32 with coupon) and figured I would give it a try. This smart watch has activity tracking, heart rate monitoring, sleep tracking, alarms, receiving and reading messages (text messages, emails, Whatsapp messages, etc.), weather, and all of the standard “smart watch” features that are expected on a smart watch. And all of these functions work really well. I also like the ability to take pictures with your phone remotely by tapping a button on watch. The watch interface is also very user friendly and easy to figure out. Overall, I would say this is a pretty solid smart watch that easily competes with other, more expensive smart watches. And for this price point, I would say that TOZO has come out with a fantastic value watch that is perfect for those new to smart watches, or those (such as myself) who want a smart watch but don’t want to break the bank. First and foremost, the 1.71'' full touch screen is absolutely stunning. The vibrant colors and crisp resolution make it a joy to interact with. Navigating through menus and accessing various functions is a breeze, thanks to the responsive and intuitive touch interface.

One of the standout features of this smartwatch is its heart rate and sleep monitoring capabilities. The accuracy of the heart rate sensor is commendable, providing real-time data during workouts and daily activities. The sleep monitoring feature is equally impressive, giving me detailed insights into my sleep patterns and helping me make adjustments to improve my overall sleep quality.

What truly sets the LIGE Smart Watch apart from others is its exceptional battery life. With a staggering 50 days of standby time, I no longer have to worry about constantly charging my smartwatch. This extended battery life is a game-changer, especially for those who lead an active lifestyle and often forget to charge their devices regularly.

In terms of durability, the 5ATM waterproof rating is a standout feature. I can confidently wear this smartwatch during swimming sessions or even in the shower without any concerns. The watch is built to withstand water pressures up to 50 meters, making it suitable for various water activities.

Furthermore, the LIGE Smart Watch offers an extensive range of sports modes, totaling 24 options. Whether I'm running, cycling, or practicing yoga, I can easily track my workouts and monitor my progress in real-time. The accuracy of the data collected gives me valuable insights into my fitness journey.

Compatibility with both iOS and Android is another advantage of this smartwatch. I was able to seamlessly connect it to my iPhone, and the accompanying app provides a user-friendly interface for managing and analyzing my fitness data.

Finally, the LIGE Smart Watch's design deserves special mention. Its sleek and stylish appearance makes it suitable for both casual and formal occasions. The comfortable strap ensures a snug fit on the wrist, and the overall build quality feels robust and durable.

In conclusion, the LIGE Smart Watch for Men is a remarkable device that offers a plethora of features at an affordable price point. With its beautiful display, accurate sensors, exceptional battery life, and extensive sports modes, it has truly enhanced my fitness journey. If you're in the market for a reliable and feature-packed smartwatch, I highly recommend giving the LIGE Smart Watch a try. It's a game-changer!

Review:
I went through Lumoid.com to try 5 different fitness trackers before I sunk a lot of money into one of them. Here are the trackers that I "rented" for two weeks:

Fitbit Surge
Garmin Vivoactive
Fitbit Charge HR
Jawbone Up3
Garmin Vivosmart

After being able to put these items through their paces, and figure out which of any of them I wanted to buy, my decision was left between two excellent units. The Fitbit Surge and The Garmin Vivoactive. They both had strengths and weaknesses, but I ended up making the final decision to go with Garmin, and I am not disappointed. Here is why the decision was made:

Fit and Finish Quality - The Garmin won hands down for the most comfortable and usable tracker I tried. I have a small wrist, and this unit just feels right on my arm. The Fitbit Surge feel most substantial by far, but it was NOT comfortable. I also like that the Garmin Unit has rechargeable bands so I can change the look up if I want to.

Reliability and Accuracy - The both have ups and downs in this category, but I had a LOT of issues with my Fitbit Surge staying connected. It dropped connection a LOT, and then was difficult to fix. I never had this issue with the Garmin unit. The GPS was flawless on both of them, and it took very little time to get a gps lock on either device, even indoors. They both accurately counted my steps, calories, and sleep! I like the integration of the Garmin Unit much better with other aps on the market. Both had excellent battery life, about a week per charge, using the GPS once per day about an hour at a time. The Garmin unit will allow me to alter my step stride if I needed to, but I found the standard to be just fine. I could never figure out how to do that on the Fitbit.

Screen - Both have excellent screens, but I have to give the edge on readability to the Fitbit. Indoors is was much better, but outdoors they both reign supreme. I like that the Garmin unit does have an app store where I can download more watch faces, data fields, widgets, and apps. There are not a ton out there yet, but those that are available are great. The Garmin unit is much more customizable, but the Fitbit is much more simple to use. I do like the color screen on the Garmin Unit, as it does break up the monotony just a tad.

Companion App - Wow, they are both great! They both have strengths and weaknesses. I like that the Fitbit can track food and water right on their own app, but on the Garmin I have to use a companion application. That being said, there are more companion apps that are able to play nice with the Garmin Unit, giving me almost endless opportunities. I like that. The fitbit application is much more simple to navigate. The ONE issue I have with Garmins Application, is that sometimes you have to do a refresh several times for the application to update. No big deal, the information is there, it just takes a bit to get it where you want it! The Fitbit application is faster for syncing.

No matter which unit you decide on, they are both outstanding products. There is NO right or wrong here, it is what works best for you. I found the Garmin Unit to be a more reliable option as a whole. I highly recommend that for $25 you to go www.lumoid.com and rent up to 5 different trackers to try for 2 weeks. This way you can get a better sense of which one works better for you. Let me know if you have questions, I'm happy to help!
