Review:
First off, i'm not a bot or some paid company writing fake reviews. Everything below comes from my own purchase of the ticwatch pro. I really want to like this watch and I'm a fan of Ticwatch, but I have to be honest ; it has some setbacks. I will try to keep it as concise as possible while giving sufficient info to help you in your buying decision.
1. Physical attributes
Metal bezel and some kind of nylon-glass composite for the body, although the overall feel is "plasticky". However it does feel strong enough for outdoor sports. The band is a 22mm "hybrid" - leather on the outside, silicone beneath. Weight is okay, not too heavy nor Fitbit-light. Have to say it is a comfortable watch for its large 45mm size. The watch looks bigger than its stated size due to its wide chunky lugs. I highly discourage smaller/thinner wrists from getting this as it may overhang. I read some reviews saying the band is too short. I have exactly 7.5 inch wrists, you can see from the attached image how it wears. There is excess.
2. Software
This is the caveat I need to highlight. It can be slow at times to open apps or switch screens. I am not sure why this keeps happening as I turned off Heart monitor, turned off Wifi etc to keep it bare bones. In comparison my Fossil Gen3 smartwatch is considerably fast; screen changes almost instantaneous, and that is a 2 year old product. Maybe it is a quality control issue affecting some pieces. Also, with the new smartwatches due out later this year (Samsung just announced their latest smartwatch last weekend), you may want to wait it out to see the upcoming competition if you are in no rush.
3. Fitness tracking
Pretty decent, does everything it advertises. Heart rate monitor is good. Step tracking is relatively okay, no glitches. However I find the Fitbit Versa is more accurate and fitness-app-friendly. Do note the Ticwatch Pro is more of a smartwatch first rather than an activity tracker.
4. Battery Life
Yes it has the famous 2 screens everyone keeps talking about. And it does extend battery life. This is one area the Ticwatch Pro really excels. You can choose either purely Essential mode (Only the battery saving screen is active), Always On Mode (only your selected watch face is shown) or hybrid; Essential mode switches to watch face when you flick your wrist or press something on the watch. I tested it in full Watch Face mode (the most draining option) and got about 2.5 days max (GPS off, heart rate off, Wifi off).
5. Additional Features
I like the ability to answer phone calls directly on the watch when I'm driving. No hassling around with the handphone. The audio is clear enough despite road noise and the other party can hear me clearly via the watch. The other thing is NFC, you can wave your hand and do Google pay with this watch. Pretty useful at grocery store or deli when you have your hands full.
6. Conclusion
Thank you for reading this far. I'll make this quick: A solid contender in the premium smartwatch market with a decent price tag. You will enjoy its battery life and some additional features. However again do note there may be some slowness in the software and there are newer models with better processors on the 2018 horizon. If this watch is $199 it is a very attractive proposition, but this coming from a Ticwatch fan - consider your options carefully if you are not in a rush to get your next smartwatch.

Review:
Like this Garmin. Had a 510, until like an idiot I left it sitting on the bike rack after a ride and drove off forgetting about it. I loved the 510 touch screen. To me there are a few real key differences between the 510 and the new 520 version. First the touchscreen. Some people hated it on the 510, mine worked great with no issues. The 520 is controlled with side buttons, which basically sucks to use while in motion Some important menu items are buried inside multiple levels of menus, require excessive scrolling, push a button, find the option, push a button again, scroll some more, find the option....you get the idea. It really isn't very convenient. This is my main beef with the 520.

On a positive note, versus the 510, the 520 will connects quickly and easily to your iphone or mobile phone using Bluetooth, and with the Garmin Connect App on your phone, it will upload your Strava ride the moment you save it on the 520. I do like this feature. No more connecting the 510 by cable to a computer to upload rides.

Generally speaking, the 520 suffers from a poorly lit display. The 510 display was easily readable day or night. At sunset the 510 display would kick over to reverse graphics that had a black background and white letters. That contrast was easily readable with litte to no need for backlighting. The 520 changed and not sure what they did to it, but it is virtually black at night, and unreadable. The only way to see the 520 at night is to set your backlight in the "on" position for night rides, and then set your display at about 30 or 40%. This does impact battery use, but so far still leaves me with 75-80% charge after a couple hour ride.

There are other features added to the 520 that are lacking in the 510 as well. These include segments, basic maps, and other features that I don't use. I don't want to take a star away for something I'm not using. Note however, I did try the segment piece and found it quite annoying and turned it off. The idea is if you have a segment created where you are tracking your time, speed, etc, the device will alert you as you approach the segment, and show your pace against your best time, and tell you if you set a new record for yourself. Unfortunately, when the segment tracker kicks on, it blocks out your screen with the map and you can't see your speed, cadence, for the length of the segment. Worse, its somehow tied to the Segments you create in the Garmin Connect app, and it isn't intuitive tying this Strava. I got a few segments set up and afterwards the 520 never updated my best time on the segment. It was forever stuck on the original segment time first loaded. Ultimately I couldn't get the 520 to add more than a couple of segments, which never updated. I also am unable to delete them. Better just to leave that feature turned off.

All that said, this is a great little cycling GPS device. I like how small and unobtrusive it is. For all the main features I use for, it works great.

Review:
When I buy a smart watch, there are certain things (features & functions) that I always look for. I do not care much for the accuracy of heart beat rate, SPO2...etc because I fully understand that these economic types (under $50) watches does not really provide accurate data. So as long as those data are somewhat accurate and useful enough, I am fine with it.

for me, the most important things are the following : a lot of useful watch faces that I can download and switch back and forth, thru the watch, not via app.
Tennis fitness app (I am a tennis coach) among other useful (at least for me) sport apps. very loud alarm and timer, so that it can wake me up. 44mm and up big size watch for my 7.4 inch wrist. Large battery....etc

As for watch faces, it has a lot. A lot of good ones that I can use. Also, I can delete pre-installed all the watch faces and upload with all new ones. Many other lower cost smart watches do not have this feature. I can only upload one or two that I like and I have to keep the pre-installed faces which I can not delete nor replace. As for this watch, Yes, you can basically delete all the pre-installed faces with your choice of watch faces, up to 8 of them.
As for the battery life, it claims that it has 300 mAh. That is pretty big size and I think that it will last for few days.
It also has a lot of fitness choices. More than 100 of them and I think that most of us can really choose what we like. Also, the app (Veryfit) can allow the watch to upload only the fitness apps that we are willing to use. Veryfit app is a very useful and well designed app for lower end watches.

And the feature that I like the most is the alarm and timer. Most of watches, including expensive ones costing over $100 or more, only comes with weak vibration for alarm and timer. But this one has the "real alarm" sound. Not vibration, but the piercing & loud sound that will really wake you up. I had a lot of smart and fitness tracker watches, but this one is the only one that has the actual alarm sound coming out of the watch speaker. I really like this feature.

This is big size enough for my wrist and the screen quality isn't so bad either. It is not amoled screen, but you really can not expect amoled for this price. However, screen is very nice and it is bright enough.
I guess that the only draw back that this watch has is the strap. You can not really change to different strap because it has its own proprietary lug designs (as you can see from the photo). However, the strap is nice and soft and comfortable though...
It comes with a very simple and cheap looking gift box and inner plastic container (which even looks cheaper) but as long as the watch works and it works great for me, I do not mind.

Review:
I am a hard-core weekend warrior. I love to race mountain bikes and run. I've been getting in to Triathlons over the last five years. I've been watching Garmin develop sport watches for several years, but i always felt the price didn't justify the technology they were putting in them. One would be good for this sport and one would do well with that. I could never find a watch that did it all. The Garmin 910XT seemed to finally meet my basic criteria. One watch that can do it all. I want a watch that i can train with and race with. As a triathlete, I've been most intrigued by the Swimming features.

Swimming:
From a training stand point, the 910XT can support lap-swimming and record distance, speed, strokes. Again, for years, no Garmin product has had the ability to gather lap data while inside a pool. But, the FR910XT does exactly that. That's some forward thinking. In practice, i'm still getting used to all the buttons and all the different screens. Again, I've never owned a Garmin. So far my favorite swim feature is the lap keeper, you just set the length of the pool and off you go. The swimming mode supports a number of different strokes depending on how you swim. It also features an open water mode. Unfortunately, it's still to cold to try it out. I'll update during my first race or open water swim.

Biking:
The 910XT has made a number of small improvements over previous watches that i've looked at. It offers the ability to now set up multiple bikes. I have three bikes, one mountain, one road, and one tri-bike. I can store different saved parameters, such as ANT+ sensor details (power/speed/cadence) and wheel size/bike weight. I ride a 29er mountain bike for run 700cc on both my road and tri bikes. Again, one watch to run them all. The 910XT is designed to be either worn or mounted on the bike. I've found i really like wearing over messing around with mounting it. The display is fully customizable. It will show up to four fields of data. I use time, distance, speed, and cadence, but i recall that you can toggle through eight measures in all.

Running:
The 910XT comes pretty well stacked for my running needs. Garmin has proven that can make awesome running watches in the past. Many of the same feature that i use for biking are the same for running. I've been trying to use the HR monitor during my running and biking training days. It seems be accurate. It has a Run/Walk feature which i've found is pretty cool for interval training. I use the distance and pace features the most. It's so much information, that i've tried to keep it simple.

Conclusion:
Over all, there is so much to learn about this watch. It's a bit like drinking from a fire hose. How does the watch work, the HR monitor, and then how do you download everything to your compute? The data it collects is endless. If you're a triathlete, then this is the watch, a single device that does it all and that's why i bought it. It should be 5 star for all the features, but for now just 4 because it's taking me a lot of time to figure everything out. It's a bit complicated, but well worth the time investment to learn how to use it.

Pro's:

Indoor lap swimming mode, recording distance/speed/strokes
Run/Walk feature
Virtual Racer feature, ability to race past performances/others
The back of the unit can twist/lock onto a traditional Garmin bike computer mount (slick)
Accurately tracks distance, heart rate, pace and a ton of other metrics
Wirelessly downloads workouts via ANT+ to computer or cell phone
Supports Training Peaks Metrics also pedal based power meters

Con's:

Doesn't record/display heart rate while underwater
Short battery life on 20 hours so it doesn't work as a normal day to day non-sports watch
Can't split between two people(husband/wife) it will only support one person at a time on watch
No touch screen. I've seen Garmin do it on other devices, so why not this one?

Review:
The DG Ares Smart Watch is between 4 to 5 stars for me. I have had a few smartwatches. All within the same price range throughout the years. I have never had a Apple Watch. I can compare it to FitBit Charge 2. Prior to this watch, I was using another Chinese Budget Smartwatch - which uses the app VeryFitPro. This watch uses GloryFit.

Overall, these watches depend heavily on apps to have a good user experience. The watch itself has basic programming that can help with daily task.

The watch has a large face. I'm not entirely sold on this hybrid circular/square shape. I would have much preferred a round watch. The display itself is round. I can deduce that the watch needs the extra bezels to house hardware. With the thick bezels, it does feel large on the wrist. It's also thick - not very flattering on smaller wrist.

The smartwatch has evolved over the years. These budget watches are never going to be as good as an Apple Watch, but you're also not paying 5-6 times that amount. They perform basic functions such as record steps, tell time, heart rate, oxygen levels and sleep. As it connects to your phone, it shares weather information. It does not tell the temperature in real time.

The battery last pretty long time. I get a large amount of notifications via Instagram/emails so it drains the battery. Unread emails/notifcation prompt reminders.

Once I got in the habit of using the watch, I found it useful.

Here are the things I dislike about it.
- instructions were super generic and not specific. I tried to email support within the app and I did not get help. I did eventually figure it out with the QR codes. The instructions are through the web pages via QR codes on the manual.
- The sleep tracker doesn't work very well - especially if you move a lot in your sleep.
- The step tracker works, but the software is a little weird. I run 6+ miles. It would track the steps on the watch. The software would automatically interpret those as runs and subtract those steps. It also wouldn't fully categorize those steps as "workout" on their workout section. The app does not automatically GPS those runs. I have not tried to record manually, as I use Strava, another app.
- I use a Samsung phone. During set up, there's a lot permissions that I have to "allow" in order for the notifications to come through. I know this is a struggle for the software developer but it doesn't help with the user experience - especially if you're not aware of these settings.
-The crown of the watch is just a button and turning it does not have any function - which I think is a missed opportunity to create shortcuts or accessibility to certain functions.

From my review, it might seem like there's a lot of challenges, which I do not deny. I do think these smart watches have been made better - where the battery last longer, it's a tad more user friendly and have more accurate information.

These watches are perfect for those who do not need a lot out of their watches. To have basic functions, read notifications (not respond to them), have a timer/stopwatch, see the weather and count steps.
If you want more out of your watches, wait for a black friday sale, where you can snag a prior year samsung watch for about $150.

Supposedly Fitbit will attempt to keep services running through 2017.

I've had my Vivofit 2 about a week and I've been really happy with it. There have been a few small issues, but overall, this has been a good purchase,

The three biggest things going for it are that it has a readable watch (as opposed some other fitness trackers that either have nothing or just lights), it is waterproof to 50 m and the price point was right. I'm not a fitness person, I'm a person who needs to get off the couch more and burn a few calories. This has helped me do that. A month ago, I was averaging between 1200 and 2000 steps a day, I'm now consistently over 10k, everyday and a lot of that is because of the inactivity alert. I like that it syncs to the app on my phone and that the app share data between my phone and my iPad. You can get it with an optional heart monitor, which is nice for people that need or want to have that information, but it doesn't apply to me. The band is lightweight and easy to wear. I wore a watch for 30 years and then stopped for a few, but this doesn't feel like wearing anything. The band also locks to prevent loss. You can also use the app to select what screen show on the band, streamlining for your personal needs.

The cons are fairly minor in the grand scheme of things. I think the biggest con is that alert tone has no volume control; it is either on or it is off and the sound isn't really loud enough. I can hear it in very quite rooms, but that is the exception around my house. Even just road noise in the car is too loud to hear the sound over. I also don't love the app. The information isn't very useful, compared what is shown on the tracker (except sleep). It is suppose to sync with my fitness pal, but is often pretty wonky. Sometimes, it would push my steps to MFP, sometimes it won't download my calories from MFP, sometimes it acts like it can't talk to MFP at all. The active calories feature of the app has been lacking as well (although I just got an app update this morning that might fix that). For example, yesterday I walked 13,658 steps. The connect app said that I had burned 1 active calorie for my effort, which I know isn't true. The other thing I've noticed is the inactivity bar takes some work to clear and some things don't seem to count. If it isn't consistent activity, it doesn't clear the bar. A few days ago, the bar was on and I ran to the grocery store. It was quick trip, I parked close, ran in grabbed the two things I needed, and came home, but because I walked in, stopped, picked out what I needed, walked to checkout, stopped, paid, walked to the car, stopped, drove home, it didn't clear the bar. It counted all the steps, just not towards clearing the bar. So once that light comes on, you have to do more than just walk to the bathroom to clear. It seems to take around 200-300 steps continuous steps clear it out. Finally, something to keep in mind, if you are doing something else with your arm, it doesn't count all of your steps. I've been tracking y steps with my iPhone and I find them to be fairly close, most of the time. In order to get my steps in, I've mapped out a small path around the inside of my house, so I can walk 1000 steps an hour. I decided to add weight training to my laps and the Vivofit didn't track any of the steps for the time was also lifting the weights. It made the steps over 1000 from my iPhone. The final drawback, for me, is that not as many people own the Garmin trackers, which limits my pool of friends I can compete with. I've been recommending it to everyone, so hopefully, I get a few more, but most everyone has a Fitbit of some kind, instead.

This tracker has good and bad, like everything, but the good really outweighs the bad and it is well worth the money for a waterproof watch step tracker.

I was one of the 60,000+ Kickstarter backers. I received mine about two and a half weeks ago and have loved it ever since. To start off, I am normally not a watch wearer nor would I be willing to spend more than $150 on a smart watch gimmick, so this watch fulfills my requirements. Good:
-Lightweight
-Not bulky or gaudy
-Interchangeable bands
-7 day battery life
-Features
-water proof (resistant) I shower with mine all the time with no problems.

Bad
-inaccurate heart rate monitor.
- Difficult to use standard watch band and spring bar if the band is 22mm. (no holes in the side to allow access to spring pin ends)

I have a ton of watch faces loaded up and they have all worked wonderfully with the watch. The decreased bezel compared to the first Pebble makes it look a lot less like a toy and more like a useful watch. the Pebble app has been great about allowing the notifications I want and they pop up on the watch with a quick vibrate. Vibration is not loud but you will notice it right away. I had trouble pairing it at first but it worked itself out and remains paired as long as I am in range of my phone. The screen is crystal clear and very easy to read. If you use a well made watch face they look great. Another feature I use a lot is the alarm feature. I matched the watch alarm with my phone, so it will vibrate when the alarm goes off. Instantly wakes me up.

Durability has been great so far. When I first got it I used a left over screen protector from a cell phone and cut it to size. Although it has Gorilla Glass 3 I didn't want to take a chance. Plus I liked the look of the matte screen protector. The watch band it ships with is made of silicone and seems to be holding up well. The end with the clasp is 2.75" long and the other end is 4.875". The clasp is made of plastic. I have messed around with the watch pretty frequently and the side buttons are holding up fine. I have some concerns that the silicone cover on the buttons may wear out but only time will tell on that one. The plastic finish seems to be durable. I have definitely bumped it against more than a few different materials and still no scratches.

The interface is snappy and I have never experienced any slowdowns or issues with it. I like that it has a workout mode that will monitor my heart rate and time of workout. I have found the heart rate monitor is not accurate. It may be interference with my hairy arms. But it seems to use the same optical sensor design as other watches so hopefully it is software issue.

I wish the app had a little more functionality to it but you can use it with other apps. The app provides the user ability to change watch faces and adjust settings, but the same can be done on the watch itself. The music control is awesome. My car stereo is on the backseat floor so I have to connect to bluetooth. With the watch I can leave me phone in my pocket and quickly open up the music control, play/pause, skip/rewind, and control volume without taking my eyes off the road.

Battery life for me has been around 5-6 days before I charge it depending on how much I use it. I think last time I charged it is was the 6th day and I was at 30% battery. You will see about a 10% drop every day at least. Full charge takes a couple of hours.

I was not looking for something flashy to wear on my wrist so the e-ink screen is perfect. There is an adjustable back light that does help you read it at night. I have used the speech-text dictation as well and it has worked great. The menus are intuitive and allow lots of adjust-ability from the watch itself.

Overall I would definitely recommend this watch. I would never pay those stupid crazy prices for a watch that you have to charge everyday. This is a nice compromise if you can do without a color screen and it won't break the bank.

I was looking for a watch to replace my pebble and settled on this one even though I knew it was more fitness than smart watch oriented. The size, continuous HR monitoring, waterproof(ness), battery life, and ability to receive smart notifications and respond with preset text was what swayed me towards purchasing this watch over the competition. I will say it is an absolutely beautiful watch. It is incredibly sleek and I love the lightweight body and silicon band. I have a 5.5" wrist and it fit just fine without looking ridiculously out of place like most smart watches do. I actually really like their silicone band design and would consider purchasing just the band in the future. The connection to my Samsung S7 was not very reliable. Many times when I would turn off my phone or watch, it had issues reconnecting through bluetooth. Again, I know this is not exactly marketed as a smart watch, but if you are going to advertise smart notifications and the ability to respond to texts, it should work consistently. I found a lot of issues with displaying of notifications from my android: a) no group chat notifications, b) if someone sent me a really long text that got broken up into multiple simultaneous texts, the watch can only open the most recent of the messages, c) you can't send a text, only respond, d) there is no ability to modify your preset replies to texts. The last two are not a huge deal, but would be nice features. Maybe I'm too used to the instant and reliable connection of my pebble, the microphone, and the ability to send texts and reply with user written text or voice. But for $300 and "smart notifications" feature, I was really expecting it to maintain a constant connection with my phone and display a group or long text correctly.

Garmin customer service was friendly and patient when I asked them a million questions. They responded within a few days but could really only tell me that they would "let the research team know" or that I could submit my suggestions for future features.

Overall, I find that this is more of an amped up and beautified fit-bit-esque smart watch. Didn't meet my needs. Looks like it's back to my trusty pebble until the new samsung watch comes out...

I was soooo excited when the Vivoactive 3 was announced. I had a FR235 and I was so excited to upgrade. I went and bought it on release day in October.

The flat HR monitor was a huge upgrade from the giant bump on the FR235. I find it to be accurate.

For running, the Vivoactive 3 is awesome. The gps is spot on, however it always took my VA3 2-3 minutes to connect, much longer than the forerunner and now much longer than the fitbit ionic I replaced it with, which takes 30 seconds max to connect. I loved the cadence and running stats on the VA3 and that’s the biggest loss I am experiencing in moving to the ionic. The battery life is great on the VA3. It is an attractive watch also.

Apart from that, the rest of the Vivoactive 3 was just flat out disappointing. The bezel scratched way too easy. I found the touch screen and scrolling to be unresponsive sometimes.

Here are the real issues and why I decided to leave Garmin (and not just upgrade to the Fenix 5):

-the sleep tracking is horrible. It’s basically the sleep data that fitbit gave you 3 or 4 years ago. No details on light/deep/REM sleep. This was a big deal to me as I’ve been having trouble sleeping the past few months.

-the watch would lose connection to my iPhone every single day. A few times a week, I would have to go into the settings in Garmin Connect and remove the device. Then spent 20 minutes trying to reconnect it and troubleshooting. It got to the point where I was just done. This made music controls basically unuseable during my runs.

-when connected, the watch would take (not kidding) 4-5 minutes to sync over Bluetooth. The fitbit takes about 30 seconds to sync.

I moved onto the fitbit ionic, which admittedly is a step down for running. No cadence data has been a big loss but I just ordered Lumo run to help with my form and cadence. For everything else I am looking for, the ionic has fulfilled all of my needs. The sleep tracking is great, gps while running is great. Notifications are great, music control is great. Heart rate is accurate.

The only downsides to the fitbit are battery life is shorter, the watch itself is ugly and doesn’t have an always on screen, I’ve lost cadence data and the data fields while running are severely limited compared to the VA3 (only 3 fields with one as a swipe through other stats field). The fitbit wins, at least for my needs, and for reliability.

Ok ive had the Tic Watch E3 two weeks and its time for a review!
TL:DR its great, go get one and try it out!

My last watch was an asus zenwatch 2, so ive been out of the game for a little bit. I was looking for something new and affordable since upgrading from a note 9 to a S22 plus. The Tic Watch E3 is really it!

Initial setup is a breeze and had everything going within minutes of taking it out of the box.

First things first,
The battery life. Its great, up to two days between a fast charge before work (takes about a half hour i think to get a full charge). Im using all the bells and whistles too. Heart rate, steps, sleep, oxygen, gps, spotify and probably more. Really quite surprised actually considering how light this watch is.

This watch is LIGHT! i almost dont like wearing watches because i like my arms to weigh the same. Lol but seriously, between the weight of my old watch and its battery life, i just stopped using it. The Tic Watch E3 is some serious hardware and weighs almost nothing by comparison.

The display, its bright and easy to read even in full daylight and adjustible. the touch sensor on the watch is very well made too. I never thought a keyboard on a display that small would be easy to use. But it is! Ive used it to log into my Tic account to keep track of my activity. And used it to reply to messages. Its surprisingly easy and accurate.

Sleep tracking is very informative, I've actually been sleeping better now that i can see how my routines affect my sleep. And when i feel like i didnt sleep well i have all the info i need to convince my self that i actually did.

Heart rate, steps and GPS are all very accurate and informative. Makes me want to do more in order to break previous records ive set or keep consistent. And when ive been sitting too long it gives me a reminder to get up and move around for a little bit. Extremely helpful when im on my pc too much. (im always on my pc too much)

Its also very easy to manage which apps are notified by the watch and to silence your phones notifications when the watch is active. Helpful so you aren't buzzing on both devices.

Ive been using the Tic apps exclusively on my watch and have no complaints. Plenty of stock watch faces available by default. And through apps like Watchmaker and more you have an endless supply of watch-faces ranging from all the data displayed you can think of to absolute minimal.

Instant familiarity if you've used any other or previous android wear product with a suite of features and options you'll find on more expensive models.

Waterproofing is very acceptable, i dont plan on swimming with it on (personal preference here, i know the watch would be fine) but i get dirty at work. Ill run it under water to wash off the grime before washing my self up and have had no issues.

The glass is tough too, its still as pristine as the day i took it out of the box. Despite the abuse my work causes it.

And last but not least, the watch band it comes with i thought i would replace almost right away. As i did with my Zenwatch and almost any other watch (smart or regular) ive owned. To my surprise i did not need nor want to do that in this case. Its just fine, it works, its comfortable and unless the band wears out or breaks ever ill keep it.

In conclusion to my review, i really like this watch. Ive become more active and generally enjoy using it. Highly recommend you try it out yourself.

If you’ve ever been to Chinatown, you can be forgiven for thinking many items sold there are junk. Every once in a while, though, you can find a gem, and nearly as good as the higher priced items out there. I think I found just such an item in this clone of a well-known Smartwatch.

I did a lot of research about this particular Smartwatch, and can give you all the specs you need. First of all, this watch is called the “T49”, and is tied to the “Da Fit” app available on Google Play. I tried to find it on the App Store with no luck. Maybe a temporary thing, but if you have an iPhone or iPad, I would give this is a pass since it relies on being paired via Bluetooth, to do a lot of the work.

I was able to pair my Smartwatch to one of my Android phones (Samsung) quite easily, and it allowed me to choose a different wallpaper than the standard pink one it came with. Note, you do need your phone to pair with the watch for certain functions, like temperature reading outside, or calling others. You don’t need it if you just want to monitor your blood pressure, how many steps you take, or your pulse. It’s excellent for sporting activities, and offers you a range of workout monitors which can come in handy if you want to play sports, but don’t want to possibly damage a $400+ watch.

It currently has no ability to add other apps, so it’s not THAT smart. However, it does have some games, and all the native apps you’ll need to function.

I’ve just ordered some bumper cases to see if they work with this version. It seems to be a size 38mm, or 40mm. I’ll update this with pics when the bumper cases arrive.

UPDATE 12-29-22: The bumper case needed will be the 45mm, which correlates to the 2022 Apple Watch version. HOWEVER, those cases are moot, since they won’t allow you to move the crown at all. Choose your watch colour wisely, as you won’t be able to customise it with a bumper case at all.

Also, same update: It takes a conventional 20mm strap watch. The Apple Watch bands are meant for that phone alone, and won’t fit it.

Just a note about safety: you have to be street-smart in life, and know there are some people out there who may not have your best interests at heart. To that end, I wouldn’t upload any photos or personal contacts to this kind of phone. If it had the capability of using some payment app, there would be no way I would input my details either. It doesn’t, so it’s moot. But it’s important enough to mention this for the younger, more trusting crowd.

I did use this phone to call relatives without storing numbers and it absolutely works. You just have to have pair it with your phone via Bluetooth, but crucially, you have to keep your phone near you for you to be able to make calls. Think of this as an extender of your phone.

Folks, this is a 40 dollar watch which can be found online for half that, and double that. Don’t expect miracles. But if you’re looking for a pretty nifty gadget which anyone would love to use, especially if you can’t afford the pricier versions out there, give it a whirl!

I've never heard the "alert sounds" for lack of movement, but knew that was likely when I purchased the Vivofit 2.The sensitivity to movement is higher than my Misfit Flash (which I loved, but retired because I wanted an activity tracker which would display my heart rate from my Scosche Rhythm Plus Heart Monitor). Consequently, the Vivofit 2 displays more hours of "light" sleep as opposed to "restful" sleep, but I think it's pretty accurate. You have to remember to press a button on the tracker to tell it you are going to start and stop sleeping, but I've never forgotten to do it. The battery is supposed to last a year or more and I've only had mine a month, so I can't comment on that. I do wish there was a screen in the display on my cell phone which showed the battery status like the Misfit software did. The Vivofit activity data syncs pretty well with SPARKPEOPLE.COM and MYFITNESSPAL.COM although I have to enter the number of hours sleeping manually, which I did not have to do with the MisFit. All-in-all, I am very pleased with this purchase. The price was right and the tracker functions as advertised.

I got this watch because I was looking for a smart watch that looked like a simple regular watch but had all features of a smart one.

The con is that you must have the app open at your iPhone at ALL times so it can be synchronized and you get the alerts on your watch. Usually I charge it every night as my battery is showing 40-50% at the end of the day. I rarely used the Essential Mode but it is indeed a nice feature to have if you only care about checking the time, steps and date. Disabling the touch and tilt actions can extend the battery life, but I like these features, so I leave them on and compromise on charging my watch every night. I tested once how long it can run on full Essential Mode and it went for 5 days. So not too bad if you have a long holiday weekend and want to still use your watch... although I did this test only because I was curious how long it would last. I still prefer having all features on the watch...
- Build Quality: this is a very nice, solid build. I like the round shape as it look and feel like a regular watch. I often get people asking me about this watch and they are surprised on how cool it looks and how well it is build. I have small wrists but it fits very well. The charger is very nice, magnetic and snaps on holding the watch well.

Overall this is a great smartwatch, functional, and nice. It's not a small watch, but not too big (in my opinion).

Review:
First of all, I will say that this is my first smartwatch so I have no others to compare it to. I mainly bought this watch for the gym and for running to use as a fitness tracker and music player. This was the best deal i could find that gave me offline music, a pedometer, GPS, heart rate monitoring, etc. I really don't need notifications and other things because I can get them on my phone easily. I mainly wanted something convenient to use when I didn't have my phone with me.

Positives:
Setup was very easy and only took a couple seconds to pair with my phone. I like the feel of the band, it is a very soft feeling rubber material. It feels light and comfortable to wear. The controls are easy enough to understand but it took a while to get the hang of a few things.

Negatives:
What really bothers me is that I cannot find the watch face from the image advertised anywhere. That was one of the main things that attracted me to the Ticwatch E, and I expected it to be the default face or at least one of the pre-installed ones. But I can't find it anywhere, and now I feel lied to and like it was falsely advertised. It just leaves a very bad taste in my mouth.

The watch itself is a little bulky, I would have preferred something a little lower profile but it's not horrible.

I had a little trouble finding certain wifi networks, but I found an app in the store that helps a little. It was a little complicated to install, because when I originally needed it I didn't have wifi so no way to install it. I ended up turning my phone into a hotspot, connected my watch to it, then installed the app, then was able to connect to the wifi network I needed.

One thing that would be nice is to be able to tell how much storage on the watch is being used. I tried to load a Google Play Music playlist but it stopped half-way through. I assume this was because I was out of storage but I couldn't really tell. I thought the 4 GB would be enough but when you account for the OS and apps it doesn't leave much room for anything else. It would be nice if I could fit some more music on it.

Battery life seems pretty horrible, it's annoying to have to charge it every night (not to mention it turns itself on in the middle of the night and wakes me up). I guess I'm just used to my old fitbit what lasted a few days. I'll try decreasing the brightness, using battery saver, and turn it on airplane mode when I'm not really using it and see how it goes.

But at the end of the day, it does what I wanted it to do. It plays music and tracks my workouts at the gym without needing my phone. It will track my outdoor workouts with GPS. It will even give me a heart rate reading but I'm not sure how accurate that is. Music players with belts, clips, or cords always seemed to get in the way, haven't had that problem with the watch yet.

First day with my new Lg G smart watch R W110 4gb 1.3" Oled screen. I just got it, and thanks to a recommendation from M. P. Mac Runnel "CPU-MD" from Sterling, Virginia, I also got mine from a traditional AT&T store. Not so much for the immediate gratification but because it is $70.00 less than at Amazon. com (thank you Mac Runnel). So I highly recommend you do the same, but beware, as you may come across clueless sales people who do not have any idea what they are selling. Take for instance the guy who sold mine, at the AT&T store in Aventura, Florida. This so call “AT&T sales advisor” was so clueless, so uninformed about the products in the store, that he kept insisting I was buying the Moto 360 (both are displayed next to each other), even though I turned the Lg G smart watch R W110 upside down and pointed at LG logo in the back. Unable to acknowledge his mistake he went to the back of the store saying, “Let me go get your Moto smart watch…” Go figure.

Anyhow, after having waited six months for this watch, after having read lots of reviews and compared it to many other smartwatches, I chose the Lg G r as my first smartwatch because of its circular shape and Oled screen. Unlike other smartwatches, the Lg G r looks and feels like a regular watch. A very nice- looking regular watch I must say. And to me this is a welcome departure from the traditional square, or rectangular screen, of most smartwatches. So if you are into this kind of look and feel of a more traditional watch, the Lg G r is the way to go. But that is pretty much where the tradition ends, because everything else about this watch screams new technology. The Lg G r has a brilliant Oled screen which allows for uncompromising viewing under any lighting conditions, many different analog and digital faces to choose from and various different wearable modes. The watch is very light, and yet feels solid and well built. My wife and I live on a mini-ranch (24 acres of wooded land). We like to take long walks with our dog and be active outdoors. Both of us are retired from medicine and have an interest in maintaining our health. I already have a smartwatch that tracks my health statistics. I ordered this VEYKY smartwatch for my wife so she can track hers.

She is very pleased with the smartwatch. The watch face and band are very feminine and lightweight. Built into the watch are quite a number of useful health features:

• Number of steps taken and compared against a daily goal (you can set)
• Total yards walked
• Total calories burned
• Total minutes spent walking
• Total hours and minutes of sleep the night before
• Charting of your full-day heart rate
• Current heart rate
• Blood pressure in mmHg (both systolic and diastolic pressures)
• Blood oxygen level in percentage
• Outdoor running (in yards)
• There is a feature you can enable to remind you to walk (to reach your goal)
• The watch can synchronize health information with my wife's "Health" app on her iPhone.

Additionally, there are some nice features that can be set with your smartphone. These features are controlled or can be adjusted by the HeroBandIII app, which can be downloaded from your smartphone's app store:

• There is are many watch faces to choose from
• Up to three alarms can be set in the watch to remind you of important events
• The watch can be used as a remote shutter for your smartphone camera
• You can set the time format
• You can set your preferred language
• You can set your unit format (metric or imperial)
• You can set an auto-lock after a selected number of seconds of no use
• You can set your location to receive weather reports on the watch
• For weather reports, you can set the temperature format (°C or °F)
• If you've forgotten where you set your watch down, there is a "Find Device" feature

To get a more accurate assessment of your health and activities, you will want to go to the "Profile" settings in the HeroBandIII app to set up your gender, height, weight, age, and length of step.

The watch comes with a proprietary magnetic charging cable that attaches to the back of the watch and a small plug-in USB wall charger. She uses the watch often, so the smartwatch requires charging every two or three days. The display is bright enough to be viewed outdoors. When she receives a phone call, the watch vibrates and shows who's calling (if the phone number is in your contacts list on your smartphone).

The print in the manual is rather small - a bit too small for my aging eyes. I have a lighted reader for small print. The manual is basic in the information it provides. It covers some of the main features of the watch and explains the initial setup to download and pair the watch with the free HeroBandIII app. The HeroBandIII app seems well thought out, intuitive, and stable.

Overall, she is quite pleased with this smartwatch, its tight integration with her iPhone, the vital statistics it tracks. It is well made, and it offers a lot of functionality, features, and value for the price.

The HOAIYO Smartwatch received had a rose gold case and a pink band. It looks quite nice and seems to be of good build quality. As I mentioned above, the watch is nice looking and powered on the screens are very easy to navigate. We went hiking and it seemed to accurately record steps. The pulse and PulseOx utilities are very easy to use, worked accurately and gave readings quickly. I was actually quite impressed by the simplicity getting these readings. If you are tracking your pulse during exercise, it maintains this data, and passes it to your smartphone with no action required on your part.

The notifications feature is very nice. It makes a quiet little vibration and displays the message received on your phone on the watch long enough for you to look at it. My wife was coordinating something with a friend, and it was quite nice to not need to keep checking her phone for a response. We tested if for both text messages and also Facebook Messenger. I assume any other app that generates notifications will also display them on the phone. This includes reminders and tasks programmed to present a notification. It has some other useful features like a timer, which is useful for everything from timing laps to reminding you to take something out of the oven. It also has a weather screen which gives you the local temperature, current weather, graphical temps and weather for the next several days. That is a very easy answer to your basic weather questions.

I must say, I owned a Samsung Galaxy watch. It had many more features. But, quite frankly, most of them didn't work very well or were difficult to use. This watch is comparatively basic. One day's use and this watch dropped from 100% to 95% which I was very impressed with. I think I can reasonably expect to see five days, or more, use on a single charge.

If it does, I am not sure how easy a replacement will be to be found. That might be no problem. I'd have to investigate how common this type of charging cable is.

Review:
As an owner of a number of smartwatches from known brands (Galaxy Watch, Apple Watch, Garmins) and currently an active user of Fitbit Sense, I got curious about how good these generic brand smartwatches became. I went ahead and gave this watch a try and I was pleasantly surprised.

The big clear LCD screen is easy to read, even in bright sunlight. It is not OLED, but it is not a huge drawback in my opinion.

The battery life is truly exceptional, which sets it apart from many 1-2 day per charge smartwatches like Galaxy watch or Apple watch. I can go for up to a week on a single charge, which is really convenient for me especially for monitoring sleep and wearing it 24/7. It is also very handy when I go on a business trip without the need to bring a charger.

The heart rate monitoring feature is okay, but it's not very accurate. I tested it while wearing an Apple watch on the other wrist and the reading sometimes can have a 10-20 bpm difference. In addition, the heart rate monitoring is not continuous and there's no option to turn it on all the time. The app provides an option to control how often heart rate is being measured, and the lowest I think I got it to is within 1-5 mins. This I am sure is to preserve battery, but it is the only watch I have that doesn’t seem to do continuous heart rate monitoring. However, the on-demand spo2 measurement is a nice addition and I appreciate being able to track my oxygen levels whenever I want.

The Alexa integration is another useful feature, but the response time can be a bit slow at times. It's not a dealbreaker, but it can be a little frustrating when I'm in a hurry. On the other hand, the on-wrist call quality is fantastic and I can easily make and receive calls without having to take out my phone. People receiving the call from me from the watch commented that the audio is very clear.

The sleep monitoring is very effective and is comparable to that of Fitbit, which is known for its outstanding/accurate sleep tracking. I have tested it a few nights of wearing it to bed on one wrist and my Fitbit on the other, and it was able to create a very similar light/deep/rem pattern as my Fitbit watch. That really surprised me.

The app is nothing fancy (e.g. it doesn’t have those comprehensive programs and challenges like Fitbit), but it gets the job done. There are a lot of surprisingly good watch faces to pick from, and I think some watch faces actually look better than the ones provided by Sense. It is also worth calling out that there is no payment integration for this watch, so if you plan to use your watch to pay often, then this is not going to support that.

Overall, I'm happy with this smartwatch and would recommend it to anyone looking for a reliable and long-lasting device with a much lower price point compared to named brands. The biggest drawback to me would be the lack of continuous heart rate monitoring. However, if you value a watch with great battery life, on-wrist call quality, cross-platform compatibility, and effective sleep tracking, this is definitely worth considering.

Review:
It took me a while to decide to purchase this. First, I wanted a fitness band but decided against it because I couldn't find a easy or reliable way of getting info into Google Fit. After purchasing one, sending it back because the app was lousy, and trying to find a reasonable alternative, I began to think that if I wanted to use Google Fit I should get a device that runs it natively (Wear OS). After looking at professional reviews and exploring other models from Mobvoi, I decided to buy the pro model over the S2 for the added functionality and because with incentives the Pro was only $20 more.

THE GOOD...

1. Looks - It's a pretty stunning looking watch, and the build quality is superb.
2. Size - I don't have a huge wrist, but I like large-sized watches. I normally wear 45-50 mm diameter watches anyway, so the size of this was a plus for me. Ergo, this might not be for you if you like your watches smaller.
3. Google Fit works great with the internal sensors - When I workout I just start an exercise in Google Fit and when I'm done I stop it. It's that simple however, I usually spend 30 minutes on an ARC trainer and there's no specific workout for that in Google Fit. I pick Elliptical instead and there's a difference in calories burned (machine vs. watch) but nothing to scream about (approximately a Hershey's Nugget difference).
4. It runs Wear OS, not a proprietary OS. I see a lot of complaints about Wear OS but I don't know what the big deal is. It's functional, constantly being updated, and the library of apps is growing all the time. I kind of reminds me of the complaints I heard when Android first came out and was competing with Apple. I'm sure it will keep getting better and better.
5. Little to no lag when using apps or navigating. The reports about lag on the watch have been exaggerated. Yes, it's main processor is not the latest/greatest but so what? It works well.
6. The "essential" screen (the black & white LCD) is super easy to read in bright light.
7. The heart-rate monitor is pretty darn accurate when compared it to the ARC trainer heart rate monitor... consistently a beat or two off but generally close.
8. You can pair Bluetooth earbuds to the watch and listen to music and/or a podcast, or answer the phone from the watch. I don't know if I'll actually do this (I carry my phone with me everywhere anyway), but it's a nice feature to have.

THE BAD...

1. The default settings on the watch are not conducive to good battery life so you need to play with them. The dual screen is a great idea, but the watch has so many things going on at the same time you really need to play with the settings to get near to the advertised battery life. I switched off tilt to wake, NFC (I'll turn it on when I'm paying for something), "Hey Google" detection. Plus, I'll take it off when I'm sleeping so that it's not measuring my heartbeat 24/7. Yeah, I know that essential mode will get you a month's worth of battery life, but if you're running around with all the cool features turned off all the time to get 30 days on one charge, you just wasted $200.
2. I'm scared to get it wet. Perhaps I should have gotten the S2 after all. Read the instructions from Mobvoi and you'll see that there's some serious butt covering going on in that book when it comes to use and care.
3. Sometimes, notifications are a little slow in coming to the watch. I can't pinpoint whether it's the watch or the phone, but I'd say there's some blame to go around.
4. The leather top / rubber bottom strap is nice looking and pretty tough, but after one sweaty workout the grooves in the rubber part of the band need to be cleaned... buy yourself a replacement band - they're abundant on Amazon and pretty reasonable too. Use the replacement band for daily wear and working out, use the stock band to go out at night and impress your friends with your uber-cool techno wrist ornament.

All in all, I like it. I'm only a couple of days into ownership and I'm still getting the hang of using it. The current sale that included $50 off and the basic but nicely functional TicBand fitness tracker were what got me to buy it. That and my gift card balance meant that it was a very little out of pocket purchase for me.

TIPS:

I got WAY more battery life by doing the following...
Turn off Tilt to Wake
Turn off NFC
Turn off "Hey Google" detection.
Turn off the notifications I don't need (my email accounts for shopping, junk account, etc.)
Set the brightness to 3

With these settings, a full day including playing around with the watch, two logged workouts in the Google Fit app while at the gym, reading notifications, etc... and the battery indicator was over 70%. I'm not a huge fan of the "Essentials" screen so switching the display to "Always On" and using the watch face's power saving (ambient) mode after 15 seconds, the power indicator after a full day was over 50%. I can put the watch into "Essential mode easily by swiping down on the watch face and tapping the watch icon. Pressing the top button cancels this so switching back and forth is easy. Anyway, since I put the watch on the charger when I go to sleep, this isn't an issue for me... I get way more than a full day on a charge.

If you want more accurate heart rate detection while working out, wear it snug and spin the watch so that the sensors are making contact with the underside of your wrist. This is true for every device I've used with heart rate sensors and it works for this watch too.

I've been getting great results with using Google Fit on my watch and phone, and an app called Lose It! on my phone for tracking nutrition. Lose It! reads exercise and step data from the Google Fit phone app and puts it in the log for you. Logging into an app everything you eat every day is a pain, but it's a great way to lose weight.

Get a cheap silicone replacement band and use it for working out instead of the leather/rubber band... I got a pack of 2 for $15. They're comfortable and they look great.

If you're hard on watches in general, get a snap-on protective cover (about $8). I got two... one black, one blue to match my bands and watch face color changes.

Watch faces from SOOON on the Google Play Store are excellent, especially their fully functional versions (a very reasonable charge to unlock everything).

Review:
NOTE: This is my first Wear OS smartwatch. I've had my watch for 10 days as of the time of writing this review. Day one, with the setup and the like, it looked like the battery would not live up to expectations. After tweaking a few settings and finishing setting up, by the time I'm getting ready for bed, I'm at 70% at the lowest.

The LCD display is casually useful. It has time, date, step counter, and bars reflecting general battery life. It's pretty easy to see even in dim lighting. I do wish the heart rate monitor that were displayed in the advertisements were on it though - it's just not there.

I don't have another watch to compare it to, but the AMOLED display is crisp, clear, and generally responsive. The built in watch faces are of decent quality - a good variety between analog and digital, tinkering options and color variations on some of the watchfaces. You can, of course, add additional watch faces via the Google Play Store.

The app selection I am guessing is standard to Wear OS. The built in GPS, heart rate monitor, and NFC options are useful. It has a mixture of built in Google as well as Mobovi apps. There's some latency periodically when doing something more taxing in the Wear OS environment but, for me, at the worst of times it has been a minor annoyance rather than anything worse.

On the phone (in my case Android) I have both the Wear OS app as well as Mobovi's proprietary app...which I don't really use. Google Fit tends to work just as well for me, and has better phone synchronization options.

Hardware wise, the top bezel definitely has a plastic feel. It cannot rotate and, while it looks nice, it doesn't feel as nice. The body of the watch does have a more solid feel and the base is metal. The buttons have a resolute firm press to them - they will rotate but that does nothing. The strap is a blend of silicone on the underside and leather (whether genuine or synthetic) on the outside - it is comfortable and feels durable.

Overall, for my first Wear OS watch, I feel this will hold up through the years and I am satisfied with my purchase. I will update this further if issues arise.

Only issue at all that I have had, and this is minor, is that the watch seems to be slightly inferior to Huawei's when attempting to detect what exercise you are doing when lifting weights. It gets close, usually correct one is the 2nd or 3rd choice when it misses, but it is slightly less accurate. Other, easier to identify exercises, such as walking or jogging seem to be pretty accurate on their tracking of distance. I like having the continuous heart rate monitor and it seems reasonable, but have not put it against a medical-grade device to test accuracy. And you can swim in it, which is great!

For Android users, I highly recommend this particular watch over other current offerings.

Review:
I've been wearing this watch for most of this week and have really liked it. I was looking for a smartwatch that looked less cartoonishly large and square, someting more like a traditional watch, and this one really fits the bill! With the three side stems it looks much more like watches I've worn over the years, and the wide band makes the watch comfortable to wear. The default face, mostly black and white with a few color details, is the one I've stayed with, again because it looks more like an analog watch. There's also a dressier metal band included with this watch, along with the tool required to remove links to adjust the fit.

Setting this up to sync with my iPhone was very easy, just downloading the Da Fit app from the Apple Store and opening it up to pair with the detected watch. There are permissions to grant in the iPhone for the app's access, one paired, and some personal data to fill in on the DaFit app, as well as the usual choices of 12 vs 24 hour time, metric on imperial measurements, etc. And there are dozens and dozens of alternative watch faces available, providing more or less information on the screen.

I don't think I've mastered all of its capacities yet, but it has the usual clock functions (timer, alarms, stopwatch), health monitoring (pulse, blood pressure, heartbeats per minute, calories burned), exercise (steps taken per day, time spent running, distance covered), along with a sleep monitoring function on the Da Fit app. Plus time, local weather, text message reading, and some phone functions like dialing from the watch, recent calls, and a list of a contacts.

Blood pressure monitoring is a great deal more accurate than with my last smartwatch: I checked it several times against a cuff, doing readings on both the watch and cuff, and it gave me very similar results, only 2 or 3 points off the home monitoring device. Well within parameters I'd get if I checked a second time on the home blood pressure device. (It did give me one extraneous and absurdly low reading between those two correct ones, however.)

The watch's pedometer function is one I don't quite yet understand. I was impressed this morning to see it very accurate, within 10 steps when checked against my iPhone's health app step meter, both around 8000 paces, and I'd been wearing the watch and carrying the phone throughout the morning. I'm less impressed later today in finding it nearly 3,000 paces below my iPhone's reading, showing 9800 rather than 11700, again with neither leaving my person. (I assumed they would sync with DaFit when the app was opened, but apparently not.)

The sleep analysis function in DaFit is one that's entirely new to me, so I have nothing to compare it to. The time asleep is accurate, and this is certainly more data that I've ever had before.

I'm impressed with the look and the varied functions of this watch, and might well buy it as a gift.

Review:
I owned the TicWris Max for over a month before I sold it. I then bought the Max S. This review will cover the features common to both models, as well as the differences.

Both watches are unique in that they run under the Android operating system. In addition to the smart watch type of interface both models have, you can also install apps from the Google Play Store that allow you to change the look and feel. Personally, I use Square Home launcher.

Here is a summary of the pros and cons of each watch:

Pros:

1. Feels comfortable on my wrist in spite of its size. Able to wear all day. The Max S, being slightly smaller, is a bit more comfortable.
2. Able to run many applications from the Google Play Store. Most importantly is running a launcher that can completely change the device's interface.
3. Good battery life - about 2 days with normal use for the Max. About 1 day for the Max S. Both charge in about 2 hours.
4. Using a sim card (I am running under T-Mobile) it is able to make calls, texts and all other things a cell phone can do.
5. Has WiFi, Bluetooth and USB connectivity.
6. By wearing on your wrist as a cell phone, it frees up both hands and eliminates the need to carry a large cell phone.

Cons:

1. The small screen (compared to a cell phone) makes it difficult to see many apps. It also requires apps to run in landscape mode. It takes a fair amount of time finding apps on Play Store that run in landscape and that also allow the size of the font to be enlarged. It should be noted that the smaller screen size of the Max S makes it very difficult to read some apps.
2. Smart watch fitness functions are limited to steps and heart rate. The device cannot read blood pressure, oxygen level and temperature.
3. The standard interface that comes with the device is that of a smart watch - the problem is that applications installed on the watch show up as a lot of icons not sorted in any particular order. This is why getting a launcher from Play Store is important.
4. A very large number of free watch faces are available when running under the smart watch interface.
5. Screen brightness could be better. Not a problem indoors, but outdoors is another matter.
6. While it can pair with your cell phone using bluetooth, you cannot make calls or texts. You have to have a sim card to do that.

These devices are not for everyone. They would not work well for a heavy cell phone user. For me, however, it is perfect. The occasional text, email and phone calls I make and receive make this practical with the advantage that my phone is always with me.

The photos attached show different views of the Max. The first 3 are from the standard interface. The second 3 are using the Square Home launcher. Note how you can display calendar and weather widgets.

As I mentioned at the beginning, I had the Max, then sold it to get the Max S. After a few days of using the Max S, I am returning it and buying another Max. The screen on the Max S is just too small for my eyes. I also miss the longer battery life of the Max. The Max S does come with an additional camera which the Max lacks, and there are some additional watch faces lacking in the Max.

Overall, both models are good choices if you want a smart watch that offers more customization options than anything else on the market.

THE GOOD: Let's face it: for a smart watch, Garmin nailed the size with the slimness of the watch. Hands down, it looks good. I bought the white watch, and it looked great on my small wrist. That's where my excitement ended.

THE BAD: For the price, I wanted to like this Garmin product. Garmin is a respectable brand, and I was excited that they created something less bulky for smaller wrists. Taking the watch out of the box, already the screen lighting was quite dim, and I couldn't even respond to the questions on the screen for setup because I couldn't read them. There is no brightness adjustment for Garmin. Eventually I went to a well-lit area of the room and could see the screen. This is already problematic for me because in my mind a watch should be seen at any time. Thankfully, there is a backlight button for a few seconds, but that unpleasantly took me back to my 80s digital watches. (Casio is looking good now…) Within minutes of setup, the menu icon was already non-responsive, and the side buttons had to be pressed quite hard to get any response. Keep in mind that this watch is smaller and feels more breakable, so you'll understand why pressing anything too hard makes the wearer feel like it will be broken.

WOULD I BUY IT AGAIN IF THEY MADE CHANGES? I still have high hopes for Garmin products, and hope that in the near future they'll make a more responsive watch that perhaps has less battery life in order to power it with more speed and light. Hopefully, they'll also make their app even more intuitive in the process. Verdict is out, but knowing how great Garmin is with GPS and exercise gear, I'm sure they'll figure this all out.

Review:
My first smartwatch and this TOZO was a great place to start.

It was easy to set up and sync with my iPhone and I love the quick and easy magnetic charger (takes about 40 minutes to fully charge). Speaking of charges, it holds a charge for a long time (roughly 7 days of usage), I was surprized and impressed.

The only con I have is that the imperial measurement system (for USA), the abbreviation for pounds is incorrect, as it says "LiBS". I'm sure they'll correct this soon, if they haven't already.

Overall, I like the watch and it seems a great entry level product for the price. I've purchased other TOZO products that are great value for money, and the company stands behind their products, as anytime I have a question or concern, they are quick to respond. Thanks, TOZO!

Review:
I purchased this watch 8 months ago and have not had any problems. I had been wearing FitBit for years and had various versions but sick of the ugly look of the fitbit and after awhile the fitbits seem to not keep their charge as long.

Functionality: I wanted something that looked like a watch, was light, and could track my activity, sleep, and have a silent alarm. Pebble accurately tracks both and the alarm works great, plus it has added benefits of being able to see texts and emails from the watch and incoming calls. You can respond with voice or canned messages right from the watch as well and send a text easily from the watch. You can also easily pick from your phone app (I have Android) which apps you would like to notify you, i.e. if you wanted your work email to send notifications to your watch, but not your personal email, you can very easily turn off the personal email notifications. You can also set the alarm right from your watch, you don't need your phone to set it which I had to do on the FitBit. The interface is super easy to use and doesn't take long to get used to. The ones I use most often are the Health monitor where I can easily see from the watch my steps & sleep, the timer, and torch/flash light. The sleep also tracks "deep sleep" and keeps track of your average sleep and average deep sleep. Both the activity and sleep will send a notification to your watch after exercise or when you wake up with things like, "your rockin' the shut eye! You slept for X hours and X mins. Make it nightly ritual. You deserve it." or "Enjoying the great outdoors? You walked for X mins and burned X calories. Way to keep moving." The torch/flash light is not bright like a phone flashlight at all, but is useful in the middle of the night if you just need a little extra light. You can also set reminders to yourself using your voice, i.e. Remind me to go to my appt at 11 am (Slate is an app you can add, but Pebble comes with this capability). There are a ton of other apps you can add like Uber, drink/water counters, games, other sleep and activity apps. The apps add easily and instantly. You can easily reorder the apps that show on your pebble as well - easiest way on your phone app just touch and hold the app and drag it up or down. And you can set two apps to be available by pressing and holding the up and down buttons on your watch for immediate access.

Look & feel: The stone band was not very comfortable to me. I immediately ordered the silver metallic band and watched the video on the Pebble website for how to change it. I love that band, but have not changed it out since as it wasn't super easy (for me at least) to change the band the first time and get it to the right length. There are a lot of watch faces, but I don't really love any of them and you don't see the watch face when its just on your wrist very well at all unless the back light is on. Otherwise it's extremely light and comfortable, looks like a real watch, and durable. I work out with it on, play tennis, have done heavy yard work and have had zero problems and I do not have a protector on it.

Battery life -- States it will last two days which it may if you don't have many notifications otherwise closer to a day, but just make a habit of charging it while you are taking your shower and you'll be all set. It does send notifications to you that reminds you that it will only last until tonight, for example, which annoyed me a lot in the beginning but now I'm used to that.

Review:
This replaces a Fitbit Charge HR that failed after 3 days (Fitbit service's response to my e-mail was "we'll get back to you in 2 or more days! After going back and doing further research, I bought the Garmin Vivosmart w/heart monitor and have been extremely happy with it.
It is a great tool for reminding you to "move" if you've been idle for and hr. or more, mates with "MyFitnessPal.com" so you can estimate your calorie intake and approx. what you've burned, against a daily estimated goal. Also tracks your steps and distance, and, based on your previous day's totals, gives you a new goal each day,(instead of the more common 10,000)
Using the heart rate monitor chest strap during my daily exercise, I can get a much better idea of how my heart is doing than I could with the Fitbit. The Charge HR wrist-based heart rate was erratic, at best, and, many times didn't work at all.
Extremely easy to tell it that I am going to sleep, and it records a visual graph of activity vs. inactivity.
It is waterproof to 50 meters (about 150 ft,) so you can shower, swim, etc. without concern.
It is light-weight, great secure strap (with or without the little rubber keeper they provide.) The display responds with 2 taps and scrolls easily in both directions for heart rate (if using the heart monitor strap}, mi. traveled, calories burned, idle time "move bar", steps left and daily step goal (even vibrates and indicates you reached your goal, with a little fireworks display!)
It would be nice if it would just commnicate with my PC without having to attach it to the usb/charge cable, but that is really the only "con". It will talk to smartphones via "smart" bluetooth, which I thought my Samsung android tablet had, but it didn't. Mainly works with the later smartphones, but they provided a list of compatible devices - I just didn't read it closely enough.
If I had a compatible smartphone, the Vivosmart would vibrate and notify on the display of many different messages, e-mails, facebook posts, etc., and this is a feature you can regulate or turn off altogether.
I haven't needed Garmin support yet, (they have been in the fitness watch business for over 10 years). They do have a really great forum, and much more refined fitness watches, should I desire to increase my monitoring levels in the future.
I've always had a Garmin GPS, and I am looking forward to a long future with them in the fitness monitoring end of their business.
I am really enjoying my new tracker, and would recommend it to everyone. (I just bought a Garmin Vivofit 2 for my better half.) It is just lacking the "smart" messaging and comes with many fancier band selections.) In the short time I have used it, I am already much more interested in what I'm eating, my calories burned, exercise results, and I've lost 5 puonds in the last two weeks in the process! Hope this review helps.... my review of the Fitbit Charge HR was not nearly as positive.

Because I had to reset services on my phone I chalked up the C2 not pairing to the same issue. After playing around with the Fossil for a day I sent it back. The only watch rated above it was the Samsung one but that runs Tizen and has limitations. Ticwatch had the Pro on sale for $50 off. I order it and haven't regretted it. The watch is big,so if you do not like big watches I'd suggest the C2. The screen is great nice and bright and lot of real estate. The watch is very responsive even though it's running the old Snapdragon 2100 chipset and not the 3100. The battery life on this watch is great! I get a full 2 days off the watch. This is an excellent smart watch that exceeded my expectations.

When I first got this watch, the setup was a little difficult at first as the app it had me install, initially would not show the watch in the options to pair despite being connected to my phone's Bluetooth. Luckily, the manual mentions this could happen and tells you to factory reset the watch and it should show up afterwards; which thankfully it did. After that issue with setup, everything else was a breeze. With this watch, all your main customization and features have to be adjusted and set with the app. This is where you will be able to download and set various clock screens, set up weather data, and more. I also had a couple firmware updates on my initial setup, so it was nice to see that the company is making sure their product stays up to date.

Once I had everything personalized how I wanted, I began to use the watch. The first thing I noticed is that depending on the clock face you choose, there are areas on it that will also display your calories burned and steps taken for the day. Or on some watch faces, it will display your O2 and heart rate levels by default instead. I was already really impressed at this point. Aside from the main watch face, you can also swipe left and right to additional screens where you find dedicated spaces for reminders, calendar, checking your heart rate and O2 levels, weather info, stopwatch and timers, and more. The watch itself has an AMOLED display, which is quite shocking to me. The display is vibrant, crisp, and colorful, yet still has a long lasting battery life. The touchscreen is also super responsive and doesn't require extra force like on some others. It looks good and works really well.

As far as the features themselves, they are very good. The step counter works precisely to how my old Galaxy phones did, and the o2 and heart rate sensors work great but do take a few seconds to give you a reading.

Overall, it's hard to find things to complain about. I highly recommend it to anyone who is looking for a good smart watch. While it can't do everything, it is the best for those of you that are looking more for fitness style watches but it will still be good enough for most casual users.
