Review:
Background on me is that I used to workout a lot. Now, with small kids and time crunch, I am not hard core and pretty much just walk to run errands. With a regular stroller, not even a jogging stroller. I am more like an active regular person. Still I walk to and from work or the grocery store when possible, and try and keep active. I'd gotten the watch because I wanted a heart rate monitor, and I feel like a fitness oriented watch would give me that plus a grab bag of extras. I have no background in smart watches, but have previously used pedometers, heart rate monitors, and phone apps that do health oriented things like remind me to drink water throughout the day. Ultimately, I want to more efficiently work exercise into my daily routine. I'm not swimming or running. So, that's where I'm coming from.

This watch has been great other than being HUGE on my wrist, and sometimes uncomfortable. In watches, I tend to get the smallest face possible with an all metal band. But, a small watch couldn't have a big touch screen, so can't be helped.

I got what I wanted: a heart rate monitor plus a grab bag of features. This seems like a fantastic watch for a regular person looking to be more fit. In general, the watch is good for measuring things it detects from you, and bad about info you have to tell it. It's just horrible and inadequate for calorie tracking, because you have to tell it. Then it does these extras like track when I'm asleep. It also is a fitness device, not a straight up smart watch and doesn't have speakers and that kind of thing. If a feature is not fitness oriented, then this watch won't have it or it will be poorly developed.

Battery life is maybe 3 days optimistically. 2 days for sure. It takes less than 3 hours to fully charge. I'm not keeping it connected to a phone, and not fiddling with it much.

Also, here's my disclaimer: it feels like Samsung is actively developing the apps for this. For some problems I list below, like not being able to see older notifications, I would expect Samsung to correct those problems some months out. I tend to say if I've updated my review. Still, this review may go out of date regarding what features the watch actually has.

Pros:

Interface is pretty good. You rotate the metal band on the outside of the watch then tap. It becomes pretty easy to do things as long as they are doable.

Doesn't need to be connected to a phone or a data plan or anything like that. It can work solo. You initially do have to install Samsung Gear app on a phone and do a first connection. Before that, the watch is a brick and won't do anything other than show you a screen saying to connect to phone. But, after that, you can take the phone to another city, turn off Blue Tooth, whatever. The watch will do stuff and tell you info. You do need to reconnect to the phone periodically to make changes to settings. The watch won't let you get to most settings. Still, the watch is a device by itself and not just input output for a phone. Also, you would never have a need for a data plan specifically for the watch. Any data is to the phone.

Pedometer: It's really accurate. No false positives when I'm not walking. From other reviews, if you are pushing something with wheels, like a stroller, it may detect that as a different activity than walking. Like, it might think you are riding a bike.

Tracking water and caffeine drinks: An app for counting these is included. I've previously used a phone app for this. Having it on my wrist means I am much more likely to use it consistently.

Sleep tracking: Not totally accurate, but totally interesting and accurate enough that I could do more with it. It detects when I'm asleep and then gives me a report for each sleep that I can click into. When I say not accurate, for me, if I wake up and stay in bed on my phone or something, it records that as restless sleep. It even has recorded me getting up, feeding a baby, and using the restroom as a period of "restless" sleep. Whoa! Each sleep time is divided into motionless vs light vs restless. When I look at sleeps in the phone app (the watch will only show me a recent sleep not a dashboard), the dashboard shows me sleeps with restless counted as sleep. I would have to click into each and see the real sleep time which is just the "light" and "motionless" times. Nevertheless, very interesting to look at.

Heart rate monitor: It has this. If you are looking at this watch because you are coming from the smart watch angle and not the fitness angle, then right now please google for fat burning zone and heart rate. Lower intensity exercise actually burns more fat. And, if you are doing some endurance thing like long distance bicycling, then you can keep at a lower intensity to be able to go 30 miles or whatever and pace yourself to make it. Heart rate lets you do this. The built in heart rate monitor makes you tap for it to read your heart rate. It's supposed to have a setting to automatically take heart rate at intervals, but that wasn't reliable. Maybe it will miss a scheduled check or several of them. You also have to set that up from the phone app, and not from the watch. For me, since I walk to get to work and do errands, the heart rate monitor is great for checking up on intensity.

Cons:

You need the phone for lots of things. Like, I can't set or change my age, weight, etc. from the watch. I need the phone to do this. Weight changes. I should be able to check and change it from the watch. Pretty much, you have to use the Samsung Health phone app pretty regularly to really use the watch.

It's hard to figure out what the watch does. If you ask me can it do something, the answer is either yes or maybe. To find out whether it can do something, you have to poke around on the phone app and google to find forum posts. Maybe I can't do something because I don't know how and there aren't good instructions.

Style: Watch faces look kind of bad. They all match the big black chunky "I'm a Smart watch" look and style. This watch also has a definite device look and feel to it.

Calories: When it calculates calories burned, it seems off. But also, for this watch, you should already have a system for tracking this and just use the watch to get info on workouts.

Calories: The only way to track calories eaten is by a screen where you turn a dial and say a total number for the meal. It adds that to breakfast lunch or dinner based on what time of day you turn the dial. What?! This is really awful. There's no calorie look up for common foods and no itemized list. For me, it's paper log that I enter manually into myfitnesspal . I wish I could look up how many calories common foods have. Michelle Obama's Let's Move initiative released that big XML file of nutrition info for foods. It seems like they could just grab that and whip up a calorie look up screen.

Can't do much with music and calls: OK, this is not really a con, but many people act like it is. This watch doesn't have mic nor speakers unless I'm missing something huge. You can use the watch to pull up the phone's music playlist. But, then the phone has to be connected to the watch by BlueTooth and the phone also has to be connected to a speaker. So, the phone is in the picture, and you may as well use the phone to click play/pause/next. Like I said, this watch is fitness oriented, not general purpose smart watch.

Only shows most recent notification. Once you check it, it's gone off the watch. Once a new one comes in, the old one is bumped, even if you didn't read it. There's no way to find a log and skim it.

Review:
*Edit* After further use of the watch and interactions with Customer Support I have lowered my previous 2 star review to 1 star. None of the issues I brought up in the first review have been fixed or addressed, nor has any timetable for addressing them been put forward, and I have found several additional problems.
-The "create workout" feature is extremely buggy. Fails to save certain exercises with no clear reason why.
-When in a strength workout, the watch will sometimes skip ahead to the next set and jump over the "rest" phase when the set is ended.
-The watch sometimes freezes up, often in relation to the broadcasting HR problems. This requires that the watch be reset, which looses ALL data. I have lost several hours of data this way.
-The VO2 Max feature, though nice, often fails to work. I have run several times, outside, for 2 or more miles, with the watch correctly recording the run and then come home to find that the VO2 Max (which is supposed to automatically calculate for every run over 10 minutes) fails to appear. The cycling VO2 Max has never shown to date, though due to the weather, I have far fewer cycling workouts.
-When running, I find that the watch often scrolls to the bottom set of "fields" while running and needs to be constantly swiped back up to the top. This is probably due to the sensor on the side of the watch which allows swiping w/o touching the screen. I havn't yet found a way to disable this.
Realistically, this is a 1 star product for the $199 I paid for it over the Holiday season. If I had paid the $299 MSRP I would be feel like I had been had. The fact that Garmin is trying to pass this off as a comparable product to the Fitbit Ionic seems increasing absurd.

*Original Review Below*
The last three Vivoactive models have all been the same story: great promise and impressive hardware undone by poorly designed shockingly untested software. This model continues that story line to a T.

I bout this model because all the 'expert' reviews said that Garmin had FINALLY got it right. They rejoiced that at last Garmin's software platform had caught up to Fitbit's. Well, to say it hasn't is really underselling it. There are certainly some pros in this model:

Pros:
-The stress tracking feature is a great touch and matches my physical experience well.
-The concept behind strength workout rep tracking and VO2 Max estimation are great (neither works more or less at all though).
-After a recent patch the HR measurements now seem to accurately match my actual heartrate.
-Swim tracking appears to be more accurate in this model, though still, baffelingly, they refuse to support open water swimming except for their $600 model.

However, the cons are numerous and unpardonable:

Cons:
-The "broadcast HR" feature which allows the watch to connect with other apps such as Trainer road will frequently cause the watch UI to crash and completely brick the watch for up to 20 minutes or more. I contacted support a month ago, was first rudely told "its probably the app your connecting to the watch shouldn't do that." I, as politely as I could manage, told the guy exactly how stupid that was and to pass me on to someone who knew how to open a ticket. That person bothered to take 5 seconds to look into it, discovered it was a known issue with "many others" having the same problem. I sent him a zip file of my logs along with descriptions of all the devices I had connected to (the watch crashed when used with all of them) he then added me to group ticket and then stopped responding to my messages.
-As seen above, customer support has improved very slightly since the original model, but is still poor.
-Many new features don't work. Including "Automatic rep counting" for strength exercises. It will count correctly about 1 in 4 sets. Also, in premade workouts there is a bug where all weights display in kg even if you input them in lbs and every setting on the watch is set to lbs. The issue goes back to the device's release and there are dozens of forum posts related to it. So far I've seen one Garmin rep's response indicating that a patch would be applied "soon." So far no dice.

In short, the device has good hardware, great ambitions and the start of great features, however, once again it feels like Garmin rushed breakneck to market to try and catch up with the far more polished Fitbit Ionic and didn't bother to fully alpha (much less beta) test much of the new features. Despite matching the Fitbit price Garmin once again is the sever underdog at this price point, which grows increasingly disheartening year after year. Though it has cornered a much larger share of the serious amateur and professional athlete sphere of users the company seems disinterested with bringing their superior high end capabilities down to mass market products.

BOTTOM LINE: Despite 'expert' reviews which claim the Vivoactive 3 and Fitbit Ionic are closely matched products which are nearly interchangeable aside from a few small differences real uses such as those on Amazon have rated the Ionic a full star ahead of the Vivoactive 3 and it's not hard to see why.

Review:
Let me first preface this by saying that I am in no way, shape, or form an athlete. My requirements for my watch were:
- waterproof (needed to be able to safely use it on my paddleboard)
- view notifications from my phone

My last watch was a Fossil smartwatch (Google wear platform) with the traditional touch screen functionality. Battery life was becoming an issue so I wanted to find something new that would work the way I needed it to. This Garmin was one of the few that promised me I wouldn't kill it every time I fell into the lake, and it would even track my swimming (should I get ambitious enough to start doing something like that).

For the first three days of owning the watch, I hated it and was pretty sure I was going to return it. The transition from a touch screen interface to this one was challenging for me (read: I'm old and inflexible) and I missed the customization that I had from my old watch.

However, after a week I realized I loved what this offered that my traditional watches couldn't. Having a week of battery life, pulse and o2 monitoring while I sleep (recently released from my CPAP I like being able to make sure I'm not having issues again), constant heart monitoring (and alerts so my watch can yell at me if I couldn't already tell I was freaking out) and the "body battery" feature are now things that would keep me from switching back to a "traditional" smartwatch.

There are a few things that I wish could be different/better:
- the Garmin Connect app that provides customized watch faces is hard for me to navigate. I'm unwilling to pay, so it's hard to find ones that I like that are free (and will stay free - I've had a few disappear on me because they were only free trials)
- app notifications often appear generic. Admittedly I have way too many apps that send notifications, and while I like that I can block specific apps from notifying on my watch it would be nice to always be able to tell me which app is sending the notification since it's often just the generic message logo and the text without context. Is it my kid's school app sending me a message asking when I'm coming back or Subway?
- tracking my treadmill time (I walk on the treadmill with my nose in a book) doesn't seem to work on the watch. It's probably user error (again, old and not super tech literate) but when I start a treadmill walk activity I expect it could do something more than just keep tabs on my heart rate

Overall, it's a good purchase. And I like that I don't have to worry about destroying yet another touch screen device with my clumsiness :)

Review:
I tried an android smartwatch years ago and decided they were not for me, but this watch has changed my mind. I have worn this for a little less than a week straight, and I am more than impressed. I did not know that for this price range you could get a smart watch that would do all that this does. I have worn it 24 hours a day to test all the features. I have it set to continually check my heart rate every 20 minutes (which it says decreases battery life some). I received it last Tuesday and charged it to 100%, I recharged it on Sunday and it was only down to 15%. The battery life is awesome. From what I understand, even much more expensive watches like the Apple watch do not have this long of a battery life. Having tested the heart rate monitor and oxygen side by side with a pulse/ox machine that we have at home, this reads your heart rate and oxygen level very near accurate. I have also tested the blood pressure readings side by side with one that we have at home, and it was also very accurate. I even had the opportunity to go to the doctor during this time and the BP read the same there as well.

I love how customizable it is. You can change the face to be any picture that you want, or pick from a huge library of already existing watch faces. Also, the watch interface is really quick and once you get the hang of how it operates, it becomes second nature to use and flip through all that it does. I have made and received phone calls on it, and that also works exceptionally well. Texts come through with almost zero problems (more on that later). I have used this to control Bluetooth audio, which is also awesome. I love how I can play music through my watch, or use my watch to control music playing on another Bluetooth device. For example, you can have your phone playing music on a Bluetooth speaker and pause/play/skip the song through your watch. Awesome feature. There is so much to love about this watch, especially for this price.

There are just a few things that I do not love about this. One of those things is the sleep tracking. All in all, it works great, but it has the tendency to track my sleep when I am not sleeping. I usually go to bed after midnight, and apparently my watch can't fathom that, so around 11, while I am watching TV and relaxing for the night before heading to bed, it has decided that I have fallen asleep (I have not). It then shows that I awake for an hour or so before actually going to sleep "again" (when I actually do go to sleep), so the amount of sleep my watch says I am getting is more than the actual sleep that I am getting, and I cannot go through and delete/adjust that section of sleep to say "No, I was not asleep." I used to wear a fitbit that also tracked my sleep, and it would allow you within the app to delete sections where you knew you were not asleep so that it would more accurately track your sleep. I wish this app did that. It seems like that would be an easy fix. Is this a major flaw? No, but it is somewhat annoying.

Another dislike would be that the instructions that come with it are definitely lacking. A lot of me figuring it out was just from using it and playing with it. I tried to look up several things on how to change or work with the different menus, and the instructions don't really explain everything well enough. With enough playing with it, you figure it out, and once you learn how it works, all is good, but there was a bit of a learning curve to figure out how to swipe through all the screens and get the most out of all this watch can do.

Lastly, and this is the main reason I deduct a star is that this watch does not allow you to send a text message response. Other more expensive watches allow you to do this. I WISH so much that this watch could do this. It would absolutely be a 5 star watch if you could send a text response. It receives texts without a problem, but you cannot respond to those texts. It has voice comprehension and a mic... I have used it for phone calls, so I do not understand why you would not be able to send a text. It is awesome to get a text on my watch, but sucks to have to pull out my phone to respond (first world problems, I know). If I could just tap it and say, yes, or no, or I am on my way, or I am driving right now, it would be amazing. Nowhere in the description does it say that this is a feature, but not having it is downright annoying and until using the watch and loving it so much, you don't realize how annoying it is. Also, one last flaw regarding text messages, is that it only receives messages that are between you and one other person. It does not receive any group texts. I have an ongoing group text with my mom and my wife, and none of those texts are received on my watch.

All in all, I love this watch and how well it works for most things. I would highly recommend it, especially in this price range. If they could make just a few tweaks, this watch could easily compete with and possibly beat their high end competitors.

Review:
This is somewhere in-between a full feature smart watch and a fitness tracker. The build quality is good and it feels solid on your wrist. The battery life has been good so far. I would anticipate charging it once a week so you don't have to worry about it dying on you. The bubble menu is fun to use. There are tons of face designs to choose from. At least 50+ designs. They are interactive and add a nice level customization. The vibration for alarms is strong enough to get my attention, which is great considering this is a common issue with many entry level smart watches. You won't have any problems waking up in the morning. It uses the Da Fit app, which is one of the more established apps out there and can easily connect to Googie Fit on the Android version. I mainly use Android but I did break out my daughter's iPhone to test the iOS version. Both versions of the app worked well, easy to pair, and relatively easy to setup the notification settings to your liking. Android is always more of a pain to setup with permissions, but I found Da Fit to be easier to setup than Mi Fit (a competitor's app). The blood pressure feature is surprisingly accurate. You still need to sit upright, don't cross your legs, and keep your arm level for it to capture an accurate reading. I would not base any medical decisions on it, but it is nice to be able to check your BP when out and about. Heart rate and sleep monitoring work as they should. The app does a good job displaying graphs and so forth for the different metrics.

Issues that I hope the manufacture will address in a future update:
- There are only 3 alarms by default. I use three alarms during the day, another two in the mornings to make sure I get up early enough, and one more twice a week that I have standing appointments. Three alarms are just not enough. Please add the ability to set more alarms. I like the menu system and the features for each alarm, I just need more of them.

- Rowing or Elliptical machine is not an option under the sport modes. Even a generic option for exercise equipment. I don't need 30 different sport modes like some smart watches have but I would like something close to one of the common indoor experience machines.

Overall:
I am a fan of the design, menu system, and it's companion app. I would like to see a few features updated but they are not deal breakers. This is a solid choice for a smart watch / fitness tracker that won't break the bank.

Review:
There are so many wonderful factors this watch has that I absolutely love over an Apple Watch. First and foremost, is the price. For all the features you receive on this watch, you simply can't beat the price. It does everything it states in the description that it says it would do. I wanted an activity watch that keeps up with my steps, blood pressure, heart rate, blood oxygen level and of course, my daily notifications i get from my iPhone. It suits these needs perfectly.

The second thing I absolute love about this watch is the battery's longetivity. You seriously don't have to charge it as often as you do with an Apple watch. In the beginning when I first had the watch, my battery life would only last 2 days. I was so frustrated because I wanted a watch that has a long battery life. I contacted the seller (who by the way, is TOP NOTCH) and explained my dilemma to them. They were extremely patient and VERY helpful. Come to find out, it was the "Quick View" option that was draining my battery. HELPFUL INFO: Turn this feature off and you will have a long-lasting battery life. It makes all the difference in the world. All you have to do is touch the screen to see the time and details when you turn this feature off. Not a biggie to me.

Third thing I love about the Umidigi watch is it's so lightweight. It does not feel like you have anything on your wrist. I am NOT a watch wearer and it was crititcal (to me) for the watch to be lightweight. I actually wear this watch all the time, even when I go to bed, which is great, since it has a sleep tracker on it.

Fourth positive thing is that AWESOME display. I am visually impaired and I wanted a watch I could actually SEE the time and details. This beautiful watch has such a vivid and colorful display. I love the simplicity of the watch features. It's not hard to figure out and with the many watch faces it has to choose from, you certainly can find one that will be perfect for you.

As we all know, nothing is perfect. There are few things this watch needs improvement on:

For most of you, this won't apply. I wear Mifi (Made for iPhone) Hearing Aids. More specificially, Otcion Opn. For some reason, this watch doesn't allow the phone to ring in my ears when I receive a phone call. This watch interferes with that transmission. Granted, the watch will vibrate and that lets me know I have an incoming call. But it will NOT ring if this watch is paired to my iPhone. Bothersome, yes, but not a deal-breaker. Maybe Umidigi will see this review and take tips on it for later improvements?? (Hint, hint)

Again, this next reason may be trivial to some, but for my OCD-ness, it drives me crazy. Whenever I receive a notification and it shows up on my phone, the screen splits up the words making it difficult to read. I will include a photo to show you what I am referring to. I wish it wouldn't split up the words. Again, not a deal-breaker but definitely a bit annoying.

This next "issue" may be big deal to some: You can NOT see the display outside. No matter which angle you hold your watch or how bright you have your screen set, you won't be able to see it outside, unless you find a dark spot somewhere. I'm hoping Umidigi will come out with a watch that allows you to see the screen outside.

Finally, last but not least, this watch does not have a speaker on it. You can't speak into it nor does it speak to you. But really, for the price, do you expect that?

I hope this review doesn't deter you from buying this watch. It's a REALLY nice watch. I know, I've tested several watches out and this wins, hands down.

Coming from the original Pebble, the Ticwatch Pro 4G is the first android wear Smartwatch I have owned. I purchased the 4G variant as it also has more RAM and more resistance ratings (IP/MIL). I do not use the cellular connection, so I cannot comment on battery life and performance with that. With just wifi and Bluetooth, along with the Mixed-mode display (shows LCD when 'off' and OLED when I gesture to look at it), I can probably get up to 3 days of battery life as I usually end the first day with 75% or higher. Performance is good but it is not as fluid as the Apple Watch. The LCD is really useful as it means I can always see the time. As a student, it is also useful to have Essential Mode as I can still have a watch during tests that won't get me in trouble.

The Mobvoi app is lacking as it doesn't serve a great purpose. It would be far better if you could change the settings of the watch and manage apps from the app. It does showcase various health stats, so there is some use. I use Facer to find watch faces and I am glad to see that there are many watch faces to choose from. As for health, I usually use Google Fit over the included Tichealth but they are both equally good.

The build of the device is excellent. The watch has a premium metal feel and is made with Gorilla Glass 3, another difference from the wifi only Ticwatch Pro. My only complaint is the band that is shipped with the watch. It seems a little to easy to stretch and seems like it wouldn't need to be pulled too hard for it the snap. I have had similar watches with bands of similar elasticity and they have all snapped within a few months of use. I may look into replacing the band in the future. The charging dock and watch are both magnetic, which makes charging a breeze.

Overall, I am very happy with my purchase and enjoy the watch very much. I had my previous watch (Original Pebble) since 2015, and I can only hope that this watch can last just as long or even longer.

Review:
Nice looking basic smart watch for everyday use. It has some nice additions which can be useful and except some frustrating things, if you do not mind lack of GPS, it has a lot of things to offer for the price tag ~$30 (with discount).

Design: 5/5 It seems very similar to Apple Watch or Amazfit. Looks nice and feels good, screen has vivid colors. Strap feels also comfortable and no complains regarding this.

Sensors: 3/5 I tried to compare it with different devices. HR is usually within "acceptable" range, however, you get some strange spikes and even while you enable "continuous" it just record every few mins and you have to have HR widget on screen to show you the actual (or start the activity). SpO2, in general, every watch nowadays is not perfect in these two things. But several times I got 100%, while other device gives me average 96%. Maybe if you play more with that you will get more accurate results. Still, it is not a medical device so it's ok. But for the price tag more as 4/5 here.

Functionality: 4/5
You get touchscreen, HR, SpO2, Breathing/Stress de-load Widget, Weather Widget, Music controls, Customizable watch face, recording of the several different activities (but you need phone with screen ON for external GPS and activity on), alarm, stopwatch, and some others.
App. is also quite nice and easy to use (I would say even easier than watch itself).

Cons: The biggest downsize for me is a lack of GPS which is causing that when you record activity using your phone you have to have screen ON! During running or biking it is always an issue as often touch can cause stop the activity. It happened to me during both run and bike and it is extra frustrating. It could basically work just as strava - you can close the screen and it is running in the background on the phone. Second thing is the heart rate widget/monitoring. You enable continuous, but you get once in a 7-10 mins metrics recording at best. To see actual you have to have activity on or open the widget and wait - here I often reported that watch was unable to show it, so I have to open widget again.

Pros: However, honestly, for the price tag you cannot expect to get everything or to work at its best. So I would say it is worthy for the price as it looks really nice, you have a lot of additional functions and App. is quite good, and you can customize your watch face as you like.

Overall: 4/5

Review:
I tried out the Samsung Galaxy Gear smartwatch but after a few days returned it and decided to try the Sony SmartWatch 2. This review is a bit of a comparison of the two watches. I hands down prefer the SmartWatch 2 over the Galaxy Gear for several reasons.

1) The strength of this watch is that it isn't trying to be everything. Because of that, the price is now 1/2 of what the Galaxy Gear cost and that makes this watch a very good value.

2) Don't sweat the lack of camera or speaker phone that the galaxy gear has. The camera was gimicky on the Galaxy Gear and unnecessary. The speakerphone while useful at times in the Galaxy gear, is not something I miss at all now that I've switched to the SmartWatch 2.

3) I think the Sony SmartWatch 2 looks better than the Gear. It has a subtlely handsome look and an understated quality feel and appearance to it. You can wear this watch with almost anything and it would not clash or draw attention to.

4) I got a few compliments from women and men about my watch the first day I wore it to work. No one has any clue it's a smartwatch at first and just think it looks cool. The Galaxy Gear I thought was more eye catching in a way I didn't like or want.

5) The display on the SmartWatch 2 is always showing the time. I love it! The GG has the display off until you bring up your wrist up in front of you to look at the time, then it would delay for an awkward second, before the screen turns on and you can see the time. The SmartWatch 2 is easy to tell the time at any time.

6) I work in a hospital and must do constant hand washing. The SmartWatch 2 is waterproof, while the Galaxy Gear is not. I was very afraid to splash water on the GG and it drove me nuts as I don't have time while working to have to worry about drying my watch all the time or trying to protect it from splashes.

7) The screen on the SmartWatch looks just fine. It's not as sharp as the GG screen, but it doesn't matter. You can easily read many rows of tiny text on the screen when receiving longer messages. Yes you can see pixels up but so what. It's still perfectly decent display for the use case.

8. The SmartWatch UI acts just like Android device. There are back, home and menu keys. There is a swipe down gesture that brings down notifications.

9. The black rubber watch band is very comfortable in all day use. I couldn't say that about the Galaxy Gear at all. The Galaxy Gear irritated my wrist throughout a days. Part of the metal clasp of the Gear watch band would rub against my wrist and caused me irritation. Also you can replace the SmartWatch band with any watchband.

10. My suggestion is to NOT load a lot of useless apps for use on the Watch. I only install the free "WatchIt!" notification app, along with the gmail and text apps. The WatchIt app will allow you to send any notification that appears on the top of your mobile phone to the watch as well. I started off by blacklisting all apps so they DON'T show notifications. Then I go through and approve only the ones I want. Be conservative in what apps you allow to buzz you on your watch. It will get annoying quickly if you allow dumb stuff to bother you and buzz your wrist all day.

11. You'll want the stock text message app as it allows you to view and reply to text messages using preformatted replies. You can create your own pre-formatted replies. I deleted all of the stock pre-formatted replies and created my own. When you get a text alert on the watch, you press the menu button, and then the text message icon button to reply. Then you can swype left or right to cycle between your preset replies. It works pretty well and doesn't try and shove more functionality that just won't work on a smartphone.

12. The watch does what it's supposed to do. I can view the time at all times, and it lets me get notifications to my wrist so I don't have to pull out my phone at work (which we have a strict no cell phone policy at work). I don't miss any important calls or text or emails anymore. I know when I have to step outside and deal with a call or text and when it can just wait.

The Ticwatch Pro is my second smart watch. I have owned the LG Urbane for over 3 years, and I loved it. I've been getting random blinking on that watch and I felt it was time for an upgrade. I searched and researched thoroughly.

After reading articles, viewing watches from friends and at stores, and determining what I needed, I settled on the Samsung S3 Frontier. I sent that watch back after trying out the Samsung software and it's limited apps.
I kept searching and decided on this watch, the TicWatch Pro. While waiting for delivery, I was concerned that this watch would not be worth it. Had smart watch technology not advanced much in 3 years?

A few days later the package arrived. I liked the look of it, except for the watch band and the thickness of the watch. Since then I've come to love the thickness, it's the perfect weight and comfort. I purchased a black leather band as well. I've played with it for the last 2 weeks, and I loved it more and more each day. There's not a better Android Smart Watch out there, especially for the price. Installing a bunch of free watch faces for WatchMaker and Facer has been addicting because good watch faces are so crisp and clear and colorful. It's shocking.

Other things I've done with the watch is downloaded 3 of my favorite music albums directly onto the watch and installed a bunch of apps from the Google Play Store. If I know I'm going to be playing with the watch all day at work, I bring along the charger. If I don't play around with it much, the battery lasts a day and a half. I have not tested the battery life while in Essential mode the whole time, but I image it would be maybe 4 days. I don't understand how anyone would claim a longer battery life than that for this watch, but that is fine.

Review:
I was seeking an affordable smart watch that would allow me to make & receive calls from my wrist. Sure you can use a blue-tooth ear piece but that doesn't look quite as cool walking down the street. This smart watch allows you to pull off a Dick Tracy or an Inspector Gadget hat trick. It's just outright cool to answer a call like you're on guard duty. Just don't go doing that in a tough neighborhood or you may find yourself in a bad situation. ( I don't think the warranty will cover that scenario, I'll have to ask. lol )

In any case, the smart watch is not perfect. It has flaws but I didn't buy this to take my blood pressure, count my steps, receive water intake notifications or to play birdy games. I only got it to make and receive calls without being forced to pull out my phone just to handle my communication needs in public.

For you to be able to add contacts to the watch via the "DaFit" app, you must format the phone numbers within your phone contact list with dashes and not parenthesis. Don't forget to grant the app permission to access your contact list. Enable "Contact sharing" by clicking into your "K22_XXXX" bluetooth connection to see your options. You can then select your 8 favorite contacts via the app and save changes to have the contacts show up on your watch. Works fine with my Motorola G Play 2021 phone running Android 11.

Example

This works. >>> 1-235-345-77XX

This doesn't work. >>> 1(235)345-77XX

The "Da Fit" app offers various options but the one I like most is the ability to change watch faces. There are numerous watch faces to select from ( 25+ ) but the issue with the current app is that you can only download 1 watch face to store offline. Don't know why the developer didn't simply design the app to allow us to download all the watch faces we want offline to enable us to switch between them at will.

At this time we need to use the app in order to acquire a new watch face that replaces the previous one, it kind of defeats the purpose. On the bright side we can use a custom watch face from downloaded images or photos we take with our phone cam so that kind of mitigates the issue with customization but it's still quite limited. You can't create a bunch of custom watch faces and switch between them, it's one at a time or the default options.

The calls are clear and I have no trouble listening, speaking and understanding everything being said. The person on the other end can hear me fine too! I was surprised on how good this feature is. I'm not going to comment about all the other options because to be honest, I don't care for those & didn't really explore too deeply. I'll let someone else share their experience and thoughts about it. However, if you just want a cool smart watch to make & receive calls I highly recommend it. Just keep your expectations in check when it comes to a sub $ 100.00 smart watch. Not all the features may be suitable for your needs.

I must of looked at over 30 different smart watches before selecting this one. I didn't want to spend over $ 60.00 and this was the best I could find based on aesthetics, battery life and overall features. I sacrificed things like enhanced water proof ratings, always on screen light and enhanced GPS features found on more expensive models.

By the way, this watch charges up fast! I don't think battery life will ever be a problem but only time will tell. Already have friends and family hinting towards wanting one. : )

FYI

- You must pair your smart phone ( IOS or Android ) via bluetooth to both "K22" and "K22_XXXX"

- The "K22" bluetooth connection allows the camera shutter and the audio player to function.

- The "K22_XXXX" bluetooth connection allows you to make and receive phone calls via the smart watch.

- The "Da Fit" app is required to download a new watch face, set location for weather and to change Celsius to Fahrenheit if that's your preference. The app also contains the data collected from the smart watch for your review when setup properly.

*** It may take a few tries to detect both bluetooth connections. Toggle bluetooth on and off on your phone if you have trouble detecting it. Sometimes you just have to reset the watch itself via it's menu options.

Before heading out, disconnect and reconnect your bluetooth to make sure it's properly connected. Don't just assume it's working because the watch and the phone may unpair itself sometimes. Simply pair them again and check your phone pairing on the watch to make sure you see the dial option available.

Review:
I am an Apple user. From phones, to tablets, to laptops, desktops, and yes, the Apple Watch. Admittedly, I have been jealous of the fact that other smart watches have had a classic round watch face design as compared to Apple's odd futuristic rectangle. Now that these classic watches claim to work with Apple iOS, I decided to take the plunge and give the Samsung Gear Sport a spin and see how it compared to Apple on my wrist. Here's what I found.

The build quality of the Samsung is amazing. Totally solid, shiny gunmetal grey in color, with a hefty (but not heavy) feel to it. Even when spinning the bezel (a much better way to navigate your phone than Apple's side mounted wheel, by the way) it feels totally high quality. The included rubber strap is ok, though guys with bigger wrists will want to order a longer (20mm) band. All standard watchbands work with the Samsung, another huge plus over the Apple Watch. Overall, it feels like a solid analog watch on your wrist and that is a huge selling point for me. The display is absolutely stunning, bright, and displays vibrant colors. The number of customizable watch faces available is simply amazing and there are some that truly look like an analog watch. You can download tons more quickly and easily too. I really like the look and feel of the round screen. The overall look and feel of this watch is impressive. You use the round bezel to turn and navigate through settings and apps, but the screen is also a touch screen. It is very sensitive and responsive to the touch, but I found using the bezel is a much easier way to navigate most of the watch features and rarely use the actual touchscreen input. Just like the Apple Watch, this watch wakes as you raise it to your wrist. This could use a little improvement on Samsung's part as I find many times the watch won't wake up on the first try and I have to give my wrist more of a spin to make it turn on. A minor inconvenience, but can be a bit annoying at times. Battery life is exceptional. I'll go three days before needing a recharge sometimes.

The software preinstalled on the watch is good and comparable to Apple's included apps. I find the activity monitor and step counter to be useful, but haven't really went into much depth with the other workout apps, admittedly. Any apps or notifications you find annoying can easily be turned off. Apps pair well with Apple devices and you get notifications with a gentle tap on the wrist. It notifies you of new email or texts, though you can't reply like you can on the Apple Watch. No big deal there, because after a few weeks of having my Apple Watch, I realized just how clunky it is to speak into your watch and went back to using my iPhone for that. I don't miss the reply feature. This may seem like a limitation to some, but I truly don't miss it. Otherwise, the pairing process and app for the iPhone were both easy to use and navigate and truly make the Samsung Gear Watch a viable option for Apple users.

Which would I pick? Overall, I like the Samsung over the Apple watch. I like the clean lines, classic look, compatibility with standard watch bands, availability of hundreds of cool watch faces, and it's bezel interface. The Apple watch has a few more bells and whistles, but for my needs - it's the Samsung I choose to wear daily and not the Apple Watch. Both are great products, but Samsung wins on design alone.

Review:
So I painstakingly compare the Apple Watch the Pebble time around, and I even bought both and more each for two days to decide.
There are many things that the Apple Watch does better, my main points where the hepatic tap as opposed to the old-school vibrate of the Pebble, responding to text messages was easier on the Apple, as was accessing music and controlling play back. Also the display on the Apple is crisper and cleaner.
All that said, the Pebble significantly lighter, and has a much smaller profile, and really looks like a regular watch. When I had on the Apple Watch I found myself itching to take it off, where as the Pebble went unnoticed when I wasn't interacting with it. Also, I find the old-school graphics, wide range of watch face choices, and quirky animations to be charming on the Pebble. Another thing that I found to be a plus on the Pebble was the fact that the step counter was simple and thus I wasn't digging through information to just get my daily step count. I understand that the Apple Watch is much more comprehensive when it comes to activity but for somebody that just wants to track their steps and not have to wear a Fitbit, this was perfect. Another huge perk for the Pebble was the battery life, one of the main things I wanted to do was use it as a sleep tracker, and though the battery life is nothing compared to the regular Pebble time, it recharges in about 15 minutes for a whole day, so I was able to charge it while I shower, and wear it for the rest of the time without worrying that overuse would make it so I would have to charge and miss steps etc. Also, the Apple Watch doesn't have a sleep tracker at all, and all of the apps that you can download to do so suggest a full charge before going to bed. Not to mention the fact that as I said before the Apple is bulky and not something that I feel like wearing overnight.
I have to admit it was difficult to return the Apple Watch, as It is beautiful and does do some things much better, but after just a few hours of wearing it I found myself wishing I had on my Pebble instead. I guess I also think there's something to the fact that we don't need to be 100% connected all of the time, and the Apple Watch is just begging to be interacted with well on my wrist, whereas I can just let the Pebble be a watch and step counter. I hope the pebble will address some of the things that the time round lacks in their next round of development, as I really think it's a great watch.

Review:
I've only had the watch for a few days. I've successfully configured it and used it for two workouts. I thought I'd share some of my observations. Before that, let me qualify my review. I paid full price for my watch and I am under no obligation to write a review. This is just an attempt to share my thoughts for others looking for opinions.

I have a Samsung S8+ and was looking for a smartwatch that would seemlessly integrate with the phone for email, messages and fitness tracking. I normally use my Polar H7 chest strap with iCardio 4 to track my workouts.

I found that the configuration was fairly straight forward. I watched a number of Youtube unboxing, configuration and review videos before purchasing my watch. Consequently, I knew what to expect and what to do when the box showed up at my house. I would highly recommend you do the same as the documentation is lacking... they know that most people won't read it.

I turned off GPS and location services. I am not a jogger/runner/walker... I do not need anything tracking my movement through the gym. I turned the heart rate monitor to monitor continuously. My display is set to "7". Going from fully charged at 6:30am to put back on the charging cradle at 11pm with 58% left on the battery. I get LOTS of emails and quite a few text messages on my phone... all of which were forwarded to my watch; including pictures sent to me by my 7yo granddaughter. So, no problem with battery life for me... 5 stars.

I didn't buy the watch for its fitness tracking only. I wanted it for the convenience of getting notifications and email without having to pull out my phone. Not only am I able to see my email and messages, I am able to respond to them as well using S-voice. Since I'm not reviewing S-voice, I won't tell you how much I wish that Bixby worked on this watch. My wife has an Apple iWatch and quite frankly, when comparing Siri with S-voice, I feel like the poor cousin. However, it meets my requirements for both email and messages... 5 stars.

I am trying to work with the text entry interface. I am trying to write my message into the screen and the interface recognizes all the U.S. letters and numbers I type. Unfortunately, I have not been able to get it to do anything except upper case letters. I'll have to research the cause of this and figure out how to make it enter upper and lower case letters. As you can imagine, IT'S RUDE TO ALWAYS TYPE IN CAPS!... So, this feature is not as intuitive as I was led to believe. So, although it recognizes all the letters and numbers, there are some complications... 3 stars.

As a fitness tracker, it utilizes a proprietary bluetooth interface and therefore, doesn't integrate with iCardio... a BIG issue for me. If I want to continue to utilize iCardio, I still need to wear my Polar H7 chest strap. Since this is not my primary use for the watch, it is an inconvenience rather than a non-starter. It integrates with S-health, which I find to be somewhat archaic in its design... not impressed with its user interface. For me personally, I will continue to utilize my chest strap for my workouts... 1 star

There has been some discussion as to the accuracy of the Gear Sport heart rate monitor. Having used both the Gear Sport/S-Healt and Polar H7/iCardo, I can give you some numbers. I did a HIIT workout:

Gear Sport: 499 Calories, 112 Avg BPM, 143 Max BPM
Polar H7: 749 Calories, 117 Avg BPM, 156 Max BPM

I have a theory about the differences and I will share it. I believe the Gear Sport measures heart rates every second. At the same time, it calculates the calorie burn and accumulates accordingly. I believe the Polar H7 measures heart rates more frequently and therefore, gets a more accurate measurement of calorie burn... as well as peak heart rates. To the average person, a one second interval between readings should be accurate enough (assuming the Polar H7 is the gold standard of heart rate monitors). I am a computer software developer myself and most people wouldn't realize that computers measure things in microseconds... that is 6 digits to the right of the decimial (.000001). As you can imagine, a lot of things happen in the real world and on a computer within a second. When averaging heart rates and calorie burn between intervals, more data points allow for more accuracy.

In any case, I don't really care about calorie counting... I am more interested in getting a workout completed in the correct heart rate zones. I consider the heart rate monitor to be important and calories burned to be of monumental inconsequence. I've measured my heart rate on three different pieces of hardware at the same time; the Polar H7, Precor Elliptical and my blood pressure cuff. All were within a couple of BPMs. Consequently, I consider the Gear Sport to be close enough to keep me in my heart rate zones and therefore, it gets 4 stars. I would give it 5 stars for this feature if it were a bit closer (less than 5 difference).

To summarize, the apps I needed (Messages, Email) work fine. The fact that I can control my Spotify is a plus. As a fitness tracker, the hardware keeps me in my zones however, the software (S-health) is truly lacking. I'm hoping that Samsung is able to get more developers working apps for their Gear products.

Suggestions to Samsung would be:
1.) Provide customized workout types on the watch. Kettlebells, Weights, HIIT, Core... etc. Seriously, who does crunches as a workout???
2.) Provide the ability to measure recovery after the workout is complete... measure and track heart rate for a two minute recovery window.

Overall: 4 stars... limited number of available apps.

Review:
The watch itself is great. Battery lasts at least 12 hours with GPS active with a good 30%+ of charge left; great for long hikes and running ultras, etc. The triathlon functions are great. The swim functions and data are really useful and interesting (automatic indoor lap counter, swim efficiency, etc) and help guide your training.

It is Garmin Connect and the process of uploading activities that I have a problem with, which must be done wirelessly and with an internet connection that is active; usually in and of itself not a big deal. It is finicky though, to put it mildly. Garmin seems to make changes internally at its Connect website frequently (it is buggy), that render the process unworkable until they fix it. You will be wasting precious time doing menial tasks like reinstalling software; removing/re-adding devices; trying different workarounds, etc.; not to mention going back to the website every so often to try again. Not the type of stuff a time-crunched person will be relishing doing. It has gotten so bad recently (last 2 weeks) that I am prompted and motivated enough to waste precious time today to post this review. You can get most of the critical data off the watch's screens without uploading, but can't get all the data, or the charts or maps.

It is also easy to forget (when traveling) or misplace/lose the little ANT agent USB stick (and very expensive to replace). A simple upload process via the separate USB charging cable would have been convenient (like the older Garmins). There is nothing more convenient about having to use yet another piece of equipment to wirelessly upload data, when you have to connect the watch by USB cable everyday you use it ANYWAY to charge the darn thing. Garmin seems to be intent primarily in building their social universe via Garmin Connect (essentially Garmin's Borg), at the expense of their user's time and convenience. Even if you don't care about the privacy issues (I don't care at all), the problem is that you have to deal with the finicky and unreliable Garmin Connect website's uploading server.

I will be hard-pressed to buy another Garmin product ever again. i have bought/owned (gifts) many Garmin products with varying degrees of satisfaction from very low (e.g., 405 watch) to extremely high (e.g., 510 bike GPS). I no longer trust that this company has its act together enough to provide the utility and convenience I would expect for their premium prices.

Review:
Ok, here we go.

I bought this product because I wanted a Smart Watch, leaning toward the side of an Activity Tracker. To clarify: I wanted more Activity tracking features than smart watch features. This eliminates the Moto 360 and Apple Watch.

I bought the version with the chest band, because as I said before, I wanted the activity tracking abilities and the Chest Band Heart Rate sensor is the best way to get this data accurately. There are a lot of flaws with the optical sensor (again, Apple Watch), so this method is much more reliable. Do the research, you'll find it pretty easily.

I love that there is a GPS in this watch. It's so cool the turn that on and go for a walk around the woods. It tracks all the data and sends it over to your phone and computer for easy read-outs. Same goes for running. I have yet gone for an outside run with this guy yet, but when I run on the treadmill, it tracks the data with the heart rate monitor really well. It shows all this data POST-workout and lets me break it down. I bought this one because I wanted this data, and it delivers.

You can customize the watch faces with some that are built in the "store". There are some nice ones, and a lot of ugly ones. Total preference. I like a clean look when I'm not working out. Simple - time and date.

The vibration notifications are a great feature. It's how the Alarm works and how it alerts you to important notifications from your watch (mile markers, etc). You can also have it reflect EVERY notification from your phone, which is good and bad. First off, it's good because I don't have to get my massive iPhone 6+ out of my pocket to see (and clear) notifications. It's main drawback is now you have to be very particular about which notifications you receive - because they are going to all show up on your wrist. Recently I subscribed to NHL GameCenter Live and now I get game scores from my fav. team on my wrist. Heck yes! You can also pick up or decline calls from your phone. It's a simple feature that allows you to decline a call from your pocket or pick it up (if it's been ringing) from your pocket - so when you take your phone out, you are already on the call. I use this feature more then I thought I would and when I figured out that accepting the call via watch was useful, I use it all the time. Also be advised that if you let your notifications build up - they will ALL be on the watch until you clear them. It really forces you to be more intentional about your notification phone features.

The pedometer is a great added feature. You set your daily goal and I am obsessive enough to try and get as close as I can to it every day. It's a fun challenge and, to be honest, I use the restrooms in a different building now so I get a few more steps in drive the number up.

The Move Bar is going to drive you nuts. It is a suggestion for when you've been sitting too long - and it's a helpful reminder to walk around. But it doesn't clear very fast - so you need to walk about 1000 paces just to get it to clear. That's all well and good - except if you work a desk job or drive a lot. Last week I was on a trip in my car and every 20 minutes my watch insisted that I was sitting too long - which was true, but there was nothing I could do about it. Aren't you a SmartWatch? Aren't you connected to my phone? Couldn't you detect when I was traveling at 70mph and realize that maybe I was in a car and moving around for 1000 paces was not an option? Maybe future gens of this watch will be a bit more smart.

Also, this thing..... it disconnects the bluetooth sometimes, and then won't reconnect without a restart. I restart her about once every other day. This is truly the bummer about this watch. I restart her way too much. Way too much, Garmin. Once she powers back on, she's ready for anything. One star off of this review for this problem.

The battery: Good Stuff. This thing lasts a long time and in full operating mode (GPS, Heart Sensor, etc) it can go for 10 HOURS. That beats the Apple Watch any day of the week (which doesn't have a GPS). Without the GPS and Heart Sensor, I've for 5 days of heavy Notification use. Love the battery. Charging it is also amazing. I have the magnetic holder attached to my desk at work. I come in (about) once a week and rest it on there for a few hours. Back to 100% and I'm good for another 5-7 days. Oh yeah, and you don't have to have a phone to own this watch. It can work independently (so SUCK IT, Apple Watch) - although the SmartWatch features are great when paired to a smart phone.

Be warned: I did take this thing home on a weekend (friday night) at 30% and thought "Aw man, I'm good til Monday morning." Saturday afternoon, she was completely dead. Had to come back to work on the weekend and get the charger. Once you get down to the bottom of the battery, she dies FAST.

The screen is surprising on this one. By the photos you think it's going to be "meh" but actually, in the sun, car, shade, night, living room, restaurant she holds up and I can always read the screen - and one touch of the button lights up the display - bright! I am kind of happy about it. I don't need an Apple Watch screen on my wrist with this thing. It's just a better use of the tiny battery in a Smartwatch.

The interface is a bit clunky. I find that I have to swipe once to "wake" the watch up to touch, and then the second swipe works. Not a deal breaker - not a star taker, just.... meh. There is no clicking or vibration with button presses, so it feels a bit... empty.

Speaking of feel - this thing is LIGHT. I really like that about it. It takes no energy to wear this watch - even with it's larger size. It's super light and feels like a floor model when you first pick it up - but it's on purpose because you don't want added weight when working out and exercising.

About that size: fits me perfectly as a 6 ft., 170 lb male, but for a smaller female, it might feel bulky. Just throwing it out there - you get to decide in the end.

About that exercising comment: I really like the run/treadmill/walk/cycling feature. It's just cool to have a GPS on board and get all that data in conjunction with the heart rate monitor. The heart monitor feature can also work with several other 3rd party monitors, so if you already have one, see if you can pair it with the watch. Might save you some cash.

The thing the activity module lacks is a dedicated activity for Cardio or Weight Lifting. There is no non-pace option until you run the exercise and then manually change it online. This is a needed feature that needs to be added quickly. Gym goers would benefit from owning this watch, but it needs to natively show and display this data for these activities before it makes sense for them to purchase this watch. Calorie burn, timer, time, rep time. Seriously Garmin, this needs to happen. I would give you a star on this review if it did this.

Overall, I really love this watch. Yesterday I forgot it at home and when I got to work, I checked my wrist (what must have been) 1000 times for my steps and the time. I felt naked. No joke. It's become a part of my life and I really enjoy it. If you're looking for an Activity Tracker with SmartWatch features, get this one - and don't go cheap - get the Heart Rate Monitor. You'll be happy you did.

**UPDATE - 7/25/16 - FYI - The little rubber clasp is pretty cheap on the watch band. This past weekend, it broke. I have had to order an entire new band to replace it. Extra ten bucks - and the watch band apparently lasts for a year and a half. Not a deal breaker - still really love this watch.

All the promise of a Garmin product but it falls terribly short when you put it to the test. I love Garmin products and had been waiting to purchase a D2 for several years but wasn't putting up with Garmin's higher price points. This one hit the right value range to me so I decided to purchase it.

My reasons for buying this watch were to have emergency and backup nav capability, a backup altimeter, and the wrist pulse ox capability. All of it seemed fine on the ground, but when I flew the watch for the first time, the shortcomings became apparent.

The pulse ox had a hard time performing and required me to be very still to get a reading. Even while hand-flying a light aircraft in smooth air, it was having a hard time apparently from the natural vibration of the engine and airframe (note the pic from the Garmin reference materials). This defeats the purpose of it being an aviation watch. It also gave me readings of such variation that I did not trust it.

It had a hard time locking on satellites in the plane. I understand it needs a good view of the sky, but again its an aviation watch which, by default, means it will be in the cockpit. If its only supposed to be an open cockpit watch, then Garmin needs to state that. Once it did lock on, navigation worked fine when I had the time to enter my waypoint, etc - however the menus are very cumbersome if you are in an emergency scenario which was another premise of my purchase.

The altimeter was excellent - no complaints on that. It bluetoothed to my phone and adjusted for local barometric pressure perfectly and very close to the aircraft instrumentation. This they got right.

Additional issues are as follows, but I would have lived if had better results with all three areas noted above:
- Software is cumbersome - too easy to exit the app while flying inadvertently; cant get back to widgets while in flying app
- Too many different apps needed to setup and use the watch
- Watch casing and strap are very cheap feeling - plastic - Pulsar and Timex do better for less than $50
- Lack of integration outside Garmin Pilot and the Garmin world. I was a Garmin Pilot believer and happy with it, but USAF has gone with ForeFlight and all my W&B info is preloaded in it, so I have let Garmin Pilot go. I know Garmin wants to link its products, but you guys need to try and compete in other ways as this will not be sustainable for you. I think your profitability would increase if products could be chosen more freely such as the watches. To be clear - this is not the reason I am returning it. I would have lived with this, but you guys can do better.

If Garmin is reading this, let me help you develop this watch and test it in real world conditions. I want a watch that works too and happy to pay for it, but let's get it right please. No reason to keep fumbling this.

Review:
After many positive experiences with Tozo's various fantastic earbuds and charging pads, I saw they produced a smartwatch that seems to check a lot of the basic boxes for a smartwatch that was within swinging distance of what my old Pebble Smartwatches offered, but for a vastly smaller price than the original Pebbles were ever sold for. I figured giving the S1 a shot would be worth it while going in with the basic reservations of what to expect from a Smartwatch that is cheaper than $50.

After some time with the watch, I can say it still does offer some great value for the price, but it does have a few shortcomings that may or may not matter at this price point and possibly some could be remedied with software updates.

First the Good.

The device looks and feels rather well made. The body of the watch is a mixture of metal and glass and feels solid and really well made. The watch band is a nice soft touch rubber that feels and fits well on the wrist. The screen is capable of being very bright and easy to read and has good view angles. It's not a high res screen so don't expect a lot to fit on the screen in sharp detail, but comparing to a pebble, its perfectly usable for a smartwatch.

The Interface while simplistic and lacking any animations, is actually quite fast and responsive. Button clicks and screen swipes and taps are all really quickly responded too and makes using the watch a breeze. There are a collection of watch faces to choose from as well with some decent analog and digital faces that range from detailed digital to pretty relaxed analog and a range in between.

The vibration of the watch for notification and alerts/alarms is solid and works well. It's not adjustable in strength but it seems adequate without running overly long or harsh for a smartwatch. I didn't miss any notification that came through when wearing this watch due to not feeling the buzz, just be sure you turn on DnD mode in a time range in the app or else expect any notification that comes to the phone over night to wake you up with a buzz in the middle of the night.

The App that pairs with the watch from my Android Phone is reasonably laid out and while a little bare, doesn't ask too much for personal information except for what it needs for workout/sleep tracking. The one thing that may seem odd but is pretty standard for smartwatches to provide notifications, is that the app ask for nearly all the permissions possible to function and will always seem a bit odd. But considering what the watch needs them for, it does make sense. Even when it ask about Camera access, you can actually use the watch as a remote camera shutter button because why not right? Other things like Location data help the app to look up weather info, and there are a few you have to allow for notifications to be sent when the phone screen is off and to keep the app from being put into sleep mode from the battery management, etc.

I haven't had any chance to really try out the workout tracking features of the smartwatch but the step counting seemed to be relatively on par with my other watches and tracked them accurately as long as you wore the watch morning till night.

The one fitness feature I did really like and worked really well was the heart rate tracker. It takes readings at a set time you can set in the app (from once every 10 minutes to 60 minutes) and you can track it in real time by going to the heart tracking app in the watch itself. It seemed to be really accurate and can give you heart rate readings throughout the day in a little chart in the app to show you how your rate seems to change throughout the day. I assume it tracks a little more real time when using the workout apps, but for normal daily tracking it still is useful when you are just going about your day. I had no issues with it on my wrist taking a reading or feeling like it was way off on the high or low end.

The battery life of this watch is fantastic. Once fully charged and even with the lift to wake option turned on, the watch will last you about as long as a pebble (about a week) and with the lift to wake turned off, it can probably go much longer. Things like screen brightness turned down and maybe taking heart rate checks at longer intervals might extended it to be even longer. But overall any watch that can best 3+ days on a charge is pretty good in my opinion.

Now for the not so good.

Unfortunately being the budget smartwatch that it is, and a first shot for Tozo, that does take it a little bit outside of the wheelhouse of earbuds and wireless charging, there are a few bits that keep me from wanting to use the watch as my daily driver to replace my aging but still fantastic Pebble Time Steel.

I think for one is probably similar to many other reviews here, why is the watch stuck in Military time with no ability to switch it to 12H AM/PM? There is even a watch face with AM/PM on it but it still reads out in Military time. An odd oversite for a "Watch" at all and if there is a way to swap it, I couldn't find it after spending a good chunk of time searching for a way. The analog watchfaces are an alternative way to get around that, but this is something that could and should be fixed in an app/fw update for sure.

While the UI is responsive, it is a little bit, odd in the choice for things like the pulldown menu which allows you to see if the watch is connected, go to settings, or adjust the brightness, but being unable to change things like DnD mode or see anything about an e-mails contents/header is a bit of an odd limitation. Text messages are shown properly but do seem to disappear quickly and going back to read them is technically quicker and easier with your phone then using the watch itself.

Lastly, the sleep tracking seems to be about as good as my Pebbles is, however I have had it on occasion just completely not track sleep whatsoever and well, not knowing how exactly it knows when you are sleeping vs not (same question I have for the Pebble) but the Pebble has pretty much never missed a sleep session in the years I have had it. When it does work though it seems pull up roughly similar and accurate numbers to my Pebble so it does work, when it works. It may have just been a fluke though so I will continue to test to see if it was just a bad night sleep that made it think I was still working instead of sleeping, ha!

Wrap Up.

Overall while it does have a few points against it, the overall experience with this little smartwatch has been a positive one. For the price you get a watch that does nail all the basics rather well, and if they can add a 12/24hr option, this watch would make the perfect starter watch, or gift for someone who wants to give a wearable a try, without breaking the bank. It looks good, offers most all the basic features you want with a smart wearable without being too complex or difficult to use. Is it a replacement for a true WearOS, Apple Watch, or even a Pebble? Not quite, but it does come rather close and considering those can easily be $100+ more than this watch, that is saying something for sure.

Good on Tozo for branching out into other devices. I continue to look forward to other neat innovations they put out, maybe even an upgraded and improved S2 watch...

Review:
First, I'd like to discuss the pro's to this watch.
- Price is outstanding for what you get
- The watch band is very comfortable, and the watch face and body aren't too large or obstructive to get caught up in a long sleeved top.
- Perfect for someone who doesn't like wearing a watch, but wants to get more health data (me)
- Great entry level smart watch, which displays the key features one would like in a smart watch
- Keeps time, and is great for controlling music without having to fish your phone from a pocket or bag. The audio controls controlled Spotify on my phone, which I thought was awesome.

Next, the cons -
- Proprietary charging magnetic method, and once attached you need to be pretty sure it doesn't move
- Battery life is unpredictable, if you're looking for a device that can hold a charge for many days, this is not that
- The functionality is close, but leaves a lot to be desired. For example, I was never able to get my text messages to show up. I was able to get incoming phone calls to show, but trying to use the watch as a speakerphone was not a great experience. Often times one of the 2 bluetooth connections would re-enable without my intervention, this happened overnight and I didn't hear my regular alarm go off.
- I'm not convinced the health sensors are accurate. I was checking my blood pressure regularly, and it was fine. At the doctor's office I was reading completely different on their blood pressure cuff, and I even tried some tests while waiting there, and the results were way different.
- I'm also not sure if the sleep sensors are accurate. I know I get poor sleep, but this told me that I average 8 to 26 minutes of restful sleep a night, with the remaining time classified as light sleep.
- While in the shower, I noticed that the screen's touch sensitivity was sensitive enough to be triggered by water, and every time I looked the watch was kind of going crazy, or moving through menus on its own.
- It doesn't interface with the clock app on my phone for alarms, instead it has 6 pre-defined timers (like a 1 minute timer, and a 5 minute timer). I found that to be a little bit of a challenge, and ended up using my phone instead.

Other thoughts
I picked this up because I don't like wearing watches, but wanted fitness data as I've been working towards some health goals, and it's nice to have additional metrics. This does integrate with the Apple Health app, and provides useful data directly to the app with little configuration.
Although this is not a garmin or apple watch, for the price it's definitely a good smart watch for the cost. If you know that going in, I think you'll be satisfied with this product.

Review:
I've been a Garmin fan for years; never spent much time with TomTom before Amazon sent me this one via the Vine program. After getting used to the menus and taking it on a 8 hour trip this is my impression of this GPS device:

Things I liked about it:
Big screen, easy to read. Touch screen is very sensitive, though; easy to bump the wrong thing till you get used to it.
Search for attractions includes phone numbers. When I got close to the restaurant I was looking for, I called and made my carry out order.
Emergency numbers and hospital, police, & fire info handy; first aid instructions.
Many small customizable details such as sounds, etc.
Maps have lifetime upgrades, something I wish my Garmin had. Also allows user to make corrections to maps for others to access.
Speedometer and display of current speed limit. This was even accurate in construction zones, showing the temporary speed limit.

Things I didn't like:
Mounting gadget not easy to use. I gave up after a while and just propped it on the dash. On subsequent trips I got the hang of it, but it is still harder to attach to the windshield than my Garmin.
No detailed instructions. Is this online somewhere? The user guide was very basic and didn't adequately cover all my questions. Example: I couldn't find a volume control anywhere, and the user guide didn't tell me anything. I just stumbled on it by accident. (FYI, volume is controlled by running your finger along bottom of screen and touch pad appears.)
Directions are not always accurate. I used both the Tom Tom and my old Garmin Nuvi at the same time on an 800 mile round trip. When they differed on how to get somewhere, I tried to follow Tom Tom directions but kept getting lost and had to use my Garmin to find my way back on track. The restaurant that Tom Tom gave phone number for? It wanted me to go a half mile the wrong way. Garmin kept pointing the other way, so I finally called them back, and the restaurant was right where Garmin said it was.

Bottom line: fancy features, bells & whistles, but less accurate on the one thing I want a GPS for: finding where I am going.
