Review:
I purchased this watch with the intent of gifting it to my girlfriend for her birthday. I have not yet given it to her, but I know I don’t have to to know she will be impressed.

Garmin watches are top quality, and well worth the buy. I myself own a Garmin Fénix 5x, and love it. I’ve never owned a more technologically advanced, durable, long lasting watch. This Vivoactive 3 is a bit different from mine, but it still has a multitude of amazing features, that might even beat mine!

The watch is beautifully crafted, and can be worn on all occasions. Whether it be at the gym, at the beach, or even at an extravagant event. It’s design is meant to be casual, but with that little extra flare that makes people say “wow, nice watch!”.

Like I said before it has a multitude of features, that are extremely convenient, and you will end up appreciating more than you know later on. If you’re an active person, being able to track your runs, trace routes, see how many strokes it takes on a paddle board to get you 100 meters, and more, makes working out even better than before. It helps you retain your progress, and strive to to better. It promotes over all better body health. It tracks your steps, heartbeat, and more, which helps you keep note on your activity, and helps remind you to go and get out there if you’re not meeting your goals.

Also, besides all of the neat sports features, it’s extremely tech! I used to laugh at people with Apple watches because they constantly checked their wrists for texts, but now that I own a smart watch, I completely understand! (Btw I’m not comparing these to apple watches, because Garmin blows them out of the water, but well get to that in the next paragraph.) it’s extremely continent to be able to have your phone somewhere else, and be able to quickly check texts or answer calls. Not only that, but have you ever been in the middle of a good workout, and a song you don’t like comes on, and you have to get up to change the song on your phone? Well you can do that from your watch without moving. Like I said, you’ll appreciate this watch way more than you know.

Now, when it comes to competing brands, garmin in for the Win. If you have an IPhone, no need to fear, Garmin is 100% compatible. Not to hate on Apple watches, but don’t buy an apple watch just because you have an iPhone, and for a few reasons. First being that Apple doesn’t have the extensive list of features garmin does. Secondly, apple watches die after 3 days, and take almost a whole night to charge. I can wear my garmin for a week and some change, then charge it in an hour and a half. It’s insane. And finally, apple watches just don’t have that extra pop that Garmins do. The square body shape doesn’t compare to the look a garmin gives off. Garmin watches are almost like ford raptors. Yeah it’s a truck and you can work in it and get it dirty, but at the end of the day it’s a $100k truck that’s built for racing.

All in all, I think Garmin Watches are top notch, and there’s nothing else like them. It’s well worth the buy, and you won’t regret it.

Review:
This will be a Christmas gift to my Mom.

I will give my impressions of the watch.

Quality. The build quality of this watch is good.

I like the styling and I'm sure my mom will love it.

It comes with a USB-A charging cable that attaches to the back of the watch for charging. No adapter needed.

It comes with two watch bands. One metal band for dressing it up and a rubber watch band. That way she can switch it up when she wants.

This watch uses the FitCloud Pro app.

I have other watches in this company's line up that use the FitCloud Pro app so I can speak about the ease of use.

Using the FitCloud Pro app you can set up the watch to track whatever health data you wish to track. Things such as steps, heart rate, sleep tracking, checking bp, exercises such as cycling, running, climbing etc...

I am only using the Fit Cloud Pro app for sleep tracking but I have tried the heart rate and bp. The tracking for those I believe are fairly accurate but I cannot say for sure since I have no way to test for accuracy. It's not something that I would totally rely on. So on the occasions I do check my bp for an example, it's only to get an idea of where I am until I can have it measured with medical grade equipment.

The sleep tracking I can say is accurate for me. The app shows how many hours of light sleep and how many hours of deep sleep. I find this information very useful since my sleep is all over the place.

Being that this is a smart watch, you can use it for calls and messages and music control.

Once you download and set up your account with the FitCloud Pro app, it's easy to bind the watch in the app using bluetooth. From there you can go through the settings to get the watch set up to use the features you are interested in.

So this is a good smart watch and offers very good value. My wish is that the app would allow more than one watch to be added.

I will update this review after my mom gives me her feedback on using the watch.

I recommend this smart watch.

I hope this helps.

Review: I was debating between the vivofit 2 and a Fitbit Flex -I read a ton of reviews on both which gave me pretty good ins and outs of what the trackers do, pros and cons of each, and which will best fit my needs. I love the Garmin vivofit 2 tracker!!  As a first time tracker, the vivofit 2 fits the bill perfectly! It cost a little less than the Fitbit, IS waterproof (can wear in shower, pool, ocean), tracks your sleep, counts steps, calories burned, has a light, comes with 2 size wristbands, a USB port and is a watch too. I also like that you don't have to charge it every night; the battery life says it will last for a year and once the battery dies, you go buy a normal watch battery and have a jeweler install it like any other watch. I couldn't get the Garmin Connect app on my iPhone (thanks to updating on my software - its a hand-me-down phone), so I put it on my tablet at home - it was so easy to set up the account, not to mention using the app, plus I don't want to obsess at work about what my stats look like. You have to sync the information yourself manually (it does not do that automatically, but it doesn't take long!) but if you forget to do it daily, it saves your information from previous days until you sync the next time. I don't mind having to sync my vivofit manually, but the fact that you can look back at previous days information is great. Now, I don't know how 100% accurately the vivofit 2 tracks everything (steps, sleep, calories) but I've been really impressed with the whole concept of it. Looking at the sleep pattern charts in the app has been cool - it shows how many hours you're in deep sleep, light sleep and awake, and the chart has different colors for each category of sleep. Again, I'm not sure how accurate it is, because when you set up your account, you put in what time you go to bed and what time you wake up on average and it will base your tracking on that. As for the step counting, the vivofit 2 will set your daily goal based on your average for the week, so your step goal is never the same. Now, I don't care if its not 100% accurate (what tracker is?) - I feel like I'm getting my needs fulfilled with my purchase more than I expected. I highly recommend as a first time tracker for someone who doesn't want one that's crazy high tech, and easy to use AND its affordable.

Review:
After way too much research, I ended up buying Garmin 265WT for my wife and Magellan 1470 for me to use. After using them both for several months, I found wanting hybrid of Garmin and Magellan. The thoughs...

Likes & Dislikes on Garmin compared to 1470:
(1)Power cable routing is much better.
(2)Speaker quality is much better (maybe because Magellan is thinner?).
(3)Screen is much easier to see during day light.
(4)Choices and sound of women's voice (Magellan sounds like a robot).
(5)Re-route/calculation speed is faster.
(6)In night use, both map screen AND menu screen get darker.
(7)Menu is easier to use at beginning, but lacks choices compared to Magellan's. My wife and I enjoy and trying out different food (Indian, Japanese, African, etc.). Magellan offers many options, but Garmin is very limited.
(8)POI is outdated-It does not even show Costco in Toledo, OH!
(9)Maybe my phone? Bluetooth function works fair, but not really useale while driving.
(10)Adjusting volume takes many pushes... Magellan is quick & easy.
(11)Getting back to map screen (after searching POI) is pain in the rear end.
(12)FM Traffic is pretty good, but re-routing is some what questionable.
(13)Advertizements you get & see on Garmin is less annoying(you get this in exchange for "free" traffic). Maybe I notice more and annoyed on Magellan because its screen is bigger?

Likes & Disikes on Magellan:
(1)Big screen for the price.
(2)Menu screen is much for thoroughout with variety of options. I really like short-cut icons that you can create. I have "Jimmy John" and other favorite places I tend to visit during my road warrior work days.
(3)Thin & sleek design
(4)Finding restaurant, hotel, etc. at specific city/area is much more easier than Garmin.
(5)Lane guidance is nice, but gets too much at busy intersections
(6)Crashes (freezes) after about 5-hrs of straight operation. Magellan's new software update (just downloaded) is supposed to correct this. I'll find out next week.
(7)The woman's voice is robotic
(8)Speaker is weak
(8)Only map screen goes dark in night time. Menu screen stays bright! What the heck?

In conclusion, neither Garmin nor Magellan is perfect.
I want Magellan's useful menu options, but want Garmin's auto dimming screen, speaker and guide women's voice :o)

This smartwatch appears to be of good quality. It has smooth a silicone band that can be removed for cleaning and comes with a magnetic charger that's specific to this watch. The watch charges quickly, but how quickly it drains depends on how much it's used.

The app was easy to download and the features are easy to set. My daughter's watch isn't set up for phone calls or texts because I don't want her to be distracted by it during school. It has other features she likes using, though. They don't seem to be incredibly accurate but she enjoys seeing her sleep patterns, step count, and the weather. For a child, this would be suitable, but I don't see this being accurate enough for an adult who's really trying to track numbers.

Her favorite feature of the watch is that she can customize the face to whatever image she wants. There are preset options but uploading your own is a lot more fun. She's been enjoying changing it as she desires and it makes her feel really cool that she can truly make it her own.

I'm happy with it for her (an 11-year-old) but I wouldn't be thrilled with it for myself.

Review:
My never ending search for the perfect Smartwatch / Fitness tracking hybrid continues. So far I have tried in order..LG G Watch R, Samsung Gear 2, Asus Zenwatch, Fitbit Surge, Sony Smartwatch 3, Sony Smartband Talk, Striiv Fusion and now the Samsung Gear Fit.
First the good. The screen is so nice. Brilliant color, clear and crisp. All notifications work, including Google Hangouts, Emails, etc. Only issue is that is a pain at times to delete them all. It takes a few taps. Android Wear does it much better and easier. Battery life is ok for me, 2 -3 days. The price at $119 has come way down and now it is a very good value. The heart rate monitor when tested seemed fairly accurate.
The bad: This is a fitness band that can’t track daily calories burned. You can only track calories while exercising or walking. You burn a lot of calories sleeping or even breathing, but Gear Fit does not track them. So you can’t really tell how many calories you can eat to balance it against daily calorie burn. Also, natively they Gear Fit does not track gym workouts. Only Walking, Running, Cycling and Hiking. But they do have an integration with Endomondo which does a decent job of tracking my Crossfit workouts for calories burned. But Endomondo does not integrate with S Health where the calories burned through walking, running, etc or stored. So you really have to use 2 apps to tracking your active calories. And like I said you still will be missing your other non-active calories burned. Sleep tracking is manual and does not give you much info at all. Just when you are motionless or not. There also is no Smart Alarm to wake you when you are in a light sleep. You can use the cell phone alarm and the Gear Fit will pick it up though.
Overall: This will probably be returned too. Comfort is great. Notifications are great. Android Wear is better for notifications as you can respond to Google Hangouts texts via voice or auto text response on the watch. With the Gear Fit you can only use the canned response for true SMS texts. I use Hangouts so this doesn’t help me. The screen is the best of any fitness band or smartwatch I have tried. But the poor set up of fitness and sleep tracking to me is a show stopper on a Fitness band. Based on all the Smartwatches/Fitness Bands I have tried here is my current ranking from best to worst for my needs.
8. Sony Smartband Talk – Good for calorie tracking. Sleep tracking in automatic. The talking aspect on the band itself is nice. But notifications would not work consistently on it. They would come initially and then stop. No idea why. Sony Support did not know either. Also, the e-Ink display is impossible to read in low light and the text is very small.
7. Striiv – Ranked higher than the Sony Smart Talk Band because it is half the price. Notifications are ok, but the fitness tracking aspect is lousy.
6. Samsung Gear 2 – way too big to work out with. Tizen is cumbersome and not as easy to navigate as Android Wear. Camera and speaker on the phone for call is nice. Also, can’t respond to google hangouts texts with Tizen
5. FItbit Surge – Notifications are limited to SMS and Call Alerts. No email, no calendar, no google hangouts, etc. It is even cumbersome to navigate to them when you do get SMS texts. It is good for tracking gym workouts and heart rate. Auto Sleep tracking is nice, but the data doesn’t give you much info. Black and white screen is not as nice as other color ones or as clear as the e-Ink on the Smart talk Band. Great battery life. Never did use the GPS. Continuous heart rate monitor is nice, but it really underestimates it during the workouts.
4. Asus Zenwatch – Looks nice, but too nice to work out with seriously. Also, don’t like the awkward way it measures hear rate. See Sony Smartwatch 3 below for Android Wear Review.
3. LG G Watch R – Better battery life and heart rate monitor than the Asus Zenwatch. Cheap band. Also, too big and bulky to workout with.
2. Samsung Gear Fit – Beautiful screen! Very good on notifications. But the fitness tracking aspect is lousy. Can’t track daily calories in total. Link with Endomondo saves the device for being down to #5 on the list.
1. Sony Smartwatch 3 – true Android Wear Smartwatch. Can respond to Google Hangout texts via voice or canned text response in Android Wear. Best battery life on an Android Wear watch. Able to store music on the phone and with GPS you really can run without your phone. It is more of sportswatch, so good to workout with. Sony Lifelog is good for tracking daily calories. But you still need several less than efficient apps to track gym work outs. It would be good if Lifelog was better. Sleep tracking does not work in Lifelog with the Smartwatch 3. At first Sony told me it did and said I needed to update the firmware. When doing this it broke the watch and it would not reboot. Had to return it and get a new one. Then Sony told me that Life Log does not actually track sleep with the Smartwatch 3. The new one I ordred did not vibrate for some reason and returned it too. Decided to hold off on ordering a 3rd one. And now the price has come down..so this is definitely the Android Wear watch to get if you are going to go with that platform.
I would like to try the MS Band or maybe the Basis Peak, but neither are available now.

Review:
My Fitbit Flex recently stopped holding a charge (no more than 48 hours max.) after 2 years. After a less than stellar run in with Fitbit Customer Service, I decided to look outside the Fitbit brand. I have had a Samsung Galaxy for 3 years and love my Samsung phone. After researching several different options, the Gear Fit looked like a may be a good fit into my Samsung lineup. I have now been using it the Samsung Gear Fit Smart Watch for 3 weeks (alongside my dying but still accurate Fitbit) and can say that I truely like it. I was able to pair it with my Samsung Galaxy S7 by downloading the Gear Fit Manager App through Samsung. That app allows me to control what notifications get pushed to the gear fit (phone calls, alarms, text messages, calendar appointments, facebook messenger, google hangout, etc) via bluetooth. S Health, also a Samsung App, links to the Gear Fit via bluetooth to track steps, active minutes and heart rate (when taken - this is not a constant read out). The watch gives a little buzz at 50% and 100% of each goal you are tracking. I try for 60 active minutes and 10,000 steps a day, so I get buzzes at 30 min, 60 min, 5000 steps and 10,000 steps. I am happy to say that the step counter on the Samsung is usually within 300 steps of my Fitbit, usually less. I believe it tracks lower because it only begins counting after 10+ steps, so short walks room to room in your home may not always register. Similar to the Flex, the Gear Fit does not register flights of stairs.

I love being able to know when I am getting a call, without my phone being on me. I have a 30-45 minute commute to work in the morning and back home in the evening. I love that when I forget to turn my phone on ring, I know I have an incoming call or message, by a buzz on my wrist. The same is true when I am sitting in meetings or on conference calls, I can still receive alerts and know if something requires my attention. Getting notified of my phone calls is great since we don't have a landline in our home. I have set the screen to rotate to portrait, making it easier to read messages. No more missing calls because I'm in a different room or outside.

Compared to its competitors at the $100 price range, this is a great buy. This watch does everything that my Fitbit did and then some. There is now a Gear Fit 2 at a higher price point with a few more capabilities but the same app and software compatibility.

Have been using the watch for a week now, found that the Chicago Garmin store had a few in stock (they always sell out when they get them, so call ahead).

Have owned the 305, 310, and now the 910. I used the 310 for triathlons, actually found the 310 was pretty good with the latest update for mapping a swim. That said, the 910 rocks! Here's what I've found useful so far with it:

* Size is not just significantly smaller than the 305 and 310, it really has some measure of style as well. Also, it just feels like a solid watch and I think the black looks excellent.

* The watch band is much easier to use than the 310. There are a larger number of slots to use to fasten the band, so it feels like it fits better to me. They also provide a watchband extension if you need to wear it over some sort of bulky garment.

* Can't tell on battery life yet, but over the week of regular workouts as well as leaving it on overnight only depleted 23% of the battery.

* For swimming, the watch is amazing! It counts laps/intervals/strokes/distance per stroke/SWOLF score/efficiency (normalized value to make various types of swim workouts comparable)/stroke type with what for me has been complete accuracy. I had the Finis Swimsense watch and ended up returning it due to fogging and hard to read screen. The Garmin screen is easy to read, either out of or in the water. For swimming, it has both a lap pool and open water setting.

* It as a barometric altimeter built-in, so does elevation correction as well.

* A number of other software enhancements are nice: Virtual racer/training effect/run-walk setting.

* I use a Garmin Footpod and Speed/Cadence sensor as well.

* Immediately paired up with the Ant receiver I already had plugged into my computer, simple to set that up.

I'm quite pleased with the watch and so far it looks like they've done a very good job with the initial version of software. I was impressed by the software updates they did with the 310, so be interested to see what they do with the 910.

Excellent watch, highly recommended.

Tom

Review:
What does your device "watch"? If it is just the time then there are millions of choices, but for this purpose, I do enjoy the dual-screen on the TicWatch. I like quickly glancing at the time and peeking at my step count without having to turn on the bright screen. It is an added bonus to know that if the battery does run low, it will kick into essentials mode and I won't lose my steps.

For "watching" my phone, it is Google Wear 2.x so I knew how that worked already. I had a Asus Zenwatch2 (which I also highly recommend). Notifications are largely a matter of the user tuning things up. Speaking of that, a few tunings of a SmartWatch settings are also part of ownership, as you balance out your preferences for features vs battery life. This is not difficult, it just takes some thought and a day or two to fit the watch to your needs.

I rate how a smartwatch does "phone watching" by how much it decreases the number of times I have to pull my phone out of my pocket. Most certainly, the Ticwatch Pro has a positive metric there. Please don't underestimate that. You start noticing just how many times other people fidget with theirs, get fed up and leave their phone out on their desk or just don't bother to put it in their pocket anymore meaning they are always carrying something. Multiply this effort/energy savings by a hundred times a day and it adds to the quality of your life. I hate saying that, but it is really true if you pay attention. Plus, your phone battery will last longer, by a very noticeable percentage.

For "watching" indoor or outdoor fitness there are smartwatches dedicated to that purpose that would be better than the TicWatch Pro because they specialize in that use case. But for me, step count and activity time are the only two metrics I pay daily attention to. You can use the included software or software made for Google Wear that does much more, and I have started to use the other sensors mostly for curiosity. But I knew before buying the TicWatch Pro how I planned to use the watch most. That is key to my satisfaction with the product. As a fitness watch, I give it a satisfactory "exceeded my low expectations" score.

Beyond those areas, Google Assistant is great for asking quick questions or launching apps, quick phone calls or even map directions when walking and you don't want to carry your phone or walk the streets with headphones. It is easy to glance at my watch for directions while driving, hands on the wheel with my phone still safely in my pocket.

For battery life, I will never drop below 50% on an average day. So using advance features like directions are always available if I need them or I can just use my phone as I would have without the watch. I never use Wifi, I borrow internet access as needed through my phone. There is a remote camera app that even streams video from the phone to my watch proving the bandwidth is amazing for the low power cost of Bluetooth.

The bottom line for battery life is that I have not had to worry about it Charger accessories are inexpensive, so I have one at work and home if needed but so far I simply don't think about it much. I use the watch however I want to. BTW, the charger does have a satisfying magnetic "snap" to it, so there is no guessing it if locked in or not. I also follow the advice from the seller, and I use a low power charger, equivalent to a computer USB port. I don't know what the charge time is because it's ready before I wake up from sleeping.

Negatives: Ther is some lag, but a faster CPU means less battery life. It seems that when newer CPUs come out, their efficiencies are made up for with brighter or bigger screens. It may be a zero-sum, depending on your preferences. We can always hope for improvements, but at this point in time, the tradeoffs are more than acceptable. The lag on this watch doesn't affect me in any important way. Google assistant might be slow, but that is not the watches fault. I am asking a cloud server through a path that takes 14 different technologies to give me a "Dad Joke".

Looks are subjective, and I would wear this with a suit simply because I don't care nor care who knows that I don't care. If I split hairs looking for a problem I would get rid of the numbers on the dial, or maybe a person would just have a nice analog watch for the "unplugged" evenings and there is certainly nothing wrong with that.

I hope these ideas were helpful.

Review:
Physically, the watch is a dead ringer for an Apple Watch, specifically one of the later models where the watch’s height is about 120% of the watch’s width. It may be that this watch’s best use case is when it is used to convince someone you have an Apple Watch when you really don't. At the surface, the displays are very similar to Apple’s. Once you drill into a menu, on even one level, it becomes very clear this is not Apple’s software nor is it all that easy to interpret and use.

As I removed the watch from the box, I noticed that we were off to an interesting start: the watch had recorded 19K steps before I ever put it on. I thought little of it, after all, it probably bounced around in the back of the mail truck. Two hours later, I became a little more concerned when I noticed that my step count was up to a total of 69K steps that day, despite no exercise and never leaving the house. Whoops.

The included charger is USB-A only. If you use USB-C, you’re out of luck. The charger fits the back of the watch only one way (don’t worry, the magnets will tell you when you’re wrong) but there’s really no way to keep the charger/watch pair up and out of the way when it’s charging. The magnets aren’t all that strong so one bump is frequently enough to disconnect the charger.

The manufacturer’s instructions aren’t that well written. Don’t get me wrong, their English is better than my Chinese, but it may have been worthwhile to have a native English speaker edit the instructions. Though the app is far from intuitive, pairing the watch with my iPhone was pretty easy. When you’re setting it up, make sure you know your metric measurements (i.e., height in cm, your weight in kg, and your stride length in cm.) There is no option for English measurements, at least not one that I've found.

Claims and Realities: The listing claims that “There are 150+ different watch face styles to choose in the App.” I found exactly five watch face styles from which to choose. The list says the watch’s style is 经典的. I had no idea what that meant so I ran it through Google Translate. It means “classic.” OK, if you say so.

It is, at minimum, water resistant. I wore it in the shower with no problems. What was interesting was that every time water from the shower hit the face, it turned on the screen. So it can’t tell the difference between water and a finger.

It’s default is to turn the screen on when you make a sharp movement with your arm - as if you were pulling your arm towards you to look at your watch. OK, that makes sense. The watch also claims to be able to track your sleep and it does a sort of OK job at that. So why can’t it take that information and figure out that, when I’m asleep, I don’t want it to turn on the screen every time I rollover in bed? That screen is brighter than the sun. It probably woke my next door neighbors. If there’s a way to change that, I haven’t found it. Now I’m wondering how much longer I will be permitted to wear it in bed, the only place where it could possibly generate sleep data.

I haven’t seen it share any data with Apple Health even though I have that selected. The app gets a little pushy if you don’t select track me all the time. I get it - it wants to be able to gather your distance information all the time - but I just don’t want to be tracked all the time, particularly when I have no idea what they do with the data.

I compared its heart rate measurements to those I got from a Polar H10 Heart Rate Monitor connected to an iPhone. The results were comparable even though they use different technologies and at both normal and exercise heart rates. I’m always suspicious of the Blood Oxygen Monitor (SpO2) measurements on devices like this; SpO2 isn’t like heart rate where it varies from person to person and from time to time and activity throughout the day. If you just programmed the device to always read 98% or 99%, you’d be right 95%+ of the time. I’d love to know how this reads with someone with sub-normal SpO2. I just don’t know anyone for whom that's true. I saw someone asked about getting blood pressure readings. This watch cannot do that, nor can any other watches I’ve seen. Generating a blood pressure reading requires measuring the pressure required to physically collapse an artery. Unless this watch can contract and expand at will and measure that pressure, it’s not going to be able to do that.

As I scan Amazon, it appears there are many different “brands” of the same exact watch. This one is HuaWise but the Zuoee, Motast, Pautios, Ordtop, and others all look exactly the same, both hardware and software. OK, the Ordtop and Motast have a button instead of a dial. But it’s not like the dial on the HuaWise actually spins - it’s just a dial-looking button.

So, in the end, it's a cheap Apple Watch clone that will fool everyone except the owner.

UPDATE: Two new additional Gripes.
1. While the watch's step count seems correct, the watch's step counter drives my iPhone step counter insane, adding as many as 370,000 steps within a single hour. This started as soon as I connected the watch and phone via Bluetooth. As soon as I had my iPhone "forget" the watch, behavior ceased. Connected again, it resumes; forgot again, it stops.
2. The watch prevents me from using my iPhone to start my car. I can unlock the car and remotely control the car's AC, windows, etc. just fine but if I want to drive the car, I have to pull the key card out of my wallet and put it on the center console.
These two gripes were too much for me. I've "retired" the watch.

UPDATE 11/14/2020: Over 10 months of owning this watch. It is generally great. The biggest gripe I have is the touchy charging. Half of the time when I put it on the charge (original charger I got with the watch), it doesn't even register that it's on a charger. Far less frequently, it starts charging but stops later and I return to find a dead watch. I also wish the watch had some kind of warning notification when the battery is low, because once it switches to LCD-only mode, I struggle to get it to turn back on or to charge.

When the battery isn't an issue, though, the watch is great. I contemplated "upgrading" to the new TicWatch, but there's no LTE version yet. I'll likely wait another generation to see what happens with Wear OS.

UPDATE 1/10/2020: I've had the watch now for almost two weeks now. I've gotten quite used to it. I usually wait until it's below 20% or so to charge it, and it takes about 1.5 hours to charge. I typically do this while I'm working so I don't mess up my step count. I really don't understand why people complain about battery life. I don't have to charge the watch any more often than I expect (I get about 1.5 days of HEAVY use out of it). This includes daily walks tracked using Google Fit, lots of music controls, and lots of notifications and messaging.

Here are my other observations so far:

-WEAR OS - still not was good as iOS, it's getting better. There aren't a lot of apps, but the ones that do exist work well (Maps, Messages, Fit, Keep, etc.) all work well. Just don't expect many non-Google apps. Tasker does have an extension for Wear OS, but I haven't explored it yet - that could offer a ton of additional possibilities.

-GOOGLE ASSISTANT - this is the game-changer here. Anything you can do with Assistant, you can now do on your watch! I can control my smart home devices, including Sonos, SmartThings, Harmony, August, etc. Like Tasker, the possibilities are endless. Related to this, the voice recognition on the watch is AMAZING. The best I've seen, ever. When I respond to text messages using voice, it has a 99.9% success rate, including punctuation!

-TIC SLEEP - I didn't realize that this is a separate app you need to install on the watch. Once I did, it works great. No issues detecting sleep or wake up. There are two areas for future improvement: (1) Google Fit integration (Mobvoi confirmed to me in an email that they're working on this); and (2) the smart/gentle alarm function (it just doesn't work as they describe; in the same email, Mobvoi said they will look into this).

-CUSTOMIZING - don't be afraid to search Google Play if there's something about the watch you don't like. I had two instances of this: (1) the screen timeout was too fast for me, so I downloaded an app (StayLit Wear) that keeps the screen on until I lower my wrist; and (2) I wanted to track my watch battery while it charges, so I found another app (Wear Battery Full) that does that (it also sends a notification when it's full, so you can get it back on your wrist). Neither of these are Mobvoi issues; they're deficiencies with Wear OS - but easily solved.

ORIG REVIEW: Great watch. I'm a prior Samsung Gear Watch user. Wear OS is great, if only because of Google Fit and Google Assistant. Fit is awesomely simple. And Assistant can do it all. So much better than Bixby. Essential mode is cool too. I use that 99.9% of the time with wrist rotation off. Couldn't be happier with a smart watch. The Apple Watch is superior, sure. But for Android users this is pretty darn good!

Review:
This review is for the Vivoactive 3 Music but most of what I post here applies to the Vivoctive 3 Non-Music except for, obviously - anything having to do with the music or WiFi. You can control music on your phone using the Vivactive 3 Non-Music but you can not store music on it.

If you’re not in the habit of sending your activities to Garmin via the app, or WiFi or via computer – the memory capacity is seven times activities and fourteen days of activity tracking. According to Garmin this is the same for both watches even though the 3 Music has more memory.

The Vivoactive 3 Music has a real barometric altimeter (versus the GPS one that many older watches have) as well as a magnetic compass and the standard accelerometers that are needed for daily activity tracking. It also has a thermometer but this isn't very useful, being so close to the warmth of the arm.

The wrist heart rate monitoring is Garmin’s new Elevate™ system and is Garmin’s version of LED’s and sensors and software for monitoring 24 hour heart rate activity tracking. For specific exercise activity-logging these same HR sensors sample at a much higher rate than the lower and variable sample rate of twenty-four hour monitoring (if you have the automatic option turned on for daily HR monitoring).

This does an excellent job at twenty-four hour monitoring, as well as use during many activities. But if you are doing plyometrics, Martial Arts or Mixed Martial Arts, or possibly running, or anything where your arms is very active; then you may want to consider a chest contact heart rate band or arm band heart rate sensor – any of which will connect to your watch of course. Once you pair them and start an activity the watch automatically picks up the previously paired device and uses it instead of the onboard HR sensors. I recommend something like the Scosche RHYTHM+ HR armband - https://amzn.to/2HY6fni, the newer Scosche Rhythm 24 HR armband - https://amzn.to/2SxuEEh, the Garmin Heart Rate Chest Strap or other heart rate straps. For regular road biking and even a regular run the onboard HR sensors work fine, maybe not so much for mountain biking and an intense road biking session and other very active exercises.

Of note here – there IS NO sound whatsoever on these watches, the only notifications are visual and vibration.

Many of the smart features of the watch like smart notifications are done via Bluetooth. You can even respond in some simple ways to texts and reject calls, etc and there are customization options for your responses. These work well and the vibration alerts of the watches is good at notifying you without bugging others around you. In addition to texts, notifications can come from Facebook, Garmin, and other things via your phone.

The Vivoactive3 Music has Garmin Pay but I have never used this so I can’t speak to how well it works or on anything having to do with setting it up, though I would imagine it’s similar to any of the other digital integrated payment methods.

BTW, charging is quite fast – with the computer as well as with a wall charger. Battery life is adequate but could be better.

Garmin says up to five hundred songs can be stored on the 3 Music (the non-Music of course does not store any music) - I haven't tested the exact number, and you are able to fairly quickly swipe over while in an exercise and control your music. It works fine but really there should have been a way to embed/add a music data field to eliminate the single extra step.

You can see what is currently playing, skip forward to the next song or back, and shuffle, repeat, adjust volume, use playlists, sort by artists; podcasts; audiobooks; genres; songs; albums, and access music apps like Deezer and others (no Pandora yet).

You can also pair more than one audio device so if you use earbuds and speakers too, or different headphones for various things/activities then you’re covered. For earbuds here’s a nice Bluetooth set that work well for me, though not the absolute greatest on bass.

Moving on to Widgets – these are little apps that can be accessed by scrolling the screen up and down to find what you are looking for. There are a number of already-installed including a step counter with full daily totals and daily charts, heart rate with charts and average heart rate time, My Day which is an overview of all of your twenty-four hour activity tracking stats, calories burned, distance traveled, intensity minutes, floors, standard calendar, clock, timer, stopwatch, weather, etc. You can also do a Find My Phone and control a Garmin Virb via widgets and apps. This covers the newer Virbs, not the original ones, BTW, like the Virb Elite (there’s also a Find my Watch in the Garmin Connect app, but it is only good to the range of your Bluetooth).

And there are a lot more you can add – both made by Garmin as well as others, via the Connect IQ store. There are hundreds of free widget apps, and some which require a small purchase or are demos/trials for paid versions. But there are tons of free ones of all sorts. Test them throuough before actually logging anything with them.

The floors climbed that the watch detects seems to be off for me, somewhat low while my wife gets what may be a somewhat higher normal than she thinks she should be getting (my wife informs me that her floors are now displaying correctly – firmware update perhaps?). This is one place that Garmin needs improvement on. My active minutes seems awfully high too, I do a lot of fitness but this seems inflated for me.

Advanced sleep monitoring is another of the features the The Vivoactive 3 series track and this seems to have vastly improved over time. There’s no installed widgets on the watch for showing any sleep display like there is for many other things, but you can find the advanced stats on Garmin Connect and through your Garmin Connect app. This is quite involved; monitoring periods of movement and restful sleep, REM sleep, etc.

The watch itself as well as the Garmin Connect app will show you an estimated VO2 Max – the measurement of the maximum amount of oxygen that a person can utilize during an exercise, which is a good measurement of your body’s ability to consume oxygen.

On the Garmin Connect app you will also find a Fitness Age calculation under the same screen where you find VO2 Max in the Garmin Connect App (under Performance Stats). This shows only under “VO2 Max” but not under Cycling VO2 Max. To get your VO2 Max for biking do some outdoor rides, for general VO2 Max do an outdoor run (or do the VO2 Max Test on the watch).

Another of the widgets that some (maybe a lot) of people may find of interest is the one that monitors your Stress Level. This also, like most of the other stat widgets, has a graph showing levels during the day. Sometimes when scrolling to it you may find that it wants to do a quick test, which last thirty seconds or a minute, and if you find yourself not able to lower your level you can do some deep breathing exercises perhaps, or consider other approaches to decreasing your stress.

This measures your Heart Rate Variability (HRV) and Garmin gets this processing of levels from First Beat, which does Garmin’s stat analytics. Having a high level isn’t necessarily bad if you have just done a high performance workout, but – for example – if you’re sitting around and doing nothing and still have a high level that may not be good…

Along the lines of steps and daily exercise there is also a move bar (option) and vibration that lets you know if you have been sedentary for too long. For those of us who sit for periods at a computer this can be a great reminder to get up and move around. Sitting is the new ‘soda pop’, ya know. This generally works well and will show you when you have cleared it too, by getting some movement and steps in. But sometimes it does work a bit flaky, in general though it is quite useful.

Goal achievements are also shown and attention is called to them by a vibration. This can be steps, stairs, intensity minutes, etc and this option can be turned off altogether or switched to toggle off automatically off when in an activity and back on afterward. You can also leave it to learn your activity level and assign auto-goals, which works fairly well.

History and My Stats are two things I use often, accessed like most things by a simple touch and scroll. History shows you exercise stats and totals and My Stats show VO2 Max and your personal records and Resting HR. There are many options and settings accessed via the touch and scroll.

You can shortcut things like turning on and off the Bluetooth, manually, syncing, and many others things in the Controls Menu – which you bring up by holding down the physical button on the side of the watch for a second or so (longer than the single press needed to bring up the activities menu). You can customize the Controls Menu in the app. More about the Controls Menu later.

Supposedly it will store seven timed activities and fourteen days of activity tracking data. On my 3 Music the numbers of activities kept onboard vary, I’m not sure how the watch decides this but it is around seven or more at any given time.

One of the great things about Garmin’s Connect IQ – which is similar to a version of the Itunes and Google Play store for downloading apps – is that many of the apps and data fields can overcome some of the limitations inherent in the watch as well as add great flexibility and customizations to the watch in general.

There is a backlight that can be turned on by swiping or when you touch the faceplate. I turned down the brightness and turned off gesture control.

To enter the mode to record your exercises, rides, runs, etc you press the physical button on the side momentarily (holding it down longer brings up the Controls Menu instead), which brings up your Apps/Fitness Activities list.

You can change how many Data Fields are displayed in each app/fitness activity, ranging from one to four in each and you can have anywhere from one to three total screens per app/fitness activity, with the HR Zone Gauge screen as an additional screen if desired.

Unlike the rest of the screens the HR Zone Gauge screen can’t be customized. The HR Zone Gauge shows what zone you are in via a gauge-like screen with your heart rate in the middle. You can edit your heart rate zones in the Garmin Connect App or online with Garmin Connect, but no other options are available for this particular screen unlike the others.

There are many built-in fitness apps like Run, Bike, Indoor Bike, Walk, Treadmill Run, Indoor Walk, Cardio, Strength Training with rep counting, Elliptical Training (your results may vary with this – many people – me included – don’t seem to have much luck with this. I just use Indoor Walk and switch it to Elliptical in Garmin Connect), Stair Stepper, Floor Climbing, Indoor Rowing, Yoga, Skiing, Snowboard, XC Skiing, Stand Up Paddleboard, Row, Indoor Row, and more.

Pool swim is another, where you can set the length of the pool (from presets as well as custom) and it calculates your pool metrics like stroke type detection and swim efficiency using the built-in accelerometer as you swim. Unfortunately there is no open water swim on this watch (only a few Garmin watches seem to have this, like the Garmin Swim or Garmin Instinct) – perhaps some variation of DC Rainmaker’s technique for tagging the Vivoactive 3 along the surface via a tethered flaoting bag or something might work with a specific marked distance?

A full-featured Golf mode is also available, I don’t golf so I can’t tell you anything whatsoever about this.

TrueUp, a fairly new feature, is included. This allows syncing of data between multiple Garmin devices – say if you switch from your watch to a bike computer. Any relevant data is synced between the devices when they are connected. A personal biking distance or speed record done on your Garmin bike computer will show up under your records on your watch, or daily activity stats recorded with your Vivoactive 3 will show up on your Fenix 5, etc.

Some of the activities also give you the option of advanced workouts like Garmin Workouts and Training Plans that can be set up in Garmin Connect. Some apps/activities give you various options, like in the Run app. For Run this includes Run/Walk if you are just starting out or doing a long run and need occasional breaks, and others. The Run fitness app also lets you calibrate treadmill distances, though it is supposed to do some self-calibration after your first outdoor run(s). Indoor Track is also a separate fitness app.

Most of the Fitness apps also have auto pause, auto lap, manual lap, lap alerts, auto scroll, and you also have the ability for touch and button lock. All pretty self-explanatory I think.

Customizable alerts are another excellent feature for some, with heart rate zone alerts, calorie, drink, eat, turn around, go home, calories, in addition to the ones you would expect like distance and speed and time, etc. Some of these can be very powerful motivators, or useful from a health standpoint and of course for training.

Any of the Data Fields can be changed to any number of built-in data points like speed, distance, Sunset, elevation, etc – there are many. In addition additional Data Fields can be downloaded from Garmin Connect IQ. And each separate fitness activity/app can have a differing number of Data Fields and various options.

In addition to adding Data Fields to existing workout apps (and in some cases replacing them with a full screen Data Field) you can also download many other apps/fitness activities as well as things like mapping, navigation, etc that do not add to or replace Data Fields but show up as a new, separate fitness app/app.

I want to mention here, one of the built-in apps is Garmin’s Navigation which is great to have handy as it can be invoked at any time – inside an existing app or separately – to navigate you to saved Waypoints or back to the beginning of your activity. This is something that I would recommend everyone try out and get used to using in case of emergency or when needed. This will not navigate you back using routing like a car GPS or Google Maps but it will point you in the right direction. And you can start it anytime to get back to your beginning point or a Waypoint. Heck, if you think you might lose your car in a large parking lot you can save it as a Waypoint…

One good fitness app to add, that is missing, is a hiking app. I recommend Hike2+ by jim_m_58 and BF Hiker Map by BeFitte.

Duplicating the built-in apps is also an option. Say you want to use the Run app for your regular running but you want to use something like the Connect IQ Race Screen app when you do a running race. So if you duplicate the RUN app you would have the original RUN app and a Run 2 app. Unfortunately there is absolutely no way to change the name of the duplicated apps, it just adds a number after it.

One of the most useful safety features that works with the Vivoactive 3 series in conjunction with the Garmin Connect app on your phone is Livetrack. With Livetrack you can share your real-time info with friends or family or acquaintances, or as Garmin mentions – your fans 😉 You start Livetrack in the Garmin Connect app and, obviously; you must be planning on doing an activity that uses the GPS. Livetrack uses the GPS on your watch and your phone’s cellular signal to allow others to see your location and keep updated, and stats. If you are trying to use Livetrack an area with bad GPS it will only show your last location(s), or may be spotty.

Manual start or AutoStart for Livetrack are options, with AutoStart all future activities will automatically start LiveTrack. Nice if you tend to forget to start it.

Also, your LiveTrack info can be shared directly to some Garmin devices that are compatible and this also ties into Strava Beacon (if you happen to have the proper Strava subscription).

A multitude of Garmin ANT+ and ANT+ compatible sensors as well as many Smart Bluetooth sensors can be connected to the Vivoactive 3/3 Music and, of course, display and process data from them. Yes, you can use nearly any kind of non-Garmin ANT+ and Bluetooth sensors with the Vivoactive 3 series.

One notable exception/caveat here; for those bicyclists out there – there is no ‘official’ bike power sensor meter display and recording – though it will connect to a power meter - https://amzn.to/2HZBuhE . Fortunately there are Apps and Data Fields created by others that allow the display of power with a power sensor that is connected, like the ANT+ Power Meter Data Field by takura87 and others. This Data Field has a way to insert the data into the .FIT file that the watch uses and uploads. Unfortunately despite the app showing power and saving neither the data the watch itself nor Garmin Connect can not use this information for calculating VO2 max and other factors. Why did Garmin not include this capability natively?

Foot pods - https://amzn.to/2t8ujtv - can be added too, and the Stryde foot pod can be accessed via one of the Data Fields from Connect IQ, like Power Meter.

The Vivoactive 3 series is compatible with Garmin’s Varia rearview radar and headlights too - https://amzn.to/2BoVEvU . Great safety devices from what I have heard.

Connecting to sensors is very easy and quick, and if you have one that has both Bluetooth and ANT+ you can select which you want it to connect through. I prefer ANT+ as I believe that it has faster data transfer (or processing) but Bluetooth is more secure.

One thing to remember here is that when you connect a sensor of any sort – if it is powered up it will be used by whatever fitness app you are using. If you have a couple of bikes with cadence sensors on them and you’ve previously connected both – you don’t want to inadvertently jiggle the bike you’re not riding as that sensor might come out of power down and be the first one the watch picks up. I would have liked to see the ability to pick the sensors that each fitness app uses, but despite this I have yet to have any problems like the scenario mentioned above.

All sensors that I have tried have been able to be set up easily and quickly and cleanly – except for an older Scosche Bluetooth Speed/Cadence sensor - https://amzn.to/2SxeJpz. This showed up as connectable device but would not connect. This is a very cheap, older Bluetooth sensor.

Otherwise everything has worked perfectly and flawlessly, and even things like the bike sensors (that go to sleep when not in use) are quickly picked up by the watch as soon as there is any bike movement. I used the excellent Scosche RHYTHM+ Armband Heart Rate Sensor - https://amzn.to/2HY6fni, Wahoo Speed and Cadence Sensors and the cheapo but just-as-good-as-more-expensive-ones CooSpo Bike Speed and Cadence Sensors - https://amzn.to/2HZ1EkV.

My wife uses the Garmin Face It app (there is a version for both Android and IOS, iPhone) and created a custom clock face on her Vivoactive 3 Music. This allows you to add your own background photo and slightly customize the clock face options.

So…my conclusion. While there are a few small features lacking that I would have liked – I very highly recommend the Garmin Vivoactive 3 or Garmin Vivoactive 3 Music for a wide range of users. From those who want to casually keep track of their all-day activities to those who want some more heavier-duty and specific fitness logging and smartwatch abilities, and anything in between. You can find a more thorough review and more photos on my blog - https://randombitsbytes.com

I got this on a lark from a meh.com deal. Turns out it is exactly what I want in a smartwatch. I also own a [[ASIN:B00NC8PMUK Motorola Moto 360 - Black Leather Smart Watch]] which is gathering dust on my nightstand. Here's what the Martian Notifier does right:

Review:
I have been very happy with TicWatch models, and the E3 is no exception. It has a great battery and is very responsive to taps and button pushes. I like that it runs Google's Wear OS, which gives a larger choice of watch faces and other apps for the watch than I would expect from a company-specific OS. When I used the always-on display (and light daily use) for a full day (for me, about 16 hours) the battery was still at about 50%. It was still at about 70% after a full day with the always-on display turned off. And it only dropped a few % when I left it for 24 hours in essential mode (with no other use).

Compared to the Pro 4G (which is an older model than the Pro 3), my previous watch, the E3 is smaller and lighter. It does not have the bezel with watch numbers that the 4G has, making it feel smoother to do gestures starting at the edge of the screen, and reducing the size. The E3 does have an "essential" mode, but this is different from the 4G's "essential" mode. The 4G has an additional LCD screen which constantly shows the time in essential mode, which the E3 does not have. Instead, in essential mode, the E3 will turn off the display (and many other functions) to save battery, but the screen will turn on when you tilt your wrist to see the time. The display that is shown is not your selected watch face, but (I assume) TicWatch's built-in face. When not in essential mode, if the always-on display is turned off, the watch will always display a face when you tilt it toward you, but if you've turned off the "Tilt to wake screen" option then the face is the built-in face, and if you have the tilt option turned on, then the face is your selected face. Tapping the face will also turn on the display with your selected face (but not in essential mode). I will say the battery on the 4G seemed better, in that with the always-on display turned on, the 4G is usually at 70% charge at the end of the day, where the E3 was around 50%, with similar usage. But the 4G is a bit bigger and heavier, so that may be the battery. It may also be due to the E3 having more sensors in use.

Review:
I purchased the unit in time for a 2000 mile motorcycle ride through Colorado, Utah and Arizona. The trip was an excellent opportunity use the Monterra as intended. My biggest mistake on this trip was leaving my Nuvi unit at home, trapping me with Monterra as my primary unit...
This is Garmin's first Android venture and it shows. Where my Nuvi feels like an integrated device. The Monterra is a collection of apps that are not glued together very well. The radio failed within a week and only would create a loud squealing sound, both the FM and Weather. I bought and loaded the North American Street App which would make the unit navigate somewhat like a Nuvi but just not as well; frequent crashes and freezes. Even in this mode the Monterra calculated straight line distance, and then when you hit go, the only way to know the true distance was to use the Nuvi option on the map display to show distance in the lower left corner. Example: from just outside Page Arizona, the unit would report distance to Grand Canyon North Rim campground as 45 miles. After hitting go, it would display the by road distance of 160 miles. If you deal with double data enough times and sooner or later it will get you. I could not reach the campsite at grand canyon for that night thinking I had plenty of time to explore Glen Canyon Dam. It was a constant hassle to not get tricked by the distance calculation, apps crashing, and general disconnected non-intuitive feel of the unit. The Monterra was a bad experience, opposite from my Nuvi 765T(automotive GPS), which I totally abused taking on multiple cross country motorcycle rides, on and off road. Easy to use and I'm amazed it still works! In contrast, the Monterra is a frustrating experience with many nuances that make you reluctant to trust it. I returned the unit.
In Summary:
+++ Display was nice
+++ mount was same as Montana unit and nice
----- Outdoor App (mapping app) crashed often or did not respond until reboot (Failure of this core app is the most important point)
----- unit would freeze, which was had to detect in bright sunlight and could cause you to miss a turn.
-- Recently found destination list always came up empty, separate app that never seemed to have the data.
---- GPS features/functions is a collection of poorly connected Android Apps.
+ wifi and camera seemed to work fine but did not really matter since nothing else worked well.
---- Primary function as a GPS was inadequate and even more disappointing given the price.
++ Accuracy of GPS unit itself was very good.
- battery life minimal
+ Once booted(long time), quick to lock on satellites.
- unit is heavy, hard to imagine a hiker wanting it.
+ topo display feature was nice
+ worked ok with BaseCamp for uploading or downloading tracks and routes
- difficulty connecting to Garmin online for updates, while Nuvi connected just fine, Monterra would come up as unrecognized device.
- paid extra for north america maps, virtually worthless with out these maps/routing capability...really, really! extra on a 799 unit? Who's marketing idea was that?

FOOTNOTE 1: I did not use the extra feature to much extent, did not want to risk crashing the unit. (Camera, WIFI, Weather Data)

FOOTNOTE 2: Garmin needs to develop the feature to allow you to pick up a Route or tracks from the nearest point to you. In both cases the GPS would try to route me to the start of a route even if I was closer to the halfway point. If that feature exists, it was well hidden.

FOOTNOTE 3: If you feel compelled to buy the Monterra, be sure use a store that will allow you to return the unit without penalty.

Bottom line: The Monterra is not ready for prime time and one has to wonder about the culture of the Garmin corporation to market an incomplete product, especially at the dollar value. Garmin is huge but the quality of their software is making them vulnerable to competition. In the case of the Monterra, it is a bunch of disconnected feature crammed into a unit with the kind of usability you would expect from 10 separate corporate high performance work teams. (Watch the online video "7 red lines", you'll get what I mean).

I want to try the Garmin 590LM next but am reluctant given $799 price tag, my Monterra experience, and what other users are writing about the 590LM product quality.

Review:
Battery is 5 stars. Some stats of battery usage with music+GPS+heart rate:
10mile run, 1 hour 40 min, 26-30% of battery
5k run, 26 min, 8-10% of battery
5k short interval (200x10) with vibration notification: 9% of battery
Comparing with Ticwatch Sports/Huawei Watch 2: a 30min 5k run with music+heart rate (always-on display) = 25% battery gone.
I am running 20 miles each week, biking to work on Tuesday to Friday (3 miles each), 1 charge lasts almost a week (slightly better than Garmin 645 music).
Based on above estimate, this watch has no problem running a 4h-5h30m full marathon with music+GPS+heart rate on, which no Apple watches nor Android watches can do.

Screen is 5 stars for outdoor, 3 stars for poorly lit condition. Unlike Apple Watch or any Android WearOS watches using OLED display, which you have to bump up the screen lightness under sunlight. Stratos is using a transflective screen like Garmin watches, the brighter the sunlight is, the clearer the image is. For indoor, the screen is good as well. The only scenario the screen's readability is sub-par is when you use the watch to track swimming during evening time.

Music experience is 2 stars. Apparently Xiaomi doesn't streamline the music experience as good as Apple Watches or Android Watches (iTunes/Google play auto playlist sync). There is even no playlist support so far. You have to name the mp3 files sequentially to play them in a certain order. The bluetooth connection is okay. I am using a Trekz Air, the signal does not drop when wearing on the right hand. I experienced occasional drop when wearing on the left hand, but still much better than Ticwatch S or Huawei Watch 2.

App experience is 3 stars. The app itself is like Garmin connect and I give 5 stars, you can customize your workout, the stat fields shown during a run/bike/swim. It has no problem on the latest Android system (8.1 on Pixel 2 XL). I am subtracting 2 stars because it asks too much permission (luckily on Android 8.1 you can customize what permission to give the app).
